Title: The key role of oxidation state and flake size in the ecotoxicological impact of industrial graphene oxide nanoflakes
Authors: Subrati, A.; Bigini, P.; De Luigi, A.; Natale, C.; Mehennaoui, K.; Houin, M.; Chary, A.; Serchi, T.; Venus, T.; Saorin, A.; Monopoli, M. P.; Zhang, X.; Zhao, K.; Alonso, B.; Estrela-Lopis, I.; Gao, C.; Zabeo, A.; Hristozov, D.; Moya, S.; Diomede, L.
Abstract: Graphene oxide (GO) is a widely used nanomaterial across various scientific and technological fields. Environmental exposure to GO and consequent ecotoxicological effects have been largely reported. Despite the significant efforts and illuminating conclusions, establishing fair pairwise correlations between material and toxicity descriptors remains challenging and controversial. Key drawbacks in GO ecotoxicological studies to date include a lack of standardized materials, poorly defined descriptors, and insufficient material variants. Here, we establish the first comprehensive framework to tackle the multidimensional ecotoxicology of GO. We perform thorough material characterization to derive descriptors that precisely define four key GO variants used in industrial scale-up, with differing flake granularity and oxidation extent. These GO variants are evaluated against toxicological endpoint descriptors across two animal models (Daphnia magna and Caenorhabditis elegans) and two plant models (rice and pepper). Our findings underscore the inherently multidimensional nature of GO toxicity by identifying key physicochemical properties associated with it. This study provides an unprecedented platform for parametrizing GO materials using material and toxicity descriptors to contribute to nanomaterial safety.

Title: Distinct changes in brain and peripheral oxygen levels induced by synthetic opioids of the nitazene family
Authors: Arce, A.; Nguyen, N.; Gomez, J. L.; Sulima, A.; Rice, K. C.; Michaelides, M.; Kiyatkin, E.
Abstract: Nitazenes are a category of synthetic opioids, some of which have high analgesic potential but also high toxicity, which has historically prevented their development as therapeutic drugs. Like fentanyl, nitazenes induce respiratory depression, a primary factor in their toxicity. Recently, a nitazene derivative called N-desethyl-fluornitrazene (DFNZ) was shown to have high analgesic properties with weak hypoxic effects. To better characterize the hypoxic effects of DFNZ relative to its parent, fluornitrazene (FNZ) and the prototypical nitazene etonitazene, we used amperometric oxygen sensors in freely moving rats to examine oxygen dynamics in the nucleus accumbens (NAc) and the subcutaneous space, using fentanyl as a comparison. All drugs induced similar patterns of subcutaneous hypoxia, with rapid dose-dependent oxygen decreases. In the NAc, all opioids, except DFNZ, at low iv doses (1-5 g/kg) induced moderate but significant brain oxygen increases. At higher doses (>10 g/kg), oxygen levels for all opioids, except DFNZ, showed a biphasic response; robust hypoxia followed by a weaker rebound-like hyperoxia. Etonitazene at 30 g/kg had the largest and most prolonged brain hypoxia compared to the other drugs, without the rebound-like hyperoxia. These findings indicate that etonitazene and FNZ mimic the effects of fentanyl, inducing dose-dependent brain and peripheral hypoxia. In contrast, DFNZ induces very weak hypoxia seen minimally at very high iv doses (300-1000 g/kg). Our findings substantiate the low hypoxic potency of DFNZ and indicate that not all nitazenes are characterized by high potential for toxicity. As such, the development of nitazenes as analgesics should not be categorically dismissed.

Title: The activation-deactivation cycle of human PIEZO1
Authors: Massa, J.; Frieg, B.; Tyrchan, C.; Koch, O.
Abstract: PIEZO1 is a cation channel that is primarily activated through mechanical force, and activation has been shown to be influenced by membrane curvature. PIEZO1 is ubiquitously expressed and plays critical roles in various patho-/physiological processes such as inflammatory diseases or red blood cell volume regulation. Here we combine coarse-grained and atomistic simulations in which human PIEZO1 is embedded in a curved membrane and subjected to simulations under controlled membrane tension and a physiological transmembrane potential, allowing the gating cycle to be reconstructed at atomic resolution. Systematic pressure adaptation identifies an activation regime in which the channel flattens progressively, and ion permeation quantitatively reproduces the experimental conductance of 36 pS. Furthermore, the R2456-E2117 salt bridge couples pore lipid retention to the anchor domain and disrupting it reproduces the phenotypes of the disease-associated R2456H and R2456C variants. PIEZO activation is transmitted through an interconnected network of contact rearrangements that ultimately reshapes the yoda1 binding pocket at the THU8/THU9 interface. This state-dependent remodelling rationalises the pharmacology of yoda1 and offers a framework for the structure-based design of PIEZO1 modulators.

Title: Chimeric antigen receptor T cell therapy targeting CD94 for cytotoxic T/NK cell malignancies
Authors: Le, C. C.; Weng, J.; Liu, J.; Aletti, F. M.; Cherng, X.; Tang, Y.; Patchva, S.; Richard, M.; Balakumaran, M.; Piubelli, M. M.; Solis Soto, L. M.; Lu, W.; Lin, C.-Y.; Chu, F.; Cao, J.; Rehman, A.; Singh, K.; Agbedia, O.; Gouni, S.; Chohan, K.; Darbaniyan, F.; Kolsuz, S.; Balakrishnan, K.; Saini, N.; Green, M. R.; Flowers, C. R.; Iyer, S.; Vega, F.; Neelapu, S. S.
Abstract: Chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T cell therapy against pan-B-cell antigens is highly effective, but analogous approaches for T-cell lymphomas risk prolonged T-cell aplasia. We developed a CAR-T therapy targeting a post-thymic antigen, CD94, a receptor with restricted expression in normal tissues and immune cells but enriched in cytotoxic T/NK-cell malignancies. Second generation CD94 CAR T cells generated using a specific and high-affinity anti-CD94 monoclonal antibody showed potent and selective cytotoxicity against CD94-positive tumor cells in vitro and completely eradicated NK-cell leukemia xenografts and patient-derived xenograft models of hepatosplenic T-cell lymphoma and NK/T-cell lymphoma in vivo. Incorporation of truncated B-cell maturation antigen (BCMA) as a safety switch enabled rapid elimination of CAR T cells using anti-BCMA T-cell engagers or anti-BCMA antibody-drug conjugate. Super-resolution microscopy demonstrated intracellular sequestration of CD94 by the CAR, preventing fratricide. Collectively, these findings support anti-CD94 CAR-T therapy as a promising and novel treatment for cytotoxic T/NK-cell neoplasms.

Title: Computational identification and in vitro evaluation of astragaloside II as an inhibitor of dengue virus NS1-induced endothelial hyperpermeability
Authors: Jantrachotechatchawan, C.; Chawnawa, W.; Leephatarakit, N.; Maneepitasut, W.; Maneerattanasak, S.; Manoret, P.; Poyseungnoen, K.; Boonarkart, C.; Puttikhunt, C.; Avirutnan, P.; Noisakran, S.; Auewarakul, P.; Duangrattanalert, K.
Abstract: Background Dengue is a mosquito-borne viral disease in which severe cases are marked by leakage of plasma from blood vessels. The secreted nonstructural protein 1 (NS1) of dengue virus damages the endothelial barrier and is a drug target, but no approved antiviral exists. We aimed to identify compounds that target NS1 and to test whether the selected compound, astragaloside II (ASII), counteracts NS1-induced endothelial hyperpermeability. Methodology/Principal findings We built a deep learning model that predicts compound-target binding from chemical fingerprints and protein sequences, and used it to prescreen 177 natural compounds against NS1 of the four dengue virus serotypes. The model outperformed the DeepConv-DTI baseline in recall and F1-score on a BindingDB holdout set and on two independent test sets. ASII was predicted to bind NS1 and was docked onto the NS1 dimer. In human microvascular endothelial cells (HMEC-1), NS1 reduced the relative trans-endothelial electrical resistance to 0.56 (P < 0.001), whereas ASII at 10-30 {micro}g/mL kept resistance close to control levels without detectable cytotoxicity. ASII did not reduce NS1 internalization. In a competitive enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay, ASII inhibited NS1 binding to heparan sulfate in a dose-dependent manner (half-maximal inhibitory concentration 51.12 {micro}g/mL; 95% confidence interval 47.91-56.24 {micro}g/mL), although inhibition at the protective doses was only 8-26%. Conclusions/Significance ASII is a candidate for further study as a modulator of NS1-induced endothelial hyperpermeability. Its mechanism remains unresolved and requires further study. Direct binding to NS1, activity in infected cells and effects in other endothelial models were not tested here, and the computational predictions require experimental confirmation.

Title: Long-term Epstein-Barr virus persistence in immunocompetent, primate-related Chinese tree shrews and inducible lytic reactivation in species-matched epithelial cultures
Authors: Avilala, J.; Dochi, H.; Wekselblatt, J.; Flemington, E.; Pierce, A.; Brown, C.; Dobek, G.; Ott, K.; Roussel, P.; Abdelghani, R.; Becnel, D.; Sides, M.; Morris, G. F.; Liu, H.; Feng, W.; Lin, Z.
Abstract: Experimental models combining long-term Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) infection in immunocompetent animals with species-matched cellular systems for studying viral regulation remain limited. Chinese tree shrews combine evolutionary proximity to primates with small-animal practicality and native immunocompetence, offering a complementary nonrodent model. We serially monitored blood and oral specimens from six animals inoculated with Akata EBV. Five were followed for approximately two years, including two beyond two years, and the sixth underwent tissue collection at approximately six months. Intermittent EBV DNA detection included blood positivity beyond two years in one animal. Viral RNA localized to liver, lung, and spleen at six months and to liver and spleen of another animal near two years, supporting persistent infection. All tested blood and oral specimens from six uninoculated controls were negative. In parallel, renewable lung-derived epithelial/mesothelial-like cultures maintained EBV infection in two immortalization backgrounds. Viral profiling identified Qp-associated EBNA1 transcription and latency-associated expression alongside spontaneous lytic transcription. Host transcriptomics identified 684 robust EBV-associated expression changes, with prominent enrichment of MYC and E2F target programs and metabolic pathways, together with reduced interferon- and inflammatory-response transcription across both backgrounds. These findings nominate MYC/E2F-associated host programs as candidate regulators of the balance between maintained infection and lytic activity. Zta expression and sodium butyrate induced lytic reactivation, with infectious virus production demonstrated after sodium butyrate treatment. This integrated platform complements humanized mice and nonhuman-primate models and connects long-term EBV persistence in vivo with experimentally accessible studies of host regulation and the latent-to-lytic transition in species-matched cultures.

Title: In vitro reduction of mineral oil hydrocarbons by Lacticaseibacillus casei DSM 20011
Authors: Miklavcic Visnjevec, A.; Pellegrini, M.; Conchione, C.; Barp, L.; Peressini, D.; Iacumin, L.; Moret, S.
Abstract: Mineral oil hydrocarbons (MOH) are food contaminants of increasing concern due to their widespread occurrence in food and potential health risks. Although various physicochemical and biological strategies have been investigated to reduce chemical contaminants in food, the ability of lactic acid bacteria (LAB) to remove MOH has not previously been explored. The present study aimed to evaluate the in vitro removal of MOH by Lacticaseibacillus casei DSM 20011 under incubation 0for 4 h with shaking at 100 rpm. Following the screening of different LAB strains, L. casei DSM 20011 was selected for in vitro evaluation of MOH removal using a representative mineral oil mixture, followed by the determination of MOH by on-line LC GC-FID. L. casei DSM 20011 reduced MOH concentrations by up to approximately 80% (p < 0.05), with comparable reductions observed for the MOSH and MOAH fractions and no clear evidence of preferential removal of either fraction. Cell wall adsorption has been proposed as a mechanism contributing to PAH removal by LAB. Given the structural similarity between PAH and the MOAH fraction of MOH, together with the lack of recognized hydrocarbon-degrading enzymes in LAB, adsorption to the bacterial cell wall may also explain the observed MOH removal, although this hypothesis requires experimental confirmation. These findings identify the food-derived L. casei DSM 20011 as a promising candidate for the biological reduction of MOH contamination and provide a foundation for future studies investigating the mechanisms underlying MOH removal and validating its effectiveness in complex food matrices.

Title: TRIDENT (Taxonomic Resolution and IDentification using Environmental dNa Traces): An Optimized Algorithm for Vertebrate Taxonomic Assignments in eDNA Metabarcoding, Integrating Molecular, Taxonomic, and Ecological Criteria
Authors: Haderle, R.; Jung, G.; Riou, M.; Ung, V.; Jung, J.-L.
Abstract: Environmental DNA (eDNA) metabarcoding has become a powerful approach for large-scale biodiversity assessment, yet taxonomic assignment remains one of its most critical error-prone steps. Current bioinformatic pipelines rely on molecular similarity searches against reference databases, but assignment accuracy is constrained not only by short marker length and database incompleteness, but also by fundamental limitations, including recent species radiations, incomplete lineage sorting, introgression, NUMTs, and the imperfect correspondence between genetic variation and species boundaries. Here, we present TRIDENT (Taxonomic Resolution and IDentification using Environmental dNa Traces), an automated and simple protocol designed to improve taxonomic assignments in eDNA metabarcoding. Developed for marine vertebrates, TRIDENT may be used with any barcode and integrates three complementary sources of evidence: molecular similarity (NCBI/GenBank and BOLD), curated taxonomic information (WoRMS), and ecological plausibility derived from biogeographic occurrence data (GBIF). The workflow sequentially constructs candidate taxon lists based on sequence similarity, expands them through taxonomic hierarchies, and filters them using spatial occurrence constraints. It further identifies possible taxa lacking reference barcodes and evaluates their plausibility through CO1-based similarity if data exist in BOLD. TRIDENT has been implemented as a source-available Python tool and tested using empirical eDNA datasets from marine vertebrates as well as simulated communities. Results demonstrate that the tool produces taxonomic assignments consistent with expert manual curation while substantially reducing processing time and attention errors caused by manual processing of large datasets. By combining molecular, taxonomic, and ecological criteria within a single framework, TRIDENT improves transparency and reproducibility and provides a robust and flexible solution strengthening confidence in taxonomic identifications in eDNA-based biodiversity assessments.

Title: IFT20 mediates trafficking of ciliary proteins to support mammalian motile ciliogenesis in testicular efferent ductules and respiratory tract.
Authors: Li, T.; Schmitt, A.; Pan, J.; Zheng, C.; Li, W.; Parveen, S.; Yadav, A.; Abdulghani, M.; Bennett, K.; Hess, R. A.; Pazour, G. J.; Kelly, C. V.; Huang, D.; Brody, S. L.; Toure, A.; Zhang, Z.
Abstract: Cilia are antenna-like organelles that extend from the apical cell membrane and are broadly present in eukaryotes. They are classified as primary and motile types; the later including sperm flagellum and somatic multiciliated cells present within the reproductive and respiratory systems. Intraflagellar transport (IFT) provides delivery of cargo for cilia assembly and maintenance. Of the multiple protein components, IFT20, a component of the intraflagellar transport-B (IFT-B) complex, is required for cargo delivery anterograde during primary cilia and mouse sperm flagellum formation, and is also known to link the Golgi with the primary cilia; however, its role in motile cilia from somatic cells is so far unknown. The objective of this study is to investigate, in mice, the role of IFT20 in motile cilia of somatic cells. We used a FOXJ1-Cre mouse to conditionally delete Ift20 only in motile cilia. We found that most Ift20 conditional knock out (cKO) mice were viable and none showed left-right asymmetry defects nor hydrocephalus, though they exhibited reduced body weight. Compared to control mice, adult cKO males were subfertile with significantly shortened motile cilia and decreased ciliary beating frequency (CBF) in efferent ductules (EDs). Examination of ciliary ultrastructure in EDs revealed partial absence or displacement of the peripheral doublet microtubules (DMTs), as well as defects in both the inner and outer dynein arms and the central pair apparatus. In addition, the lumen of EDs were significantly dilated and filled with aggregated sperm. Sperm aggregation also led to a dilatation of the lumen of the seminiferous tubules and testicular atrophy, accompanied by an increased number of degenerated germ cells that were sloughed into the lumen. The tracheal cilia were minimally shortened and had reduced CBF, however, they had normal appearing ultrastructure. In contrast to control mice, analysis of cKO ciliated cells, in both EDs and trachea, showed an accumulation of the central apparatus protein SPAG16, SPAG17, the outer dynein arm DNAI2, and inner dynein arm DNAH2 in the apical region of the cytoplasm. These data indicate that IFT20 is essential in sperm and somatic ciliated cells from ED and trachea, to sustain flagella/cilia formation and beat frequency and suggest that, IFT20 assists in trafficking ciliary structures from the cytoplasm to the motile axoneme.

Title: Artifact-guided restoration improves visualization of cellular ultrastructure in cryo-FIB-SEM volumes
Authors: Zhang, N.; Joubert, L.-M.; Wu, G.-H.; Su, G.-C.; Liu, P.; Mishra, M.; Li, P.; Sanz-Ros, J.; Einav, S.; Wang, B.; Cobos, I.; Xu, M.; Chen, M.
Abstract: Cryogenic focused ion beam scanning electron microscopy (cryo-FIB-SEM) enables volumetric imaging of vitrified specimens, but charging artifacts, high noise and weak membrane contrast hinder the interpretation of biological features. Here we present a two-stage deep-learning-based framework that translates cryo-FIB-SEM images toward the domain of conventional room-temperature FIB-SEM (RT-FIB-SEM), suppressing large-scale charging artifacts and enhancing local membrane signal. Held-out synthetic tests show improved agreement with constructed reference targets, while results on four experimental cryo-FIB-SEM datasets show reduced visible artifacts and clearer membrane features. Processed cryo-FIB-SEM volumes from our two-stage model can be directly analyzed by tools designed for RT-FIB-SEM, and an existing pretrained segmentation model is applied to our model output, yielding extensive predictions of membrane structures. This post-acquisition approach improves the visual interpretability and downstream analysis capabilities of cryo-FIB-SEM data without modifying imaging hardware.

Title: Pleckstrin Homology-based proximity-labeling reveal lipid-associated interactomes
Authors: Noack, L. C.; Vogel, P.; Neubergerova, M.; Pleskot, R.; Blaschek, L.; Persson, S. C.
Abstract: Phosphoinositides (PIPs) organize membrane-associated signaling, but the proteins associated with specific PIPs and their regulation remain poorly characterized. Here, we establish a lipid-binding domain-based proximity-labeling approach to map PIP-associated proteomes in vivo, and applied it to plant cells. We identify distinct protein networks associated with PI4P and PI(4,5)P2, linking these lipids to membrane signaling, transport, and organization. Using molecular dynamics simulations and in vivo validation we further reveal how two previously uncharacterized PIP effectors, ALTERED RESPONSE TO GRAVITY-LIKE1 (ARL1) and HYPERSENSITIVE RESPONSE 1 (HIR1), engage with PIPs to regulate their membrane localization and nanodomain organization. Finally, we outline how PIP-associated proteomes change in response to prominent abiotic stress conditions, including salt and heat, in Arabidopsis. Our work establishes a platform for investigating lipid-associated proteomes in vivo and reveals how PIP-specific and stress-responsive protein networks contribute to membrane organization and cellular responses.

Title: Endogenous cAMP production within tissue fibroblasts is required for spontaneous fibrosis resolution
Authors: Fortier, S. M.; Speth, J.; Walker, N. M.; Baas, J. D.; Wang, K.; Wong, V. T.; Guzman, S. D.; Liu, Y.; Pan, H.; Ren, H.; Verma, P.; Huang, S. K.; Gutor, S.; Blackwell, T. S.; Varga, J.; Aguilar, C. A.; Zemans, R. L.; Peters-Golden, M.
Abstract: Pathologic myofibroblasts (MFs) are pivotal effector cells in the development of persistent tissue fibrosis following parenchymal injury, and their activation and accumulation has been linked to a failure to phenotypically dedifferentiate and thus to resist apoptosis. The second messenger cyclic AMP (cAMP) has been shown to induce MF dedifferentiation and restore their sensitivity to apoptosis in vitro, but its endogenous role within MFs during fibrosis resolution in vivo has not been explored. To test the hypothesis that cAMP generation and signaling within fibroblasts is essential for fibrosis resolution, we leveraged the spontaneously resolving nature of the single-dose intrapulmonary and subcutaneous bleomycin models in mice with an inducible and fibroblast-specific abrogation of cAMP generation owing to deletion of the stimulatory G protein (Gs). Abolishing cAMP generation in fibroblasts after peak lung fibrosis was established led to a failure of the resolution with single-cell RNA seq demonstrating conspicuous differences in pathway enrichment and cellular cross-talk not only in fibroblasts, but also within macrophages and epithelial cells. Spontaneous resolution of skin fibrosis in a model of scleroderma similarly required cAMP production in dermal fibroblasts. We conclude that cAMP generation within fibroblasts after tissue fibrosis has been established is required for its spontaneous resolution in the lung and skin. Our findings provide new insights into factors governing the outcome of tissue fibrosis as well as a mechanistic basis that helps to explain the therapeutic efficacy and ultimate potential of newly available and emerging cAMP-elevating agents.

Title: Polarized Canine Liver Organoid Monolayers Capture Features of Western Diet-Induced Hepatic Metabolic Reprogramming Across Transcriptomic, Lipidomic, and Biogenic Amine Signatures
Authors: Giebelhaus, R. T.; Zdyrski, C.; de la Mata, A. P.; Nam, S.; Bourgois-Mochel, A.; Corbett, M. P.; Cho, H.; Ward, J. L.; Guillot, E.; Douglass, E.; Harynuk, J. J.; Mochel, J. P.
Abstract: Liver responses to Western-diet (WD) exposure remain incompletely defined, partly because conventional rodent models and immortalized hepatic cell lines incompletely recapitulate species-specific features of liver biology. Here, we established polarized epithelial monolayers from canine liver organoids derived from healthy beagles and beagles exposed to a WD for 8 weeks. We then used this platform to characterize diet-induced hepatic reprogramming and to explore differential responses to two SGLT2 inhibitors, dapagliflozin and bexagliflozin. The monolayers developed reproducible apical-basal polarity, with transepithelial electrical resistance (TEER) values of 123-335 {Omega} cm2, enabling compartment-resolved sampling. Bulk transcriptomics, lipidomics, and biogenic amine profiling each independently separated WD-derived from healthy monolayers. Periodic acid-Schiff staining provided qualitative support for this diet-associated molecular signature, showing increased carbohydrate-rich material consistent with glycogen accumulation in WD-derived monolayers. By contrast, 24-hour apical exposure to dapagliflozin or bexagliflozin at 20  M produced no detectable transcriptomic differences and only weak, context-dependent metabolomic separation, which was restricted to the apical compartment in the untargeted metabolomics dataset. These findings establish canine liver organoid-derived polarized monolayers as a tractable in vitro platform that captures WD-induced hepatic reprogramming across transcriptomic, lipidomic, and biogenic amine readouts, while providing a foundation for future targeted studies of candidate interventions for diet-associated hepatic dysfunction.

Title: COPS5 maintains spermatogenesis gene expression and piRNA-mediated transposon silencing
Authors: Huang, J.; Huang, Q.; Zheng, C.; Li, Y.; Millikin, D.; Swanson, G. M.; Yap, Y. T.; Li, W.; Chen, C.; Krawetz, S. A.; Chen, Y.; Shi, S.; Zhang, L.; Zhang, Z.
Abstract: COPS5 (CSN5/JAB1), a multifunctional subunit of the COP9 signalosome, is required for male germ cell survival, but how it acts is unclear. We combined a germ cell specific Cops5 conditional knockout (cKO) mouse model with transcriptomic, proteomic and small RNA analysis of P16 testes. Cops5 loss caused progressive spermatogenic arrest after postnatal day 16. At both the mRNA and protein levels, 59 genes were downregulated, including piRNA biogenesis factors such as PIWIL1/MIWI, PIWIL2/MILI, Tudor domain proteins, DDX4, MAEL and MOV10L1. In Cops5 cKO testes, pachytene piRNAs decreased in abundance and diversity, falling from about 56% to 18~30% of total small RNAs, while the 1U bias was retained. Consistent with this, the transposable elements LINE1 and IAP were activated. In human testes, COPS5 was high in spermatogenic cells but reduced by 56.4% in the germ cells of patients with non-obstructive azoospermia (NOA). Thus, COPS5 maintains piRNA homeostasis and transposon silencing, and its loss may contribute to human spermatogenic failure.

Title: Granger-causal inference to study crosstalk between two actin regulators in live cell imaging
Authors: Godana, A.; Isogai, T.; Bhatt, K.; Doyal, M.; Danuser, G.; Noh, J.
Abstract: Dynamic actin filament assembly at the cell membrane drives cell migration. Its regulation is governed by functionally overlapping actin regulators and complex feedback loops that hinder conventional perturbation-approaches from dissecting actin regulatory pathways. Here we present an extended, perturbation-free statistical framework based on Granger causality (GC). The framework rests on statistical models that capture the interdependence among subcellular fluctuations of molecular and cell morphodynamic activities extracted from three-channel live-cell imaging. Applied to the inference of cause-effect relationships among actin, its regulators and cell-edge movement, the GC analysis identifies distinct regulatory hierarchies of the actin regulators Arp2/3, VASP and mDia1 on actin dynamics and cell edge movement. Notably, we find that mDia1 plays a critical role in translating actin filament assembly into cell-edge movement, whereas Arp2/3 and VASP function primarily as regulators of polymer extension. By imaging three actin reporters simultaneously, we also demonstrate that the GC framework can distinguish the distinct causal roles of filamentous vs monomeric actin in driving cell edge movements.

Title: Re-evaluating donor-cell identity after hiPSC-RGC transplantation in mouse models of optic neuropathy
Authors: Vrathasha, V.; Nikonov, S.; Bell, B.; Dine, K. E.; Liu, Y.; Khan, R. S.; Shindler, K. S.; Ross, A. G.; Chavali, V. R. M.; O'Brien, J. M.
Abstract: Glaucoma is a neurodegenerative disease characterized by permanent visual field loss caused by the death of retinal ganglion cells (RGCs). Glaucoma is the leading cause of irreversible blindness worldwide. We investigated the potential of transplanting human induced pluripotent stem cell-derived RGCs (hiPSC-RGCs) in two mouse models of optic nerve degeneration: N-Methyl-D-Aspartate (NMDA) and optic nerve crush (ONC), and characterized their ability to survive, integrate, and form synaptic connections in a degenerated retina. Follow-up studies, including immunohistochemistry and patch-clamping experiments, one year after intravitreal injections, determined the location, identity, and function of the donor GFP+ve fluorescent cells within the mouse retinas and their similarity to native RGCs. Upon closer inspection, some GFP+ve cells detected in a few retinal sections did not stain for the human-specific marker and were detected in retinal layers outside the expected ganglion cell layer (GCL)/ inner nuclear layer (INL) regions. These findings highlight complications in the interpretation of RGC transplantation studies.

Title: From Sensor Design to Force Maps: A Systematic Evaluation of FRET-based Tension Sensors
Authors: Aytekin, S.; Vorsselmans, S.; Vankevelaer, G.; Poedts, B.; Hofkens, J.; Hendrix, J.; Rocha, S.
Abstract: Mechanical forces transmitted through focal adhesions regulate cell behavior and disease progression, yet remain difficult to quantify at the molecular level. Genetically encoded FRET-based tension probes enable measurements of piconewton-scale forces across specific proteins in living cells, but their quantitative interpretation is highly sensitive to probe design and measurement modality. Here, we systematically compared vinculin tension sensors under identical experimental conditions, evaluating unloaded reference constructs, fluorophore pairs, mechanical sensor modules, and circularly permuted variants. Unloaded controls established a common no-force baseline and validated force-dependent readout. Among the fluorophore pairs tested, the green-red combination Clover-mScarlet-I yielded a higher unloaded FRET efficiency and hence a broader measurable dynamic range. Comparison of six mechanical sensor modules identified the binary-response sensors FL and CC-S2 as the most responsive, showing the largest force-dependent FRET changes and broadest FRET distributions. At the sub-focal adhesion level, CC-S2 reported the steepest proximal-to-distal tension gradient, indicating that vinculin tension increases sharply along peripheral adhesions and exceeds 10 piconewton. Circular permutation experiments revealed that fluorophore orientation has a strong, module-dependent influence on the measured FRET readout. Together, these results establish a comparative framework for interpreting FLIM-based vinculin tension measurements and provide practical design principles for selecting and engineering molecular tension probes.

Title: A Senescence-Like State is associated with the Immunosuppressive Phenotype of Tumor-Infiltrating Regulatory T Cells
Authors: Zhang, W.
Abstract: Regulatory T (Treg) cells are essential mediators of immune suppression within the tumor microenvironment (TME) and represent a major barrier to effective anti-tumor immunity and to therapeutic efficacy of immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs). Cellular senescence is traditionally characterized by stable cell-cycle arrest accompanied by distinct molecular and functional changes, yet whether tumor-infiltrating (TI) Treg cells acquire senescence-associated features and how these features influence their immunosuppressive activity remain poorly understood. Here, we demonstrate that TI-Treg cells exhibit both apoptosis- and senescence-associated phenotype while retaining, and in some cases likely enhancing, their immunosuppressive capacity. Compared with peripheral Treg cells, some TI-Treg cells from solid cancers display elevated canonical senescence-associated markers, including p16 and p21, DNA damage response pathways, senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP) and anti-apoptotic BCL-2 family genes, as well as activation of secretion associated beta-galactosidase (SA-beta-Gal). Though physiological Treg senescence leads to diminished immune suppression, TI-Treg cells paradoxically maintain the expression of key immunosuppressive molecules. These findings identify a previously unrecognized senescence-like state in TI-Treg cells that is functionally distinct from the loss of fitness typically associated with senescence in other cell types or aging-associated Treg senescence. Our study establishes senescence-associated reprogramming as a defining feature of TI-Treg cells and highlights the senescence-like state of Treg cells as a potential therapeutic target for selectively disrupting tumor immune suppression while preserving systemic immune homeostasis.

Title: Development of lentiviral vectors specifically targeting CD4+ cells
Authors: Cox, D.; Almeida, N.; Khan, H.; Chanas, S.; Marongiu, M.; Vink, C. A.; Malim, M. H.; Apolonia, L.
Abstract: Because of their central role in immunity, CD4+ T cells are a key target for genetic modification in many therapeutic applications, and lentiviral vectors with a VSV-G envelope are often used for this engineering. However, due to their broad tropism, these vectors are inadequate for cell-targeted in vivo gene delivery. Here, we explored using HIV-1 Env, which has a natural tropism towards these cells, as an alternative. We describe a three-plasmid vector production system to incorporate a panel of CCR5- or CXCR4-tropic Envs. These Env proteins are expressed from pCAG, a plasmid with reduced HIV-1 elements. We identify HIV-1 Env-incorporating vectors that can be produced with sufficient titres to specifically transduce primary CD4+ T cells in the context of in vitro mixed populations of peripheral blood mononuclear cells. We show efficient and specific transduction of HIV-1 Env vectors delivering an anti-CD19 chimeric antigen receptor (CAR). We demonstrate functional activity of the generated CD4+ CAR T cells, leading to the targeted killing of B cells in those mixed cell populations. Our methodology enables the production of HIV-1 Env-incorporating lentiviral vectors with defined CD4 targeted delivery, opening avenues for direct in vivo CAR T cell generation.

Title: Dog shelter facilitated transmission and maintenance of benzimidazole resistance-associated alleles in canine hookworms
Authors: McDonald, A.; Woo, S. Y.; Ward, M. P.; Kirkwood, N.; Slapeta, J.
Abstract: Anthelmintic resistance in canine hookworms is increasingly recognised; however, environmental settings that maintain and disseminate resistance-associated alleles remain poorly defined. We hypothesised that urban dog shelters act as hotspots for transmission of benzimidazole resistance-associated alleles in Ancylostoma caninum. Residual faecal samples (n=173) were collected from a Sydney, Australia metropolitan shelter over four sampling periods and analysed using coprodiagnostic methods and deep amplicon sequencing targeting ITS-2 and isotype-1 {beta}-tubulin loci. Hookworm eggs were detected in 41% of samples, with A. caninum identified in 97% of sequenced infections and U. stenocephala in 8%. The isotype-1 {beta}-tubulin F167Y mutation was detected in 83% of A. caninum-positive samples, although high allele frequencies (>70%) were uncommon. Longitudinal sampling identified ten dogs that acquired A. caninum during shelter residence, nine of which acquired populations carrying the F167Y mutation. These findings support the role of dog shelters as hotspots for maintenance and dissemination of benzimidazole resistance-associated alleles in canine hookworms. While the impact of this dissemination remains uncertain, ongoing surveillance and targeted anthelmintic stewardship are likely to be important in high-density dog populations.

Title: B-RANKO: An ncRNA Foundation Model with Bidirectional Decoder-Only Architecture
Authors: Vucenik, F.; Penic, R. J.; Sikic, M.
Abstract: Ribonucleic acid (RNA) plays central roles in gene expression, regulation and catalysis, and has emerged as an important target for therapeutic design. While recent RNA foundation models have achieved strong performance on representation learning tasks, relatively few approaches support both native sequence generation and transferable representation learning within a single framework. We present B-RANKO, a 150M-parameter bidirectional decoder-only ncRNA foundation model that introduces a novel bidirectional autoregressive attention mechanism, enabling a single architecture to support both de novo sequence generation and representation learning. Pretrained on a large corpus derived from RNAcentral, Rfam and GARNET, B-RANKO generates biologically plausible and thermodynamically realistic RNA sequences that exhibit strong novelty relative to their closest matches in the pretraining corpus. We further show that B-RANKO can be efficiently fine-tuned for aptamer generation and achieves competitive performance on BEACON, with particularly strong results on RNA engineering tasks. B-RANKO is publicly available on GitHub at filipvucenik/B-RANKO, together with usage examples and instructions for downloading model weights and datasets.

Title: Rapid generation of marsupial induced pluripotent stem cells suitable for use in next-generation conservation
Authors: Tarulli, G. A.; Hansen, D. K.; Adithya, P.; Tatt, P. R.; Zheng, L.; Kolaitis, N. D.; Filimonow, K.; Scase, E.; Tappe, N.; Cottingham, E.; Jaichander, P.; Hoyt, S. J.; Hartley, G. A.; Tillquist, N.; O'Neill, R. J.; Youngson, N. A.; Carone, B. R.; Ord, S.; Pask, A. J.; Frankenberg, S. R.
Abstract: Marsupials account for a disproportionate share of recent and impending mammalian extinctions, that has prompted investment in the development of "next generation" conservation biotechnologies. These include the generation of genetically selected/modified individuals for improved population fitness. Given the inherent limitations of working with threatened species, a flexible vehicle to develop these technologies is through the generation and editing of induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs). However, it is deemed necessary to derive transgene-free iPSCs for conservation target species, which can be highly time consuming and expensive. This study describes the generation of iPSCs from the marsupial fat-tailed dunnart (diPSCs) that serves as a model species for next generation conservation initiatives. These diPSCs exhibit features of totipotency when cells are maintained with exogenous reprogramming factors for long periods, until differentiation potential is required. Neonatal dunnart fibroblasts were reprogrammed using doxycycline-inducible Oct4, Sox2, Klf4, Lin28 and Myc, and the resulting iPSC lines were characterised at the transcriptomic, epigenetic and functional level (trilineage differentiation, embryoid body formation and mouse blastocyst injection assays). Dunnart iPSCs exhibited robust transcriptional and epigenetic activation of core pluripotency factors (POU5F1, POU5F3, SALL4) as well as factors associated with the naive and primed states of eutherian pluripotency (TBX3, KLF2, TFCP2L1, SOX11, DNMT3A). Dunnart iPSCs readily differentiated in trilineage and embryoid body formation assays, where they expressed markers of all three germ lineages. When injected into 8-cell mouse blastocysts, dunnart iPSCs integrated into both the inner cell mass and trophoblast, reflecting a capacity to contribute to embryonic and extra embryonic lineages during early development. Further, we show that diPSCs can maintain their potential in the presence of exogenous pluripotency factors, until required for differentiation. This robust iPSC generation and maintenance approach is a valuable avenue for the rapid application of next-generation conservation technologies in threatened species.

Title: Characterization and Evaluation of Hypoxia and LPS Preconditioned Placental Stem Cell Extracellular Vesicles in Immune and Intestinal Cells
Authors: Guglani, A.; Ellison, M. A.; Weis, V. G.
Abstract: Background: Human placental stem cells (hPSCs) have demonstrated therapeutic potential in experimental necrotizing enterocolitis (NEC). Extracellular vesicles (EVs) secreted by the hPSCs contribute to these effects through paracrine signaling, however the molecular composition and biological activity of EVs can be influenced by culture conditions of the hPSCs. This study investigated whether hypoxic or lipopolysaccharide (LPS) preconditioning of the hPSCs alters the characteristics, protein composition, and biological activity of hPSC-derived EVs. Methods: hPSCs were cultured under normoxic conditions, exposed to hypoxia (5% O2), or preconditioned with LPS (50 {micro}g/mL). EVs were isolated from conditioned medium using ultrafiltration and size-exclusion chromatography, followed by characterized via nanoparticle tracking analysis, transmission electron microscopy, and single-particle detection of CD9, CD63, and CD81. Biological activity was evaluated in HIEC-6 intestinal epithelial cells through MTT, scratch wound closure, and nitrite detection assays. Immunomodulatory responses were examined in primary healthy neonatal rat CD4+ T-cell cultures using flow cytometry. Results: EV preparations showed comparable particle concentrations and size distributions across all three culture conditions, with no statistically significant differences. Vesicle-like morphology and EV-associated tetraspanins were detected in all preparations. All three EV groups improved epithelial metabolic activity following LPS exposure, enhanced scratch wound closure, and reduced nitrite accumulation compared with their respective controls. Flow cytometric analysis showed no statistically significant differences in TNF-, IL-17A, or FoxP3 expression among EV-treated CD4+ T-cell groups. Conclusions: Hypoxic and LPS preconditioning did not significantly affect the measured physical characteristics or secretion concentrations of the EVs. Although EVs from all three conditions showed beneficial effects on intestinal epithelial cells, neither preconditioning approach demonstrated a clear functional advantage over naive EVs in these simplified culture model. These findings suggest that preconditioning influences EV molecular cargo but more comprehensive biological function assays are required to delineate potential differences in effects on intestinal epithelial or T-cell functions. These data provide a basis for further studies examining its potential relevance to EV-based therapies for NEC.

Title: The program STRUCTURE is good at detecting contemporary hybridization
Authors: Pelletier, D.; MacPherson, A.; Mooers, A. O.
Abstract: The program STRUCTURE is widely used in conservation genetics to detect human-caused hybridization between previously isolated populations. However, its performance at this specific task is not yet known, and methods used to interpret the model output vary widely among studies. We simulated hybridization between two populations on the timescale of real-world cases and tested STRUCTURE's ability to correctly detect hybridization based on a simple "hybrid signal": inferring the presence or absence of a minimum of one hybrid. Overall, this returned the correct result in 100% of scenarios when Fst between the two populations was between 0.05-0.15 when using an optimal Q-threshold of 0.10. Performance was slightly reduced when divergence was very weak (Fst = 0.01, with an optimal Q-threshold between 0.30-0.35) or when the population receiving migrants was substructured, but it still returned the correct result in 89-100% of cases, depending on simulation parameters. We conclude that STRUCTURE, paired with this hybrid signal and our recommended Q-thresholds, is an appropriate tool for detecting contemporary hybridization.

Title: TEV Induced Cleavage of Nuclei Tagged in Specific Cell Types (TIC-TaC) reveals histone profiles of activated neurons
Authors: Lukasak, B. J.; Shing, K.; Crawford, C. E. W.; Beyer, J. N.; Sangree, A. K.; Burslem, G.; Korb, E.
Abstract: Epigenomic profiling methods such as CUT&RUN/Tag are commonly employed to evaluate the genomic localization of histone modifications, transcription factors, and chromatin regulating proteins. Numerous transgenic mouse models also exist that label specific cell populations by leveraging Cre-based recombination and fluorescent reporters to allow for cell type specific epigenetic profiling in vivo. However, none of these systems allow for rapid, parallel processing for cell-type-specific CUT&RUN/Tag. Here, we report the development of TEV Induced Cleavage of Nuclei Tagged in Specific Cell Types (TIC-TaC) in which we leverage a recombination-based system that results in conditional expression of a Sun1-GFP fusion protein with a TEV site introduced between Sun1 and GFP. Like the existing INTACT system, nuclei tagged by cell-type specific Cre recombinase activity can be efficiently purified using immunoprecipitation to allow for rapid, efficient, and in parallel nuclei isolation. However, with the addition of TEV protease, TIC-TaC nuclei can be subsequently removed from the beads allowing for downstream CUT&RUN/Tag. We applied this system to neurons isolated from the cortex to define the effects of seizure induced neuronal activation on numerous histone modifications and histone variant proteins and identified concordant shifts in H3K27ac, H3K27me3, H2A.Z and H2BE at seizure responsive genes. Together, through the development and application of TIC-TaC to allow for parallel processing of tissue for cell-type specific analysis, we uncover activity-dependent regulation of chromatin in the brain.

Title: PlantTV: a versatile user-friendly software to explore RNA-seq data across plant species
Authors: Pertuy, M.; De Coninck, B.; van Buren, L.
Abstract: Bulk RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) has become a central tool in plant biology for studying genome-wide transcriptional responses. However, interpretation of differential expression results remains challenging, particularly for non-model species where functional annotation resources are fragmented, heterogeneous, or incomplete. Existing user-friendly RNA-seq analysis platforms often rely on predefined annotation databases, limiting their applicability across the diversity of plant species. We developed Plant Transcriptomics Viewer (PlantTV), a free web-based platform for interactive exploration of plant RNA-seq datasets. PlantTV integrates differential expression analysis, expression visualization, functional enrichment analysis, and co-expression network exploration within a single graphical interface. A central feature is the Annotation Builder, which allows users to generate reusable annotation tables from diverse resources, including GFF/GTF files, EggNOG annotations, BLAST results, and custom tabular datasets. Using case studies in Arabidopsis thaliana, Malus domestica, and Eucalyptus melliodora, we demonstrate that PlantTV supports transcriptome analysis across a range of annotation scenarios, from well-annotated reference genomes to de novo transcriptome assemblies. PlantTV provides an interactive and species-independent environment for plant transcriptome analysis. By combining RNA-seq exploration tools with flexible support for custom annotation resources, PlantTV facilitates biological interpretation of transcriptomic datasets in both model and non-model plant species.

Title: Spectrast: a multiscale spatial statistics toolkit for single-cell spatial transcriptomics
Authors: Gingerich, I. K.; Frost, H. R.
Abstract: Spatial transcriptomics resolves gene expression in physical space, but the spatial statistics typically used to quantify spatial organization scale poorly to imaging-based datasets with hundreds-of-thousands of cells and thousands of genes. We recast the standard spatial-autocorrelation statistics as convolutions on a rasterized representation of the gene expression matrix and evaluate them with the fast Fourier transform. Measuring spatial statistics across multiple length scales becomes tractable for every gene using this approach, which extends naturally to differential reorganization testing between two tissue conditions.

Title: Machine Learning-Enhanced Mucosal Luminal Interface Metaproteomics Reveals Diagnostic Potential of Microbial Proteins in Pediatric Inflammatory Bowel Disease
Authors: Ghanbari-Maman, L.; Fekrirad, Z.; Meyfour, A.; Kavousi, K.
Abstract: Abstract: Background: Inflammatory Bowel Disease (IBD), a chronic gastrointestinal disorder with two main subtypes, Crohn's Disease (CD) and Ulcerative Colitis (UC), is associated with more aggressive phenotypes and greater diagnostic complexity in pediatric patients. Conventional diagnostic biomarkers, lack sufficient distinguishing power between IBD subtypes. This study aimed to investigate and compare proteomic and metaproteomic profiles of pediatric IBD (PIBD) patients and healthy controls to develop a diagnostic panel capable of accurately diagnose IBD and distinguish its subtypes. Methods: We performed an in-depth evaluation of mucosal luminal interface samples from PIBD patients and healthy individuals, separately analyzing both the human proteome and microbial metaproteome data. The study involved selecting appropriate protein sets, employing feature selection techniques and machine learning across three intestinal regions: the terminal ileum, ascending colon, and descending colon. Results: Notably, panels composed solely of microbial biomarkers outperformed both human-only and combined human-microbial panels, achieving highly accurate results. Furthermore, the ascending colon emerged as the optimal sampling site, a result that aligns with the rich microbial diversity revealed in its taxonomic profile. Conclusions: Using a machine learning-based strategy on combined proteomics and metaproteomics, this study uncovered disease-relevant signaling pathways and delivered taxonomic as well as functional insights into the microbial dysbiosis of PIBD. A diagnostic panel built around microbial proteins (particularly those originating from the ascending colon) emerges as a promising tool for more precise stratification of PIBD subtypes. Larger, prospective studies are now needed to validate these candidate biomarkers and translate them into clinically deployable diagnostic panels. Keywords: Metaproteome, Biomarker, Pediatric Inflammatory bowel disease, Machine learning, Mucosal luminal interface.

Title: Nanodisc-Enabled Dissection of GxxxG- Mediated Amyloid Beta Oligomerization Mechanisms
Authors: Sarkar, D.; Roy, D.; Biswas, K.; Chakraborty, S.; Majumder, S.; Krishnamoorthy, J.; Sahoo, N.; Maity, N.; Singh, C.; Ghosh, D.; Biswas, R.; Senapati, D.; Bhaumik, P.; Bhunia, A.
Abstract: Extracellular deposition of amyloid plaques is a major hallmark in Alzheimers disease, in which amyloid-beta fibrils are key constituents. Fibrillation of amyloid-beta is modulated by several key sequence motifs, among which the G33LMVG37 motif located in the C-terminal is particularly significant. Moreover, the interaction between amyloid-beta and cellular membrane can be determining factor in its oligomerization. Here, we present membrane scaffold protein encased lipid nanodiscs as a model membrane mimic to investigate the roles of G33 and G37 in membrane-mediated amyloid-beta40 oligomerization. Using a combination of spectroscopic and microscopic techniques, accompanied by molecular dynamic simulations, we demonstrate that these Gly residues are crucial in regulating both self-assembly and membrane-associated oligomerization of amyloid-beta40. We report the formation of structurally distinct amyloid-beta40 oligomers upon interaction with nanodiscs. Our mutational studies reveal a direct involvement of G33 or G37 residues in membrane interaction, leading to prolonged oligomer lifetime.

Title: Multimodal conformational landscape and thermodynamics of coupled folding and binding in an intrinsically disordered protein region
Authors: Akulov, V.; Rizzi, V.; van Noort, J.; Mashaghi, A.
Abstract: Intrinsically disordered proteins and peptides, as well as flexible protein regions, often bind folded protein partners through coupled folding and binding, but the underlying conformational landscapes and thermodynamics remain challenging to resolve. The large conformational space of the unbound molecule and its interactions with the folded partner make it difficult to identify and efficiently sample the slow collective motions governing association and folding. Here, we use enhanced-sampling molecular dynamics to investigate the coupled binding and folding of the intrinsically disordered region of FCP1 phosphatase upon interaction with the folded transcription factor Rap74, a process that modulates the activity of RNA polymerase II. OneOPES enhanced sampling simulations reveal a multimodal binding landscape comprising native, flipped and disordered-bound states, and identify hydrophobic contacts as early determinants of association followed by progressive helix formation. Circuit topology analysis further elucidates the FCP1 folding mechanism by identifying a characteristic topological transition accompanying helix formation and its stabilisation upon binding. To resolve the thermodynamics of the process, we introduce Divide et impera, a thermodynamic decomposition that separates the free-energy cost of folding from the binding free energy of the folded conformation. This approach reduces the conformational complexity of individual calculations while preserving the thermodynamic connection between unbound and bound states, enabling the calculation of absolute binding free energies in close agreement with experiment. These results establish a framework for connecting conformational heterogeneity, binding mechanisms and thermodynamics in coupled folding and binding of disordered proteins, with potential applications in the rational design and development of peptide therapeutics.

Title: Multi-omic longitudinal profiling of companion dogs reveals cross-omic coordination and structured aging trajectories
Authors: Bamberger, T.; Algavi, Y. M.; Muller, E.; Peleg, O.; Baum, S.; Greenier, A.; Adjangba, C.; Slikas, E.; Brassington, L.; Mariner, B.; McCoy, B.; Harrison, B. R.; Partida-Aguilar, M.; Marye, A.; Harris, A.; Rout, E.; DAP Consortium,  ; Avery, A.; Promislow, D. E. L.; Snyder-Mackler, N.; Borenstein, E.
Abstract: Aging is a systems-level biological process shaped by coordinated changes across molecular, physiological, and environmental domains, yet how these domains interact and impact aging remains poorly understood. Companion dogs offer a powerful model for addressing this gap, combining shared human environments with diversity in genetics, lifespan, and disease susceptibility. Here, we present a longitudinal multi-omic analysis of aging in 965 companion dogs from the Dog Aging Project, integrating microbiome, epigenome, blood metabolome, and immune phenotyping with extensive clinical, environmental, and lifestyle surveys. We reveal an interconnected cross-omic architecture, with age emerging as the dominant axis of biological variation. We further identify a predictive multi-omic aging signature, distinguish linear from non-linear aging trajectories, uncover breed size-dependent dynamics, and characterize omic-specific mortality risk. Collectively, our findings reveal organizing principles of aging, many paralleling human observations, provide a unique resource for integrative geroscience, and establish dogs as a translational model for aging research.

Title: Gas6 signaling via its cellular receptors is essential for homeostasis in response to endotoxemia and infection
Authors: Caku, S.; Prince Eladnani, R.; Burnier, L.; Li, B.; Roger, T.; Chanson, M.; Diab, R.; Etzensperger, R.; Tripodo, M.; Knopp, T.; Liaudet, L.; Introini, E.; Iype, J. M.; Keragala, C. B.; Medcalf, R. L.; Pfortmueller, C. A.; Allam, R.; Messmer, A. S.; Angelillo-Scherrer, A.
Abstract: Sepsis is a life-threatening syndrome characterized by infection-induced organ dysfunction and dysregulated host inflammatory responses. Despite advances in supportive care, effective pharmacological therapies remain lacking. Growth arrest-specific protein 6 (Gas6), a vitamin K-dependent ligand of the TAM receptors (Tyro3, Axl, and Mer), operates at the interface of inflammation and coagulation. Here, we investigated the role of Gas6-TAM signaling in endotoxemia and infection in humans and mice. Plasma Gas6 levels increased rapidly during sepsis in patients, during experimental endotoxemia in both humans and mice, and during infection in mice, and these elevations correlated with disease severity and poor clinical outcomes. In both species, circulating Gas6 remained closely balanced with soluble Axl (sAxl), suggesting that much of plasma Gas6 is sequestered in soluble complexes, thereby limiting activation of membrane TAM receptors. In mice, deficiency of Gas6 or individual TAM receptors increased susceptibility to endotoxemia, and Gas6 deficiency additionally heightened vulnerability to bacterial infection. Gas6-deficient mice displayed reduced mean blood pressure, exaggerated cytokine release, altered early leukocyte dynamics, and enhanced macrophage activation. Mechanistically, macrophages secreted Gas6 in response to LPS, and Gas6 acted as an autocrine negative feedback signal limiting inflammatory cytokine production, at least in part through regulation of TLR signaling. Although Gas6 is strongly involved in immune regulation during sepsis, our data do not support a major direct role in coagulation activation. While circulating Gas6 and soluble Mer levels in septic patients were associated with sepsis-induced coagulopathy and impaired thrombin generation, this likely reflects disease severity rather than a causal effect on the coagulation. Consistently, in a murine endotoxemia model, Gas6 deficiency resulted in only minor changes in coagulation markers and did not lead to disseminated intravascular coagulation, suggesting that Gas6 primarily reflects systemic inflammation rather than directly driving coagulation abnormalities.

Title: An HWE/HisKA2-family kinase-phosphatase pair differentially regulates two paralogous PhyR response regulators to shape the General Stress Response specificity in Sphingopyxis granuli TFA
Authors: Pires-Acosta, A.; Garcia-Romero, I.; Reyes-Ramirez, F.
Abstract: The general stress response (GSR) enables bacteria to withstand diverse environmental challenges. In Alphaproteobacteria, the GSR is controlled by a partner-switching mechanism involving the extracytoplasmic function sigma factor EcfG, its anti-sigma factor NepR, and the response regulator PhyR. Phosphorylated PhyR binds to NepR, releasing EcfG to activate GSR gene expression. However, how upstream signalling coordinates multiple PhyR paralogs remains poorly understood. Sphingopyxis granuli TFA is a pollutant-degrading bacterium able to use the organic solvent tetralin as a sole carbon and energy source. TFA contains two copies of each core GSR regulatory component, including two PhyR paralogs with distinct contributions to GSR activity and stress resistance. Using genetic, physiological and biochemical approaches, we identify two HWE/HisKA2-family proteins, HK_3483 and HK_1165, as major positive and negative GSR regulators, respectively. HK_3483 functions as a histidine kinase required for effective GSR activation through either PhyR paralog and for resistance to oxidative stress, copper and desiccation. It directly phosphorylates both PhyR proteins in vitro, with a preference for PhyR1. In contrast, HK_1165 preferentially dephosphorylates PhyR2. Consistently, deletion of SGRAN_1165 in a {Delta}phyR1 background increases PhyR2 phosphorylation in vivo under oxidative stress and stationary phase. Loss of HK_1165 causes a pronounced growth defect that is suppressed by deletion of either PhyR paralog while the remaining PhyR paralog supports elevated GSR activity and broad stress resistance. Our findings support a model in which differential regulation of PhyR phosphorylation, mediated by the opposing activities of an upstream kinase-phosphatase pair, contributes to functional specialization within bacterial stress signalling networks.

Title: A negative role for transcription factor Bcr1 in Candida albicans hypha-associated gene expression
Authors: Sharma, A.; Mitchell, A. P.
Abstract: Filamentation, a central virulence trait of the fungal pathogen Candida albicans, is required for host cell damage, tissue invasion, and biofilm formation. The transcription factor Bcr1 was first found to be required for biofilm formation but not filamentation. Subsequent studies revealed a negative role for Bcr1 in filamentation in opaque cells, a cell type that is required for mating, under hypoxic conditions, and in a wor2del/del mutant background. Here we characterize a new context in which Bcr1 negatively regulates filamentation and present its associated gene expression impact. We compared the wild-type and bcr1del/del mutant cells in the SC5314 reference strain background at 30 degrees C in glucose media, conditions that do not induce filamentation. The bcr1del/del mutant displayed increased invasive growth in a solid medium, and some filamentation ability in a liquid medium. The bcr1del/del effect on filamentation was augmented by overexpression of hyphal cyclin gene HGC1, which caused pseudohyphal growth in wild-type, efg1del/del, or brg1del/del strains, yet caused hyphal growth in the bcr1del/del strain. RNA-sequencing (RNA-seq) analysis of 30 degrees C cells shows that the bcr1del/del mutant has elevated expression of two genes that drive filamentation: HGC1 and UME6. In published data these same two genes have decreased expression in the bcr1del/del mutant at 37 degrees C, the temperature at which biofilm formation is typically assayed. A growing cadre of biofilm/hyphal regulators can have both positive and negative effects on hypha-associated gene expression, including Bcr1, Efg1, Ndt80, and Nrg1.

Title: DNA and H3K4 methylation act cooperatively to protect regulatory elements
Authors: David, A.; Morales-Franco, M.; Hounani, N.; Monteagudo-Sanchez, A.; Perdrix, S.; Richard Albert, J.; Scarpa, M.; Bozdag, B.; Damagnez, T.; Greenberg, M. V. C.
Abstract: Histone H3 lysine 4 methylation (H3K4me) is associated with transcriptionally active regulatory elements: H3K4me1 is typically found at enhancers, and H3K4me2/3 at gene promoters. In mammals, the presence of H3K4me can reinforce expression programs, but it might also help protect from epigenetic silencing complexes. To wit, H3K4me antagonizes the binding of the de novo DNA methyltransferase enzymes, which catalyze the repressive 5-methylcytosine (5meC) epigenetic mark. To determine the extent to which H3K4me protects regulatory elements from 5meC deposition - and how this influences genome regulation - we used mouse embryonic stem cells (ESCs), which are resilient to the complete absence of 5meC. Employing an inducible dominant negative transgene that globally reduces H3K4me, we assessed the impact in both presence and absence of 5meC. Surprisingly, while ESCs could withstand reduced H3K4me or 5meC, their combined loss led to catastrophic cellular phenotypes in pluripotency and during differentiation. Genomic analyses revealed that H3K4me and 5meC work in concert to protect regulatory elements from Polycomb-mediated silencing. Thus, this work unraveled an unexpected functional cooperation between two epigenetic marks typically viewed as antagonistic in safeguarding transcriptional programs.

Title: Nuclear-Cytoskeletal Uncoupling in Aging Capillaries Disrupts Endothelial Nuclear Flattening and Lumen Formation
Authors: Francis, C.; Leser, F.; Lopez, R.; Eichmann, A.
Abstract: Loss of small blood vessels compromises tissue perfusion during aging, but the underlying mechanisms remain unclear. We investigated microvascular integrity in physiologically aged mice and in Hutchinson-Gilford Progeria Syndrome, a genetic disorder of premature vascular aging. Progeric and aged mice exhibited capillary loss and impaired perfusion, caused by cell autonomous defects in endothelial nuclei that failed to flatten and instead obstructed vessel lumens. Progerin expression in endothelial cells altered LINC complex composition by increasing SUN proteins and reducing nuclear-envelope Nesprin engagement, disrupting coupling to cytoskeletal actin and vimentin. Experimental disruption of nuclear-cytoskeletal coupling impaired nuclear flattening and lumen formation, whereas restoration improved nuclear morphology and vessel formation in progeric cells. Aged mouse and human endothelium exhibited changes in LINC complex and vimentin expression. Pharmacological Progerin inhibition restored nuclear-cytoskeletal coupling and lumen formation in patient-derived endothelial cells. These findings implicate defective nuclear-cytoskeletal coupling in microvascular dropout in Progeria and physiological aging.

Title: MAFA Phosphorylation Controls Beta-Cell Identity and Sex-Specific Pancreatic Disease Outcomes
Authors: Ka, M.; Druillennec, S.; Chabi, S.; Roulle, C.; NG, D. Y.; PECHOUX, C.; Messaoudi, C.; Walczak, C.; Soler, M.-N.; Besse, L.; Lecoin, L.; Majo, S.; Gradwohl, G.; Eychene, A.; Terris, B.; Pouponnot, C.; DUVILLIE, B.
Abstract: Mafa is a critical transcription factor in pancreatic beta-cell biology, orchestrating insulin expression in response to glucose elevations. As a member of the large MAF protein family, MAFA's stability and activity are intricately regulated by GSK3-mediated phosphorylation. To decipher the functional roles of these phosphorylations, we engineered knock-in mice (Mafa4A/+) in which MAFA is rendered non-phosphorylatable. In all Mafa4A/+ animals, MAFA stability was markedly enhanced. Under high-fat diet (HFD) conditions, Mafa4A/+ males rapidly developed glucose intolerance, which was attributed to impaired glucose-stimulated insulin secretion. Bulk RNA sequencing revealed disrupted beta-cell identity, characterized by increased expression of MODY-associated genes and a delta-cell signature, suggesting beta-to-delta cell reprogramming, a hypothesis supported by lineage-tracing experiments. Conversely, Mafa4A/+ females exhibited hypoglycemia and, with age, developed pronounced inflammatory cystic ducts including mucinous cystic neoplasms (MCNs). Strikingly, MAFA protein was also detected in MCN biopsies from female patients, linking our findings to human pathology. Our results unveil a sex-biased impact of GSK3-mediated MAFA phosphorylation. The male phenotype closely parallels the MODY-like diabetes observed in patients with MAFA S64F mutations, implicating defective phosphorylation in disease etiology. The emergence of MCNs in female mice suggests a novel role for MAFA stability or mutations in the pathogenesis of these enigmatic neoplasms, providing a fresh molecular hypothesis with clinical relevance.

Title: Pharmacologic IRE1 Activation Rewires Cholesterol Metabolism to Suppress TH17 Differentiation
Authors: Sanchez Ortiz, K.; Chatterjee, P.; Dion, W.; Pannikkat, M.; Kutseikin, S.; Basso, T.; Sun, J.; Mathur, P.; Dikiy, S.; Thaxton, J. E.; Wiseman, L.; Mendoza, A.
Abstract: T helper 17 (TH17) cells are a subset of CD4 T cells that coordinate immune responses against extracellular bacterial and fungal pathogens. Dysregulation of TH17 cell responses drives excessive inflammation and contributes to the development of chronic inflammatory and autoimmune diseases, including psoriasis, inflammatory bowel disease, and multiple sclerosis. Here, we demonstrate that pharmacologic activation of the IRE1 signaling arm of the unfolded protein response (UPR) selectively reduces differentiation of TH17 cells without impacting the differentiation of other helper T cell subsets. We show that IRE1 activation suppresses TH17 differentiation by limiting intracellular cholesterol in differentiating TH17 cells through the increased degradation of the rate-limiting cholesterol biosynthesis enzyme HMGCR. Our findings identify IRE1 as a metabolic checkpoint regulating cholesterol biosynthesis in differentiating TH17 cells and demonstrate that its pharmacological activation suppresses TH17 differentiation, highlighting a potential therapeutic strategy for limiting TH17-driven inflammatory diseases.

Title: Revealing the transcriptomic organization of extrasomatic interfaces using SCOUBI
Authors: Aggarwal, B.; Jain, S.; Sinha, S.
Abstract: Spatial transcriptomics (ST) generates substantial transcript signal outside segmented cell bodies, which is generally discarded by analysis tools. This is especially problematic for brain ST data, as neuronal mRNAs can be localized far from somata - in axons, dendrites, and synaptic compartments - and up to half of the transcripts in ST data may lie outside cell bodies. Here, we present SCOUBI, a computational framework that identifies axon-dendrite interfaces from extrasomatic RNA in ST data, revealing a hitherto overlooked layer of molecular function in neural tissues. It first partitions extrasomatic space into axon- and dendrite-enriched compartments based on known marker genes, using a neural network trained to maximize marker specificity and inter-compartment communication signals. It then defines interfaces as loci where predicted axonal and dendritic compartments converge and exhibit ligand-receptor colocalization. Applied to mouse brain, SCOUBI creates maps of axonal and dendritic compartments and their interfaces that align with known spatial patterns of neurite and synaptic distribution. It identifies transcriptomic differences between interfaces and the surrounding extrasomatic space, revealing region-specific signatures of neuronal signaling and synaptic plasticity. By comparing interface transcript enrichment with local somatic expression, SCOUBI identifies genes that preferentially localize at sites of intercellular communication rather than simply reflecting nearby cell bodies. SCOUBI reveals interface-associated transcripts beyond established synaptic genes, with molecular signatures reproducible across independent samples and imaging platforms. In summary, SCOUBI transforms a substantial and often-discarded aspect of ST data into an interpretable readout of subcellular organization and neural signaling.

Title: Comparative Profiling of Cytosolic Accumulation of Cell-Penetrating Peptides in Mammalian and Bacterial Cells
Authors: Bhandari, S.; Newkirk, S.; Ocius, K.; Liu, Z.; Sharifia, M.; Naick, A.; Starnes, C.; Dash, R.; Kelly, J.; He, Y.; Ongwae, G.; Lucas, N.; Fitzgerald, C.; Bursum, H.; Kenyon, R.; Pires, M.
Abstract: Delivering molecules to the cytosol remains a major bottleneck in antibacterial therapy, as both the Gram-negative bacterial envelope and host-cell membranes restrict intracellular access. Cell-penetrating peptides (CPPs) offer a potential strategy for overcoming these barriers. However, selecting CPPs for conjugate development remains largely empirical, in part because conventional fluorescence-based uptake measurements can misidnentify cellular association as cytosolic delivery. Here, we used our recently developed Chloroalkane Azide-tagged Membrane Permeation (CHAMP) assay, a HaloTag-based flow cytometry platform that directly reports cytosolic arrival, to systematically compare 40 CPPs in mammalian cells and Escherichia coli (E. coli). In mammalian cells, cytosolic accumulation varied substantially within each peptide class, indicating that uptake depends on individual sequence features rather than class membership alone. Among peptides with measurable accumulation in both systems, none exhibited greater apparent accumulation in mammalian cells than in E. coli. Complementary assays showed that several peptides reached the bacterial cytosol without detectable membrane damage, whereas others accumulated in association with compromised membrane integrity. Together, these findings provide a quantitative comparison of CPP-mediated cytosolic access in mammalian and bacterial cells and establish a framework for selecting peptide carriers for antibiotic conjugates.

Title: Cardiomyocytes in Persistent Cancer Therapy-related Cardiac Dysfunction Show Contractile and Natriuretic Peptide Signaling Signatures
Authors: Chan, A.; Hansen, J.; Iyengar, R.
Abstract: BACKGROUND. Anthracycline and trastuzumab therapy of HER2-positive breast cancer causes cancer therapy-related cardiac dysfunction (CTRCD) in a subset of treated patients. Some recover cardiac function, others do not. Whether persistence is a cardiomyocyte-intrinsic property is unknown. OBJECTIVES. We sought to determine whether induced pluripotent stem cell-derived cardiomyocytes (iPSC-CMs) from patients with persistent CTRCD respond to these drugs differently from those of patients with reversible or no CTRCD, and to identify the functional pathways involved. METHODS. iPSCs were derived from 23 women with normal baseline cardiac function treated with doxorubicin-based chemotherapy followed by trastuzumab: 5, 11 and 7 with no, reversible, and persistent CTRCD, respectively. iPSC-CMs were exposed to 7 drug regimens, generating 161 transcriptomic profiles that we resolved by singular value decomposition and subjected to pathway enrichment analysis. Reliability was tested by 100 clinical label permutations and leave-one-patient-out downsampling. RESULTS. Persistent CTRCD responses clustered more tightly and separated from reversible and no-CTRCD responses to a higher degree than expected by chance (P = 0.04). Reversible and no-CTRCD responses did not resolve from one another. Genes encoding guideline-recommended biomarkers, including natriuretic peptides and cardiac troponins, were more strongly induced or less repressed in persistent CTRCD cell lines, while natriuretic peptide receptor signaling was lower. Contraction, calcium handling, cytoskeletal and glycolytic pathways differed between CTRCD groups. Comparison with signatures induced by cardiotoxic kinase inhibitors in healthy donor cardiomyocytes documented high functional similarities. CONCLUSIONS. Cardiomyocytes display a cell-intrinsic signature of persistent CTRCD that centers on contractile homeostasis and natriuretic peptide receptor signaling, supporting patient group-selective cardioprotective intervention strategies.

Title: Carbon-nitrogen metabolism drives the predatory dynamics between myxobacteria and prey bacteria bytrophic interaction
Authors: Zhang, L.; Yang, K.; Yang, G.; Zhang, L.; Jiang, S.; Hou, M.; Pang, F.; Ye, X.; Huang, Y.; Cui, Z.; Li, Z.
Abstract: Interkingdom interactions represented by microbial predator and prey are crucial for soil food-web community structure and ecosystem function. However, bacteria predatory dynamics derived by metabolic interplay remain understudied. Here we examine the trophic interactions between predator myxobacteria and prey bacteria where we find that glucose input leads to predator-prey oscillations between Corallococcus sp. EGB and Escherichia coli depending on the presence of other soil microbes. Co-cultural assays revealed that glucose consumption by E. coli inhibits EGB predation by rapid environmental acidification via the phosphoenolpyruvate-dependent carbohydrate phosphotransferase system (PTS) and disruption of membrane homeostasis through citrate-mediated ionic chelation. In response, EGB adjusts its amino acid metabolism by producing volatile ammonia, leading to alkalinization that counteracts glucose-mediated acidification. Additionally, ammonia serves as a nitrogen source for prey bacteria growth, thereby providing a stable food source for myxobacteria by a possible farming strategy. Moreover, EGB also ingeniously exploits soil microbes Meyerozyma guilliermondii and Xanthomonas to metabolize glucose and citrate, thus adapting the predator to metabolites derived from prey in natural environments. This complex metabolite-based interplay depending on cell density and carbon-nitrogen sources leads to predator-prey oscillations between predator EGB and prey E. coli until a stable population equilibrium is reached. Our findings highlight the critical role of carbon-nitrogen metabolism in driving bacterial predator-prey dynamics that have implications for trophic interactions between myxobacteria and prey bacteria in soil microbial food webs.

Title: Morphology and phylogenomics of Leucomyxa quisqueyensis sp. nov., a colorless freshwater amoeboid ochrophyte (Stramenopiles) from the Dominican Republic
Authors: Tekle, Y. I.; Ghebrezadik, S.; Smith, A. A.; Petit, H.; Vasquez, C.; Plasencia, E.; Reyes, C.; Franco, E. F.
Abstract: Amoeboid ochrophytes (stramenopiles) exhibit diverse cell forms and plastid states, yet many lineages are known primarily from environmental sequences. We describe Leucomyxa quisqueyensis sp. nov., a freshwater amoeboid ochrophyte isolated from a freshwater drainage channel in La Chinola, Santo Domingo Oeste, Dominican Republic. In established cultures, the isolate consistently formed extensive multinucleate reticula, with fine strands linking densely branched regions. The largest networks exceeded 2 mm. Confocal imaging revealed longitudinal microtubule strands along the reticulopodia. Rounded cysts measured 6.47-15.43 um in diameter. SSU rRNA and nuclear phylogenomic analyses identified Leucomyxa plasmidifera as the closest sampled named relative. Their sister relationship received 100% ultrafast bootstrap support in the phylogeny inferred from 124 nuclear protein markers. The two species differed by 2.50% across comparable SSU rRNA positions and by 15.26% across 25,619 comparable amino-acid positions in the nuclear marker alignment. Transcripts with similarity to Tic110 and PPP1, together with matches to plastome-derived protein queries, support the hypothesis that L. quisqueyensis retains a cryptic plastid. The new species adds a cultured Caribbean freshwater representative to Leucomyxa and provides a basis for comparing reticulopodial organization and plastid evolution among closely related amoeboid ochrophytes.

Title: CbrA-CbrB Activity is Sensitive to Changes in Pseudomonas aeruginosa Cellular Redox State
Authors: Conaway, A.; Shimkonis, J.; Todorovic, I.; Michaels, L. A.; Rajesh-Khanna, D.-S.; Balsam, S.; Botelho, N.; Goddard, J. M.; Mould, D. L.; Harty, C.; Bomberger, J.; Hogan, D. A.
Abstract: In Pseudomonas aeruginosa, the CbrA-CbrB two component system contributes to catabolism of diverse carbon and nitrogen sources, several virulence attributes, and is required for the elevated fitness of clinically relevant strains with loss-of-function mutations in lasR in passaged cultures. Despite its significance, the mechanism of activation of the CbrA kinase remains unknown. Leveraging the observation that LasR- strains had high CbrA-CbrB signaling that led to increased phosphatase activity, we performed a transposon mutant screen in a LasR- clinical isolate for strains that potentially lost high CbrA-CbrB signaling. Through these studies, we demonstrate that CbrA-CbrB activity correlates with intracellular cysteine abundance and activity is repressed by high or low levels of cellular reducing power. We show that CbrA-CbrB activity is elevated in late-stage cultures and also impacted by stationary phase signaling. Additionally, CbrA-CbrB activity is elevated in the {Delta}lasR mutant in competition with the wild type and this activity is critical for the {Delta}lasR mutant competitive.
