These colonoid models provide a physiologically relevant platform for investigating colonic ADME-T and reveal how microvillar architecture shapes intracellular drug bioavailability.

Title: A Manually Curated Metabolic Model of Alteromonas macleodii MIT1002 and its Ecological Implications
Authors: Scott, H.; Moyer, D.; Weissberg, O.; Kratzl, F.; Valiya Kalladi, W. B.; Smith, C. B.; Braakman, R.; Moran, M. A.; Sher, D.; Segre, D.
Abstract: Heterotrophic bacteria are a vital part of the marine carbon cycle. They interact with phytoplankton and rapidly process fixed carbon, respiring it back to CO2. Among heterotrophs, Alteromonas macleodii is notable for its colonization of particulate material and its high growth and carbon utilization rates and is commonly used as a model system to study metabolic interactions with the abundant cyanobacterium Prochlorococcus. Understanding how these traits emerge from the interplay of hundreds of reactions requires a formal encoding of the organisms metabolic network. Here, we present a metabolic model of A. macleodii MIT1002, built in a traceable and systematic way to recreate experimental growth phenotypes on 51 unique media compositions. We used this model to generate testable hypotheses about the role of sodium in the electron transport chain, the catabolic relevance of different glycolytic pathways, nitrogen recycling during cross-feeding with Prochlorococcus, and microbial carbon use efficiency.

Title: A conserved MoxR-vWA chaperone complex drives starvation-induced protein degradation in bacteria
Authors: Okano, H.; Ye, Q.; Mori, M.; Manzanarez, G.; Zhang, Z.; Hackbarth, F.; Chambers, L. R.; Balakrishnan, R.; Kannan, H.; Tian, E.; Mendez-Diaz, F.; Huo, J.; Enustun, E.; Ludwig, C.; Hwa, T.; Corbett, K. D.
Abstract: Bacteria must quickly adapt to changes in their environment, notably including the sudden loss of nutrients. We previously showed that in glucose-starved E. coli, widespread starvation-induced protein degradation (SPD) fuels post-starvation proteome remodeling, degrading a wide swath of the proteome to supply the cell with energy and amino acids for synthesis of stress proteins. Here we demonstrate that SPD is mediated by a highly conserved complex of three proteins: the MoxR-type AAA+ ATPase SpdA, the von Willebrand factor A (vWA) domain protein SpdB, and the zinc metallopeptidase SpdC. Structural modeling and in vitro reconstitutions show that these proteins form a complex with 6:1:1 stoichiometry that resembles the widespread, but still poorly understood, family of MoxR-vWA chaperone complexes in bacteria and eukaryotes. Measurements of protein degradation in glucose-starved E. coli cells show that SpdA, SpdB, and SpdC work together to mediate the degradation of SPD substrates. Instead of directly degrading these substrates, our data suggest that limited structural perturbation and proteolysis "softens" SPD substrates and promotes their degradation by the cellular proteases ClpAP/ClpXP and Lon. Thus, SPD enables extensive proteome remodeling during starvation by expanding the pool of proteins accessible to cellular proteases, rather than by increasing protease abundance. Phylogenetic analysis shows that SpdA, SpdB, and SpdC are highly conserved across bacteria, with notable homologs including the well-characterized Bacillus subtilis sporulation factors PrkA (SpdA), YhbH (SpdB), and SpoVR (SpdC).

Title: Illumina MiSeq, MiSeq i100, and Element AVITI yield concordant ecological patterns for universal 16S and 18S rRNA gene amplicon sequencing
Authors: D'Agostino, E.; Needham, D.
Abstract: Molecular microbiome analyses require high-resolution, comparable measurements, often obtained by sequencing marker genes such as the rRNA gene. Recently, new platforms and chemistries have promised to improve performance at lower cost relative to the commonly used Illumina MiSeq 2x300, but have not yet been systematically compared especially for rRNA gene amplicon studies. Here, we compared MiSeq 2x300, MiSeq 2x500, and AVITI 2x300 by sequencing mock communities and field samples via a 'universal' (16S + 18S) rRNA gene amplicons (V4-V5 region) approach. All platforms recovered similar community patterns (Mantel r > 0.93), with no major differences in recovered lineages. MiSeq 2x500 showed ~4.5-fold higher index hopping (5.9 +/- 3.8% vs. 1.3 +/- 1.5%). For 18S, MiSeq 2x500, despite longer reads overlapping the 18S V4-V5 region, only marginally improved taxonomic classification (+0.7% on average) and ASV resolution (+/-1.3%). Meanwhile, all platforms similarly biased against 18S due to its greater length, which we demonstrate can be offset by a gel-based size selection, with no apparent taxonomic bias. Overall the platforms yield ecologically similar results. We highlight platform-specific advantages to help guide decision-making and challenges that can be addressed through dedicated bioinformatic or wet-lab approaches.

Title: Recovery of a distant large DNA virus from the genome sequencing of a fish leech
Authors: Manzano-Marin, A.; Willemsen, A.
Abstract: The leech gut is known to be a viral reservoir, where viruses can persist long-term and are protected from external influences. Therefore, leeches can serve as vectors for transmission of viral disease to susceptible hosts on which they prey. Nonetheless, viral diversity and virus-leech-host interactions remain largely unknown, with hitherto no research directed at identifying viruses that use leeches as their hosts. In the present study, we report the discovery of a novel large DNA virus (phylum Nucleocytoviricota) recovered from genomic sequencing data of the common fish leech Piscicola geometra (Linnaeus, 1761). Through genomic and phylogenetic analyses, we identify this lineage as highly divergent from currently known viruses, with [~]95% of its predicted protein-coding genes showing no identifiable homology with current databases. Whether the leech is a host of this virus or a vector that transmits it to fish species remains unclear. This work highlights the value of off-target sequence retrieval for discovering novel viral lineages and sets the stage for future studies directed towards the prevalence and biology of leech-associated large DNA viruses.

Title: Loss of macrodomain catalytic activity modulates Chikungunya virus dissemination and transmission potential in Aedes mosquitoes
Authors: Bardossy, E. S.; Bergmann, L.; Lacritick, A. H.; Nigg, J.; Correy, G. J.; Ashworth, A.; Fraser, J. S.; Saleh, M. C.
Abstract: Viral macrodomains are promising antiviral targets that counteract host ADP-ribosylation-mediated antiviral responses in mammals. However, their role in dual-host viruses within the mosquito vector remains largely unknown. Here, we investigated the role of the Chikungunya virus (CHIKV) nsP3 macrodomain catalytic activity by mutating the active-site asparagine 24 (N24). N24 mutant viruses rapidly selected for compensatory second-site mutations at aspartate 31 (D31) in mammalian Vero cells, while interferon-competent human cells favored reversion at position 24 instead, suggesting adaptive responses to macrodomain functional impairment. Catalytically inactive double-mutant viruses replicated poorly in interferon-competent human cells but comparably to wild-type in mosquito cells. In Aedes mosquitoes in vivo, macrodomain mutations modulated CHIKV replication and infectivity in a mutation-specific manner: one mutant reduced them while another enhanced them. Biochemical and structural analyses confirmed that these phenotypes arise in the context of a catalytically inactive macrodomain that retains ADP-ribose binding capacity, with D31 mutations lining the substrate exit path. These findings demonstrate that macrodomain catalytic activity modulates CHIKV dissemination and transmission potential in Aedes mosquitoes, revealing fundamental differences in host-dependent evolutionary advantage for a catalytically inactive viral enzyme.

Title: GFP-Tel1 is a marker of reversed replication forks that reveals constant fork backtracking during deoxyribonucleotide imbalance
Authors: Auboiron, M.; Samardak, K.; Barthe, A.; Pasero, P.; Pardo, B.; Moriel-Carretero, M.
Abstract: The apical kinase of the DNA Damage Response Tel1/ATM participates in at least three transactions key to the preservation of genome integrity: maintenance of a homeostatic telomere length, signaling of double strand breaks (DSB) in the DNA and a yet-poorly-defined contribution at reversed forks, a structure arising during problems in DNA replication. In a previous work, by tagging Tel1 in its N-terminus with yeast Enhanced Green Fluorescent Protein, we discovered that Tel1 forms foci in close proximity to the nuclear periphery in response to both chemically and enzymatically induced DSB. Here, we explore the determinants of this localization to the nuclear envelope, and we uncover that the subnuclear localization of the foci are a discriminant feature of Tel1's roles: foci forming in the interior of the nucleus mark reversed replication forks. In contrast, Tel1's function at telomeres are not tractable using GFP-Tel1 as a tool. Importantly, and in contrast to the prevalent notion that fork reversal is a phenomenon greatly restricted to metazoan replication forks, our characterization in the yeast S. cerevisiae of GFP-Tel1 at reversed forks allows us to propose a reconciling principle for how fork reversal contributes to tolerating replicative stress across evolutionary distant organisms.

Title: A harmonized functional reference framework for GBA1
Authors: Glendinning, S.; Aslanzadeh, V.; Clarke, M.; Sari, Y.; Zeneviciute, K.; Alvarez Jerez, P.; Lange, L. M.; Blauwendraat, C.; Global Parkinsons Genetics Program (GP2),  ; Lis, P.; Lohmann, K.; Klein, C.; Muqit, M.; Alessi, D. R.; Kudla, G.; Sammler, E.
Abstract: Systematic functional evidence is lacking for most rare GBA1 variants, limiting their interpretation in Gaucher disease (GD) and Parkinsons disease (PD). Here, we used a multiplexed assay of variant effect (MAVE) to generate a comprehensive atlas of lysosome-specific glucocerebrosidase (GCase) activity for more than 10400 GBA1 variants, covering 97 percent of all possible single-amino-acid substitutions. The atlas recapitulated known structural and biochemical determinants of glucocerebrosidase function and revealed concordance between functional impairment and expert-curated pathogenicity classifications. It identified significantly reduced activity in 94 of 186 reported variants of uncertain significance and revealed a quantitative relationship between functional impairment and GD disease severity. Integration with the Global PD Genetics Program associated greater variant-level functional impairment with earlier PD onset and higher PD odds ratios. Independent measurements of lysosomal glucocerebrosidase activity in stable cell lines expressing individual variants validated the MAVE results and resolved subtle functional deficits among variants close to the wild-type range, including established PD risk alleles. These findings provide a functional reference framework linking GBA1 variants to their molecular consequences and clinical phenotypes and demonstrate how comprehensive variant-effect maps can inform genetic interpretation and precision medicine.

Title: Brain disorder mechanisms and therapeutic targets identified from developmental, cell-specific gene regulation
Authors: Rohani, N.; Kovner, R.; Liu, Y.; Garcia Guerra, A.; Markati, T.; Kim, S.-W.; Kim, Y.; Xu, Q.; Wigdor, E. M.; Weiss, J.; Lalli, J. L.; Dong, S.; Nadkarni, A.; Wang, X.; Klei, L.; Pochareddy, S.; Speckhard-Pasque, D.; Dema, C.; Canosa, S.; Cho, H.; Deveau-French, A.; Gordon, G.; Griffiths, M.; Jaisingh, K.; Kachko, J.; Kathail, P.; Li, M.; Liang, D.; Ljungdahl, A.; Ma, S.; Makkar, R.; Page, N. F.; Sliby, A.-N.; Zhang, M.; Zhao, X.; Adle-Biassette, H.; Ye, C. J.; Brand, H.; Talkowski, M. E.; De Jager, P. L.; Werling, D. M.; Girgenti, M. J.; Rinaldi, C.; Roeder, K.; Devlin, B.; Sestan, N.; Sanders
Abstract: Genetic variation influences brain physiology and disease across cell types and development. We integrated whole-genome sequencing, bulk RNA sequencing, and single-nucleus multiome profiling from 231 human dorsolateral prefrontal cortex donors spanning six postconceptional weeks to 92 years. Across 24 brain-related traits, neurodevelopmental and psychiatric genetic risk was enriched in neuronal transcriptomic and chromatin profiles, whereas neurodegenerative risk was enriched in microglia. Thousands of expression, chromatin accessibility, and splicing quantitative trait loci revealed developmental and cell-type-specific regulatory effects. Colocalization linked multiple sclerosis risk to AHI1 expression in prenatal neurons and problematic alcohol use to GPX1 expression in postnatal glia. Leveraging dynamic cis-regulatory elements, we identified therapeutic candidates for haploinsufficient neurodevelopmental disorders, including a SOX5 enhancer whose CRISPR activation increased transcript and protein abundance. Together, these findings establish a publicly accessible genomic resource for resolving the developmental and cellular contexts of genetic risk and identifying therapeutic targets in the human brain.

Title: Pharmacolibrary: Interoperable executable models for PK, PD and PGx derived from published evidence
Authors: Kulhanek, T.; Denil, S.; Izmirli, B.; Ertaylan, G.
Abstract: Published pharmacological knowledge is distributed across heterogeneous scientific literature, databases, and computational models, making systematic reuse, comparison, and reproducibility difficult. We present Pharmacolibrary v26.11, a source-traceable resource that connects pharmacokinetic (PK), pharmacodynamic (PD), and pharmacogenomic (PGx) knowledge with executable models, simulations, and interactive visualizations. A multi-agent workflow combines LLM-assisted literature retrieval and extraction with deterministic validation, ontology mapping, provenance tracking, automated model generation, and rule-based review. The system transforms published evidence and extracted parameters into executable models across Modelica, FMI, SBML, MATLAB, and CellML and provides browser-based simulations for research and education. Preliminary evaluation indicates that decomposing literature extraction into multiple stages improves parameter recovery compared with single-pass extraction and that locally deployed open-weight models can provide performance that is at least comparable with frontier commercial LLMs. Pharmacolibrary provides a foundation for scalable, auditable curation of pharmacological knowledge and for connecting published evidence to reusable computational models across research, simulation, and education.

Title: Impact of culture medium on linezolid PK/PD activity against Staphylococcus aureus in a Hollow-Fiber infection model simulating cerebrospinal fluid exposure
Authors: Prebonnaud, N.; Chauzy, A.; Martin, I.; Adier, C.; Moreau, J.; Dahyot-Fizelier, C.; Marchand, S.
Abstract: This study aimed to assess the impact of the culture medium on the effect of linezolid against Staphylococcus aureus using Time-Kill curves (TKC) and Hollow-Fiber infection model (HFIM) by reproducing cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) PK profiles. TKC were performed over 30 h in Mueller-Hinton Broth (MHB), artificial CSF (aCSF) and human CSF (hCSF) at 0, 0.25, 1, 4 x linezolid MIC. Clinical CSF concentrations after 600 or 900 mg q12h and 900 mg q8h were reproduced in HFIM over 96 h in MHB and aCSF. A PK/PD model developed from MHB TKC and HFIM data was combined with hCSF TKC data to predict bacterial counts in HFIM in hCSF. In TKC, bacterial growth was slower in hCSF than MHB. Linezolid was bactericidal in MHB, but only bacteriostatic in hCSF. In aCSF, no growth and no decrease in bacterial counts was observed. In HFIM, bacterial growth was predicted to be also slower in hCSF than MHB. Linezolid at 900 mg q8h was needed to obtain a bactericidal effect in MHB, while 600 mg q12h would be sufficient in hCSF. Despite aCSF renewal in HFIM, no growth and no impact of the treatment was observed whatever linezolid dosing regimen. Bacterial growth and linezolid effect differed between media. MHB overestimated bacterial growth and suggested higher dosing regimen than hCSF, questioning its suitability for central nervous system infections in vitro studies. Using aCSF would be a promising alternative, although its composition requires optimisation to better reproduce bacterial growth and linezolid effect observed in hCSF.

Title: HyperGenie: A method for predicting enzymatic gene essentiality using hypergraph neural networks and genome-scale metabolic models
Authors: Ioannou, P.; Duta, I.; Verma, S.; Cicuta, P.; Lio, P.; Angione, C.
Abstract: Identifying essential genes in bacteria is crucial for drug discovery and synthetic biology. Genome-scale metabolic models (GEMs) evaluated via flux balance analysis remain standard, yet they rely on the often-invalid premise that mutant strains optimize for maximum growth. Recent machine learning approaches circumvent this limitation using random forests or graph neural networks on mass flow graphs (MFGs). However, data-driven tools like random forests discard network topology, while graph-based tools like MFGs decompose multi-component biochemical reactions into pairwise interactions, misrepresenting complex stoichiometry and limiting interpretability. Furthermore, existing methods remain largely uncharacterised in data-scarce regimes and cross-environmental conditions. Here, we introduce HyperGenie, a framework that integrates genome-scale metabolic models with directed hypergraph neural networks by representing metabolites as nodes and reactions as hyperedges. Operating directly on wild-type flux features, HyperGenie eliminates post-knockout optimality assumptions, achieves a 13% PR-AUC improvement over prior objective-dependent methods, and matches computationally demanding, state-of-the-art flux-sampling baselines. Using HyperGenie to guide targeted growth curve assays, we identified latent essentiality misannotations across three genes in the benchmark iML1515 dataset, which we then reconciled and validated experimentally via PCR. In data-scarce regimes, HyperGenie retained robust predictive performance (> 90% PR-AUC) when trained on as little as 40% of the data. To isolate the value of hypergraph message passing, we benchmarked HyperGenie against an independent-reaction multilayer perceptron (MLPGenie) across diverse nutrient environments and uptake rates, where HyperGenie's hypergraph inductive bias yielded consistent accuracy gains (> 2% in glucose; > 4% across six alternative carbon sources). Notably, HyperGenie exhibits robust zero-shot cross-nutrient generalization, accurately forecasting gain-of-essentiality phenotypes on novel carbon sources, though loss-of-essentiality remains challenging. Finally, coupling hypergraph representations with SHAP attribution provides actionable mechanistic insights into metabolic rewiring, establishing a data-efficient, interpretable platform for discovering novel antibiotic targets.

Title: Biphasic glycocalyx remodelling balances immune cell recruitment and tissue damage during influenza infection
Authors: Nabi, I. Z.; Ahmed, I. A.; Dodd, R.; Parkinson, J. E.; Johnson, A.; Ridley, A. J.; Zhang, Z.; Lowe, K. O.; Park, C.; Dalgarno, S.; Le Maistre, L. J.; Allen, J. E.; Li, J.-P.; Adamson, A. D. D.; Hussell, T.; Dyer, D. P.
Abstract: The endothelial glycocalyx is a glycan-rich barrier lining blood vessels that regulates immune cell recruitment, whose role in viral infection is unknown. Using a murine influenza model, we reveal that the lung endothelial glycocalyx undergoes coordinated biphasic remodelling: early shedding followed by substantial accumulation during peak immune activation. Genetic deletion of heparanase, the enzyme driving early glycocalyx shedding, reduced immune cell lung infiltration and improved host recovery. Conversely, using a new endothelial-specific glycocalyx depletion mouse model, we demonstrate that this glycocalyx accumulation actively limits immune cell recruitment and prevents excessive tissue damage. Together, these findings reveal that coordinated endothelial and immune cell glycocalyx remodelling is an active and previously unrecognised regulator of the balance between antiviral immune cell recruitment and tissue protection.

Title: Single-cell genomics reveals genomic and functional differentiation between freshwater and saline Achromatium populations.
Authors: Remy, P. H.; Ionescu, D.; Gros, O.; Heidig, S.-L.; Woyke, T.; Schiable, G.; Volland, J.-M.
Abstract: Giant sulfur bacteria of the genus Achromatium reportedly contain extensive genomic diversity within individual cells. Most genomic data (35 assemblies) come from freshwater populations obtained from Lake Stechlin, Germany, alongside four single-cell genomes from a salt marsh and saline mineral springs. Here, we characterize marine Achromatium from mangrove sediments in Guadeloupe and compare them with freshwater and saline references. Microscopy, elemental mapping, and Raman spectroscopy revealed calcium-rich inclusions, and intracellular elemental sulfur as previously described for this genus. Scanning electron microscopy revealed two cell-size morphotypes. We generated eleven single-cell, four mixed-cell, and two metagenomic binned assemblies from Guadeloupe mangrove. Divergent copies of conserved marker genes revealed extensive intracellular genomic diversity in individual cells of both morphotypes. Multigene phylogenies provided separation between freshwater references and most genomes from saline environments, including the Guadeloupe population. Gene presence-absence analyses further revealed differences in functional potential between Guadeloupe and Stechlin cells across five functional annotation categories including PFAM, KEGG Orthologs, and CAZymes. Differences in genes associated with osmotic regulation, ion transport, carbohydrate degradation, and secretion systems suggest variation in functional potential related to environmental adaptation, interactions and resource utilization. No significant differences in functional potential between Guadeloupe morphotypes were found. Together, these marine genomes reveal genomic and functional differentiation from freshwater populations and suggest that intracellular diversity does not erase freshwater/saline population boundaries.

Title: Three novel deep-branching orphan protist lineages from the marine rare biosphere
Authors: Pohl, N.; Mendez Sandin, M.; Tuovinen Nogerius, V.; Burki, F.
Abstract: Metabarcoding has transformed our view of marine protist communities, yet many sequences in environmental surveys are not assigned confident taxonomic identity. These taxonomically ambiguous sequences may include lineages that are not within any known eukaryotic supergroup, which we refer to here as orphan lineages. These orphan lineages matter beyond taxonomy-based community analyses, because they can help us understand early eukaryotic evolution. Here we used phylogenetic inferences and sequence similarity networks (SSNs) of long-read metabarcoding data of the ribosomal operon (18S-28S rDNA) to identify three novel phylum-level orphan lineages. We designate these lineages Deep Orphan Lineages 1-3 (DEEPOLs) and show that they are exclusively marine and part of the rare biosphere, yet ecologically distinct: DEEPOL1 is a cosmopolitan generalist, DEEPOL2 a conditionally rare lineage capable of local polar blooms, and DEEPOL3 a non-polar lineage with a tendency toward the dark ocean. For DEEPOL2, lineage-specific digital PCR (dPCR) combined with catalyzed reporter deposition fluorescence in situ hybridization (CARD-FISH) provides the first in situ visualization of these cells, revealing small, flagellated, and morphologically inconspicuous protists. Together, our results show that substantial diversity remains hidden among rare lineages, and that long-read sequencing combined with targeted molecular and microscopy approaches offers a first step toward linking orphan sequences to organisms and their evolution and ecological roles.

Title: Quiescent Cells Exhibit a Senescence-Like Secretory Phenotype
Authors: Rocha, A.; Kalekar, R.; Sedivy, J. M.; Neretti, N.
Abstract: Cellular quiescence is traditionally considered a reversible state of cell cycle arrest, distinct from senescence, which is associated with a characteristic senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP). However, whether quiescent cells exhibit a comparable secretory program remains poorly understood. Here, we identify and characterize a Quiescence-Associated Secretory Phenotype (QASP) by integrating single-cell and bulk RNA sequencing datasets from human fibroblasts and preadipocytes. We find that quiescent cells exhibit increased expression of genes encoding inflammatory mediators and extracellular matrix-associated proteins, with substantial overlap between the QASP and SASP. This transcriptional program is highly heterogeneous, varying across cell types, quiescence induction methods, and environmental oxygen levels. In particular, contact inhibition induces a stronger inflammatory signature than serum withdrawal in several cellular contexts. Multiplexed cytokine profiling demonstrated active secretion of inflammatory mediators, including IL-1{beta}, IL-6, IL-15, and CCL2, in quiescent fibroblasts, with secretion levels varying by induction method and generally higher following contact inhibition than serum withdrawal. Analysis of single-cell transcriptomic data from human lung tissue further reveals increased QASP-associated gene expression in idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF), particularly in myofibroblasts, linking this phenotype to inflammatory signaling and extracellular matrix remodeling. Together, these findings identify the QASP as a context-dependent secretory program that shares features with the SASP and may contribute to inflammatory signaling and extracellular matrix remodeling in both physiological and pathological conditions.

Title: GCase deficiency impairs uptake of α-synuclein-loaded ectosome by astrocytes
Authors: Jacquemyn, J.; Rodrigues, D. U.; Iftikhar, E.; Chang, J.; Soubannier, V.; Durcan, T. M.; Ioannou, M. S.
Abstract: Parkinson's disease (PD) involves the prion-like propagation of -synuclein. One mechanism for the spread of -synuclein between neurons in PD is ectosomes. But PD is a multicellular disorder in which astrocytes also play a critical role. How astrocytes take up ectosomes and whether this is affected in PD is unclear. Here we show that GCase-deficiency, as occurs in PD, impairs astrocytic uptake of neuron-derived ectosomes containing -synuclein. The defect in ectosome uptake by astrocytes is driven by compromised macropinocytosis and can be rescued by reducing glucosylceramides or restoring lysosomal function. These findings identify sphingolipid metabolism as a key regulator of ectosome uptake by primary and iPSC-derived astrocytes. They also support a shift from the uptake and clearance of -synuclein by astrocytes in health, towards the transmission of -synuclein pathology towards neurons in PD.

Title: Maternal obesity disrupts glucose oxidation and mitochondrial fission in the myometrium at term gestation
Authors: Prifti, K. K.; Rich, J. L.; Giecek, A. M.; Gill, R. M.; Pietka, T. A.; Beatty, W. L.; Frolova, A. I.
Abstract: Women with obesity experience delayed spontaneous labor onset, slow labor progression, and elevated risk of labor dystocia, but the underlying mechanisms are poorly understood. We previously established a mouse model of diet-induced obesity that exhibits decreased uterine contractility, labor dystocia, and elevated fatty acids in the myometrium. Here, we used this model to determine how maternal obesity affects energy production and mitochondrial homeostasis in the myometrium at term. Myometrium tissue and myometrial smooth muscle cells from diet-induced obese mice at term showed decreased pyruvate utilization, inhibition of glucose oxidation, and disruption of mitochondrial fission and mitophagy. Treatment with medium-chain fatty acids in both murine and human primary myometrial cells resulted in significant decreases in abundance of mitochondrial fission proteins. Finally, mitochondrial spare capacity in human myometrial cells decreased with body mass index of the patient providing the cells. Taken together, these findings indicate that fatty acid accumulation dysregulates energy metabolism and mitochondrial homeostasis in the myometrium and may contribute to dysfunctional labor in women with obesity.

Title: Vertical transmission and community turnover in seed-borne microbiomes: lessons from an aMAIZEing model system
Authors: Henaut Jacobs, S.; Sangi, S.; Matos, J. P.; Chaves Ribeiro, R.; Petroceli-Mota, G.; da Costa Rodrigues, B.; Jario de Lima, V.; Kamphorst, S. H.; Alves de Oliveira, U.; Nunes-da-Fonseca, R.; Lopes Olivares, F.; S. Etienne, R.; M. Venancio, T.
Abstract: The seed microbiome represents a specialized ecological niche, governed by assembly processes that are only partially coupled to the surrounding soil community. While environmental recruitment and vertical transmission from the maternal plant are both recognized sources of seed-associated microorganisms, the mechanisms that determine their relative contributions and whether these contributions shift across generations remain poorly understood. Here, we used long-read metagenomic sequencing to track seed-borne bacterial community dynamics across a founding seed pool and two subsequent generations in two divergent maize (Zea mays L.) varieties exposed to contrasting organic and mineral fertilisation regimes. We recovered 112 medium- or high-quality metagenome-assembled genomes and combined MAG-level taxonomic and functional analyses with genus-level community profiling to characterize persistence and turnover dynamics within the seed microbiome. While soil taxonomic diversity was high, seed-associated communities showed a near-complete compositional disconnect from soil-dominant assemblages taxa, with a persistent Firmicutes core maintained across generations, consistent with vertical transmission. Priority effects remain a possible explanation for these patterns but were not directly tested. Genus-level source attribution suggested greater environmental recruitment under organic fertilization, with more diverse soil communities and a stronger contribution from the preceding seed generation under mineral fertilization. Seed-associated MAGs also carried genes associated with plant growth-promoting potential, although these detections could not be consistently linked to specific transmission routes. In contrast, maize genotype had no detectable effect on seed microbiome composition. Intergenerational persistence and environmental recruitment jointly shape seed-derived communities under contrasting fertilization regimes. Their relative contributions remain inferred from taxonomic overlap, and the effects of microbial source-pool diversity cannot be separated from the accompanying differences in soil chemistry in this design.

Title: The pangenome of the Arctic picoeukaryote Micromonas polaris resolves cryptic ecotypes and identifies a polar-specific gene repertoire
Authors: Jackson, V. L. N.; Harrison, K.; Derelle, E.; Chambouvet, A.; Lovejoy, C.; Monier, A.
Abstract: Micromonas polaris is the dominant picoeukaryote of the Arctic Ocean, where it sustains primary production across habitats from sea ice to open water to the subsurface chlorophyll maximum. How a single species maintains this ecological breadth has remained unclear. Standard phylogenetic markers such as 18S rRNA are nearly invariant within M. polaris and conceal any internal genomic heterogeneity the species may possess. Here we present a pangenome of 14 M. polaris strains spanning the Arctic basin, integrated with Tara Oceans metagenomes, that resolves the species into two diverged ecotypes invisible to 18S rRNA but recovered consistently by prp8, genome-wide SNPs, ANI, and orthogroup-based phylogenies. The two ecotypes coexist sympatrically, with one lineage consistently enriched deeper in the water column across the basin. M. polaris carries 990 polar-specific hierarchical orthogroups absent from temperate Micromonas, organised around one-carbon metabolism, endocytosis, transmembrane transport, and photo-oxidative stress response. Several components show phylogenetic signatures of horizontal acquisition from co-occurring marine taxa. Atlantification is bringing temperate Micromonas into Arctic margins seasonally, but the polar night likely limits their year-round persistence. M. polaris and its polar-specific toolkit appear positioned to persist through the dark season, suggesting Arctic margins will undergo seasonal turnover rather than stable replacement.

Title: KORUS: probabilistic ancestry inference beyond variant calls
Authors: Warren, R. L.; Coombe, L.; Birol, I.
Abstract: Ancestry inference typically relies on variant calling and predefined population labels. We present KORUS, a probabilistic framework that infers ancestry from sequencing-derived k-mer representations constructed using ancestry-informative reference variants and encoded in Bloom filters, without requiring explicit variant calls for query genomes. KORUS separates genomic feature representation from ancestry decoding, enabling supervised classification, fractional ancestry inference, and unsupervised population structure discovery within a unified framework. Reference models were constructed from 643 genomes from the 1000 Genomes Project and the Simons Genome Diversity Project. Evaluation on an independent cohort of 22 whole-genome sequencing samples, with comparisons to ntRoot, SNVstory, and ADMIXTURE, showed recovery of continental-scale population structure, with supervised classification accuracy of 72.7-81.8% and ancestry-fraction concordance of R2 = 0.844-0.993 relative to ADMIXTURE and R2 = 0.665-0.983 relative to ntRoot. Ancestry estimates were consistent across alternative k-mer representations. Analyses of ancient human and archaic hominin genomes demonstrated that probabilistic projections quantify affinity to the learned feature space rather than necessarily indicating modern continental ancestry. KORUS provides a unified approach to ancestry inference directly from sequencing-derived representations and is freely available under the GPLv3 license at https://github.com/BirolLab/korus.

Title: Policy-Enforced Genomic Repositories and Institutional Data Governance for African Pathogen Surveillance with UbuntuBio
Authors: Tetteh, A. S.; Salami, R. O.; Ansah, R. O.; Buabeng, K. B.; Agyenkwa-Mawuli, K.; Baah, D.; Sarpong, K.; Rathod, A.; Hodgson, J. N. O.; Akorful, R. A. A.; Miah, B. D.-g.; Ayimadu, A. A.; Amoako, E. K.; Kumordzi, S. M.; Abakah, A.; Tawiah-Yingar, N. Y.; Akakpo, D.; Adade, R.; Okekale, E. S.; Senyo, M. T.
Abstract: Research centers curating pathogen sequence cohorts often operate under constrained bandwidth, multi-institutional data-sharing agreements, and strict biosafety requirements. Global public archives keep released sequences permanently open, external viral portals enforce terms outside local institutional custody, and standard Git Large File Storage (LFS) duplicates identical binaries across repositories without validating taxonomy or geography. We present UbuntuBio (v1.0.0), a Git-native, policy-enforced genomic repository platform deployed at https://ubuntubio.org and developed at the West African Centre for Cell Biology of Infectious Pathogens (WACCBIP), University of Ghana. UbuntuBio integrates four mechanisms under a single storage root: (1) bare Git repositories storing dataset cards, sample sheets, and approximately 130-byte LFS pointers backed by prefix-sharded SHA-256 content-addressed storage (CAS) with visibility-scoped wire deduplication; (2) a four-phase commit pipeline recoverable via cross-plane reconciliation that enforces 55 African Union country codes against offline Natural Earth polygons, core MIxS-derived fields, Taxon 9606 rejection, and server-keyed targeted human-marker screening identically across HTTP commits and Git pre-receive hooks; (3) institutional custody controls combining Data Use Agreements (DUAs), revocable 900-second RS256 capability tokens, key rotation, tamper-evident hash-chained logs, and externally anchorable RS256 audit checkpoints; and (4) an embedded SQLite WAL and FTS5 catalog filtered by access tier. In single-node evaluation, UbuntuBio classified 18/18 policy boundary fixtures consistently across Python, Git, and HTTP paths; showed 0/265,157 false cross-matches on 21/22 RefSeq pathogen sequences (while cross-matching Candida albicans 18S rDNA at 0.113% and Chlorocebus sabaeus Alu repeats in ENA stool reads, confirming targeted marker detection rather than verified human DNA decontamination); matched conditional uniform (n = 2,000; 200-seed 0.01% convergence 19.0% vs. 18.13% expected) and interior (n = 1,000) detection theory while detecting all spike-ins at [≥] 0.5% (30/30); halved two-repository disk usage on 613.83 MiB Nigerian E. coli runs; passed 27/27 structured-filter correctness checks over 10,000 biosamples and reached graded NDCG@10 = 0.920 on independent free-text BM25 queries with zero private leaks; and recovered cleanly across seven injected phase-transition faults.

Title: Measuring Phylogenetic Information Content Based on Clade Support
Authors: Nylander, J. A. A.
Abstract: Phylogenetic information content is often understood as the degree to which data lend support to hypotheses about the monophyly of clades. This is most commonly expressed in terms of clade support, typically estimated by resampling techniques such as the bootstrap and the jackknife. Here, I discuss how to summarize this aspect of data quality. I show that raw bootstrap or jackknife proportions are unsuitable for this purpose and instead suggest a logarithmic transformation, which can be interpreted as translating the clade support values to the number of characters expected to give the same resampling proportion in parsimony analysis of a homoplasy-free data matrix. The distribution of the number of these "supporting characters" and descriptive statistics derived from this distribution, such as the mean (Mean Character Support, or MCS) and its standard deviation, provide powerful summaries of the quality of the underlying data set. I demonstrate for both empirical and simulated data sets that MCS accurately reflects information content, and that some popular alternative measures of data quality (the ensemble consistency index, the ensemble retention index, data decisiveness and the total support index) do not. Unlike most other measures of data quality, MCS can be applied to trees resulting from a range of alternative phylogenetic methods, including parsimony, distance and maximum likelihood approaches.

Title: Tissue-specific biotransformation shapes the toxicity of 6PPD-quinone in fish cell models
Authors: Toso, A.; Franco, M. E.; Masset, T.; Dudefoi, W.; Nair, P.; Goncalves, S.; Bergmann, A. J.; Vermeirssen, E.; Breider, F.; Ferrari, B. J. D.; Peng, H.; Schirmer, K.
Abstract: Acute mortality of salmonids exposed to urban runoff has been linked to 6PPD-quinone (6PPD-Q), a transformation product of the widely used tire antiozonant 6PPD. However, the cellular processes underlying 6PPD-Q toxicity remain poorly understood. Beyond the well-documented differences in species sensitivity, here we determined tissue-specific responses in rainbow trout (Oncorhynchus mykiss) cell lines exposed to 6PPD-Q: brain-derived cells (RTBrain) were more sensitive than gill-derived cells (RTgill-W1). To unravel the cellular mechanisms underlying such differential responses, we combined time-resolved 6PPD-Q cellular depletion kinetics, targeted biotransformation product (BTP) profiling, transporter inhibition experiments, and cytotoxicity assessments. Both cell models biotransformed 6PPD-Q, but RTBrain displayed a 6.6-fold higher cellular clearance rate than RTgill-W1. Chemical profiling identified four BTPs, including para-aryl-OH-6PPD-Q, which was selectively toxic to RTBrain but not RTgill-W1 cells. These findings reveal tissue-specific toxicokinetics as potential determinants of differential 6PPD-Q toxicity even within the same species. More broadly, this integrated approach highlights the importance of considering biotransformation and the production of biologically active transformation products when assessing susceptibility to emerging contaminants.

Title: Three-Dimensional Refractive Index Patterns Distinguish CD57-Defined Subsets of Human Memory T Cells
Authors: Ryu, D.; Dao, K. P.; Kim, K. H.; Cho, H.; Kim, Y. S.; Ahn, D.; Min, H.-S.; Kim, G.; Shin, E.-C.; Park, Y.
Abstract: Distinguishing T-cell subsets is important for characterizing immune differentiation, but label-free classification is challenging because closely related subsets have overlapping biophysical properties. We combined holotomography with a three-dimensional convolutional neural network to classify primary human T cells from their refractive index (RI) tomograms. Fluorescence-activated cell sorting defined four reference populations: CD4+, naive CD8+, and CD57- and CD57+ memory CD8+ T cells. The FishNet-inspired classifier achieved 97.04% accuracy in a cell-level held-out test of 270 cells. Dedicated binary classifiers achieved 97.70% accuracy for naive versus CCR7- memory CD8+ cells and 94.44% for CD57- versus CD57+ memory CD8+ cells. Although the memory subsets overlapped in whole-cell descriptors, their volumetric RI patterns supported classification. These findings establish a basis for investigating intrinsic optical phenotypes associated with CD57-defined T-cell differentiation.

Title: A Dysregulated Peripheral Immune Landscape Favors the Expansion of Epstein-Barr Virus positive Age-Associated B Cells in Multiple Sclerosis
Authors: Yoon, L.; Chung, S. S.; Thebault, S.; Breville, G.; Munoz, L. J. C.; MacMullen, L. N.; Gu, A.; Yang, T. H. N.; He, S.; Claiborne, D. T.; Srivastava, A.; Xian, R. R.; Ambinder, R. F.; Bar-Or, A.; Soldan, S. S.; Lieberman, P. M.
Abstract: Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) is a major risk factor for multiple sclerosis (MS), but the underlying mechanisms are not yet known. Here, we use single-cell RNA sequencing coupled with targeted EBV transcript enrichment to characterize host immune and viral transcriptional dynamics following EBV ex vivo infection of PBMCs from people with active MS compared to healthy controls (HC). Early responses to EBV were dominated by differences in monocyte and NK cells, including EBV transcripts in monocytes prior to ex vivo infection. At later time points, expansion of EBV-infected age-associated B-cells (ABCs) and increased expression of T-cell exhaustion- associated markers were elevated in MS. EBV-infected ABCs were deregulated for EBV lytic genes and cellular pathways associated with interferon-alpha responses, antigen processing and Toll-like receptor signaling. Together, these findings define an MS-associated inflammatory immune state and dysfunctional response that favors the formation of pathogenic EBV-infected ABCs.

Title: In vivo crosslinking and cryo-EM analyses suggest a revised model of conjugative pilus biogenesis
Authors: Bloch, M.; Vadakeppat, A.; Zenezini Chiozzi, R.; Thalassinos, K.; Waksman, G.
Abstract: Bacterial conjugation requires elaboration of a conjugative pilus by membrane-embedded transport machineries known as Type IV Secretion Systems (T4SSs). Recent structural findings suggested a model of conjugative pilus biogenesis in which the pilus is assembled from the VirB6-base of the T4SS Stalk, while the VirB5-apex is projected at the pilus tip. In this study, we show that in vivo crosslinking of these two Stalk segments within the R388 T4SS has only a modest effect on conjugative transfer efficiency, inconsistent with them separating during pilus elaboration. Combined with cryo-electron microscopy analyses of the homologous pKM101 T4SS, this leads us to propose a revised model, in which the sixfold-symmetrical inner membrane complex of the T4SS serves directly as a base for assembly of the fivefold-symmetrical pilus. The resulting symmetry mismatch is resolved by the sequential incorporation of pilus subunits at a continuously repositioning gap at the base of the nascent pilus. This revised model answers the long-standing question of how T4SSs accommodate a central symmetry mismatch during a crucial process of bacterial conjugation underpinning horizontal gene transfer.

Title: In the non-canonical NF-κB pathway, binding of the initiating kinase NIK to the pathway's target, p100, serves a nonenzymatic "licensing" role
Authors: Liang, X.; Scheerer, D.; Bogdanov, K.; Gardarsky, M.; Amballa, C.; Wang, T.; Morgenstern, D.; Goldsmith, M.; Reichmann, D.; Haran, G.; Wallach, D.
Abstract: The non-canonical NF-{kappa}B pathway plays pivotal roles in adaptive immunity. It is initiated by NIK-mediated phosphorylation of IKK1, which phosphorylates p100 and promotes processing of newly synthesized p100. However, IKK1 can also be activated by other kinases to mediate distinct functions. Why IKK1-induced p100 processing occurs efficiently downstream of NIK but not of other kinases is unknown. Here, we show that whereas pre-existing p100 can be phosphorylated by IKK1 without NIK, phosphorylation of newly synthesized p100 critically depends on additional non-enzymatic functions of NIK's C-terminal portion. NIK binds IKK1 and restrains its kinase activity, while its binding to p100 enhances p100 phosphorylation. Single-molecule FRET spectroscopy and XL-MS revealed that the C-terminal region of p100 adopts a folded-back conformation and undergoes structural rearrangement upon NIK binding, likely accounting for this enhancement. Thus, NIK not only initiates the pathway but also dictates its specificity through binding to its downstream substrate.

Title: Phosphorylated Pol II CTD supports histone hitchhiking during transcription elongation
Authors: Bi, L.; Tong, Y.; Yang, Y.; Wang, X.; Li, Y.; Chen, X.; Xu, Y.
Abstract: Transcription requires RNA polymerase II (Pol II) to disrupt nucleosomes while preserving displaced histones for reuse. How these histones remain available as the polymerase advances is incompletely understood. Here we combine optical trapping and fluorescence imaging to follow Pol II-nucleosome encounters in a simplified mammalian elongation system. Displaced histone particles frequently move with the advancing elongation complex, a behavior termed histone hitchhiking. Phosphorylation of the Pol II C-terminal domain (CTD) reduces nucleosomal blocking and supports histone retention during carriage. Structural predictions suggest that phosphorylated CTD repeats engage basic histone surfaces through variable, charge-complementary contacts. Carried particles can subsequently transfer to upstream DNA, and a broader combination of elongation factors increases upstream transfer. Complexes already carrying a histone particle show increased blocking at a second nucleosome. Other encounters leave one particle on upstream DNA while another moves with the complex, suggesting that transfer of one particle may enable capture and carriage of the next during successive nucleosome traversal. These observations support a model in which reversible contacts with the phosphorylated CTD help Pol II capture and carry histone particles as they dissociate from downstream DNA, keeping them available for upstream transfer and subsequent chaperone-assisted reassembly. Our findings extend the role of the Pol II CTD beyond factor recruitment to histone handling, linking nucleosome traversal to histone preservation.

Title: Large scale CRISPR genome engineering reveal principles of single nucleotide microhomology in precision editing
Authors: Shi, X.; Li, C.; Li, J.; Liu, Y.; Wu, Q.
Abstract: The CRISPR/Cas9 system has emerged as a revolutionary tool with diverse applications in genome engineering; however, the role of nanoscale hydrogen bonds between single nucleotides in precision editing remains unknown. Here we systematically compared A-rich and G-rich PAM-recognizing Cas9 editors through comprehensive analyses of ~37,000 targeting sites with about half million libraries of ~0.36 billion types of editing outcomes. We showed that the A-rich Cas9 editors exhibit stronger editing outcome predictability in comparison with the conventional Cas9 editor of the G-rich PAM. In addition, the A-rich Cas9 editors induce a higher frequency of staggered cleavages, resulting in predictable editing with donor-independent templated insertions. Moreover, we identified distinct DNA sequence motifs for predictable insertions with the A-rich Cas9 editors. In particular, we revealed single nucleotides at the -4 position as MMEJ microhomologies in precision engineering via two or three hydrogen bonds with A-rich or G-rich PAM, respectively. Furthermore, we found that PolQ plays a key role in enhanced random insertions. Finally, we developed a discrete-space diffusion model CRIfuser of deep learning for predicting editing outcomes with staggered cleavage. Together, these findings establish PAM-dependent cleavage geometry as a tunable determinant of Cas9 editing outcomes and provide a framework for predictive and precision genome engineering.

Title: Development of synthetic genetic arrays for studying interactions between the mitochondrial and nuclear genomes
Authors: Schneider, K. L.; Braam, S.; Hao, X.; Hanzen, S.; Ott, M.; Cvijovic, M.; Nyström, T.
Abstract: Mitochondria, the central axis of metabolism and energy transformation has emerged as a focal point for understanding the aging process and a plethora of human diseases. Yet, how the mitochondrial and nuclear genomes communicate is still unclear. This work aims to allow the analysis of such crosstalk by developing a genome-wide platform for studying genetic interactions between the mitochondrial and nuclear genomes. Using yeast as a model system in which mitochondrial homoplasmy and stable alterations in the mitochondrial genome can be generated by biolistic bombardment, we created a genome-wide library of yeast cells carrying nuclear deletions and temperature-sensitive mutations together with a superfolder-GFP reporter for the expression of the mitochondrial-encoded COX2 gene. Using this approach, we found links between nuclear-encoded processes and mitochondrial gene expression not previously anticipated, including a requirement for genes involved in MVB (multivesicular body) sorting/RIM signaling, vesicle trafficking/glycosylation, polarity, and peroxisome biogenesis, for maintaining mitochondrial COX2 expression. In contrast, defects in the autophagy machineries, ribosome biogenesis, and nuclear transcription and chromatin organization resulted in increased expression of COX2. While reduced COX2 expression correlated with a reduced expression of the nuclear-encoded TOM70 gene in mutants defect in mitochondrial functions, expression of the mitochondrial and nuclear genes responded differently to defects in cytoplasmic ribosome biogenesis and autophagy. When creating the COX2 expression library, we also found that cells devoid of mitochondrial DNA rely on the Rim101 signaling pathway, and many of its auxiliary regulatory factors, to maintain fitness. As mutations in the Rim101 signaling pathway also caused down-regulation of COX2 expression, it appears that Rim101 signaling is central for maintaining proper control of mitochondrial function. We believe the approach will allow for future genome-wide studies on how nuclear-encoded processes influence the translation, protein folding, and processing of mitochondria-encoded genes.

Title: Single-molecule tracking in the psychrophile Psychrobacter cryohalolentis reveals heat-shock-induced changes in ClpX dynamics
Authors: Nery, E. T.; Sui, Y.; Mäkelä, J.
Abstract: Psychrophilic organisms display a series of physiological adaptations which enable them to thrive in cold environments, yet the dynamics of these processes in living cells remain largely unexplored. Here, we establish super-resolution microscopy and single-molecule tracking (SMT) in the cold-adapted bacterium Psychrobacter cryohalolentis, enabling the investigation of protein dynamics in vivo at high spatiotemporal resolution. For controlled expression of HaloTag fusions in this organism, we developed an inducible plasmid expression system based on a galactose-inducible promoter. As a proof of concept, we followed the AAA+ unfoldase ClpX during steady-state growth and heat shock. At 22 {degrees}C, ClpX diffused as a single population with a media apparent diffusion coefficient of 0.25 m2/s, suggesting that most molecules reside in large complexes. A shift to 32 {degrees}C, above the growth maximum of this strain, broadened the mobility distribution, increasing both slow and fast populations, and transiently redistributed ClpX towards the cell periphery. During recovery the fast population returned to baseline within 5 min, whereas the slow population remained elevated for at least 30 min, suggesting that the two populations reflect distinct processes. SMT in a psychrophilic bacterium thus opens new possibilities to study how cold-adapted microorganisms respond to environmental change at the molecular level.

Title: Sidetrak: a de novo-designed miniprotein targets the kinesin-1 coiled-coil stalk to inhibit MAP7 binding and disrupt mitochondrial transport
Authors: Cross, J. A.; Bristow, S. A.; Babuji, T.; Woolfson, D.; Dodding, M. P.
Abstract: The coiled-coil domains of cytoskeletal motors contain regulatory surfaces that offer largely unexploited targets for manipulating intracellular transport. The microtubule-associated protein MAP7 promotes kinesin-1 motor activity, binding a coiled-coil surface that overlaps the TPR docking site (TDS), a regulatory interface involved in autoinhibition. Starting from an AlphaFold3 model of this relatively feature-poor surface, we used BoltzGen to design Sidetrak, a 36-amino acid miniprotein that binds kinesin-1 with nanomolar affinity. Binding requires the TDS and is abolished by mutation of the predicted Sidetrak interface, supporting the modelled local geometry of the targeted coiled-coil region. Sidetrak inhibits MAP7 binding, reduces MAP7-dependent kinesin-1 recruitment to microtubules in cells and causes perinuclear redistribution of mitochondria, a kinesin-1 cargo. Sidetrak binds all three kinesin-1 heavy-chain paralogues, and quantitative interaction proteomics revealed selective association with endogenous kinesin-1 complexes and associated cargo adaptors. These findings demonstrate selective disruption of a motor-MAP interaction by a de novo-designed protein and highlight regulatory coiled-coil surfaces as targets for manipulating intracellular transport. Beyond providing a means to manipulate intracellular transport, this work illustrates the potential of de novo protein design to test structural models of protein interfaces and probe endogenous protein networks to uncover underlying cellular mechanisms.

Title: Genetic nurture and shared environmental effects across cognitive, educational, and mental health outcomes
Authors: Lin, Y.; Ayorech, Z.; Kawakami, K.; Keser, E.; Eley, T. C.; Rimfeld, K.; Malanchini, M.; Plomin, R.
Abstract: Genetic nurture, in which parental genotype predicts offspring outcomes independent of offspring genotype, operates at the between-family level, corresponding to the shared environmental effect (C) in the classical twin design. Genetic nurture represents a portion of C captured by parental genotype. The link between genetic nurture and C has not been systematically quantified across multiple trait domains. Using 2559 families with genotyped parents and 6710 twin pairs, we estimated genetic nurture using polygenic scores (PGS) and C using the twin design for 40 educational, cognitive, and anthropometric outcomes from age 7 to 26, and for 8 psychopathology symptoms at age 26. Although genetic nurture effects were small, the largest effects were observed for educational outcomes, followed by cognitive abilities, and then psychopathology symptoms. C followed the same pattern. Across eight trait domains, the correlation between genetic nurture and C was 0.68. However, psychopathology outcomes also showed relatively low PGS prediction, which creates a ceiling for estimated genetic nurture. In proportion to PGS prediction, psychopathology showed as much genetic nurture as educational outcomes. Why does psychopathology show genetic nurture despite showing no C? Why is psychopathology PGS prediction so low? We suggest that nonadditive genetic variance could explain both.

Title: A large-scale multi-omics study of cortical miRNA dysregulation in Alzheimer's disease
Authors: Pishva, E.; Kouhsar, M.; Aslam, M. M.; Schilling, M.; Harvey, J.; Soanes, D.; Imm, J.; Thomson, G.; Pegoraro, G.; Weymouth, L.; MacBean, L. F.; Wheildon, G.; Dobricic, V.; Tiane, A.; Schepers, M.; Koetsier, J.; Laroche, V.; Vanmierlo, T.; van den Hove, D.; Troakes, C.; Al-Sarraj, S.; Parkkinen, L.; Mill, J.; Creese, B.; Smith, A. R.; Bertram, L.; Lunnon, K.
Abstract: MicroRNAs regulate gene expression, but their roles in Alzheimer's disease pathology and downstream molecular changes remain incompletely characterized. We integrated cortical small RNA-sequencing data from seven datasets across six postmortem cohorts comprising 1,738 individuals with transcriptomic, proteomic, genetic, and single-nucleus data. Meta-analysis of 405 microRNAs identified 16 associated with advanced and four with intermediate neurofibrillary tangle pathology, with miR-132-3p significant in both comparisons. Five microRNAs (miR-132-3p, miR-212-3p, miR-212-5p, miR-146b-5p, miR-3200-3p) showed evidence of mediating associations between target mRNA and protein expression and tau pathology. Consensus co-expression network analysis linked the miR-132/212 family to opposing neuronal/synaptic and oligodendrocyte/myelination-related programmes. Mediated targets were enriched among tau-associated differentially expressed genes across glial cell types, particularly astrocytes. Inferred cell-type regulatory networks further highlighted miR-132-3p and miR-146b as recurrent hubs. These findings prioritize a restricted set of cortical microRNAs and associated neuronal and glial molecular programmes for mechanistic investigation in Alzheimer's disease.

Title: The genetic regulation of thyroid hormones on immune and hematopoietic homeostasis: an integrative Mendelian randomization and colocalization study
Authors: Ansah, E. O.; Fosu, K.; Adu, I. K.; Lanidune, A.; Gyabaa, E. A.; Antwi, D.; Bonsu, P. B.; Kyei, F.
Abstract: Background: Hematological traits are closely linked to immune and inflammatory processes implicated in thyroid dysfunction. Although observational studies have reported associations between blood-cell traits and thyroid disorders, whether these relationships reflect causal mechanisms remains unclear. Methods: We performed a two-sample Mendelian randomization (MR) analysis to investigate the causal effects of 25 genetically predicted hematological traits on hypothyroidism and hyperthyroidism using genome-wide association study (GWAS) summary statistics from the UK Biobank. Independent single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) were selected as instrumental variables and harmonized before analysis. Causal estimates were primarily obtained using the inverse-variance weighted (IVW) method and complemented by MR-Egger, weighted median, weighted mode, simple mode, MR-PRESSO, and MR-robust adjusted profile score (MR-RAPS) analyses. Sensitivity analyses assessed heterogeneity, horizontal pleiotropy, reverse causality, and directionality. Significant findings were replicated using independent FinnGen summary statistics. Multivariable MR and Bayesian colocalization analyses were subsequently performed to investigate significant associations further. Results: Among the 25 hematological traits evaluated, eosinophil-related traits showed the strongest associations with hypothyroidism. Genetically predicted eosinophil counts were associated with an increased risk of hypothyroidism (odds ratio [OR] = 1.25, 95% confidence interval [CI]: 1.11-1.42, P = 4.0E-04, FDR = 0.002), while combined eosinophil-basophil counts showed similar associations (OR = 1.24, 95% CI: 1.10-1.40, P = 5.0E-04, FDR = 0.002). These findings were consistently replicated in FinnGen and remained significant after adjustment for basophil traits, body mass index, and C-reactive protein in multivariable MR analyses. No significant associations were observed for hyperthyroidism. Bayesian colocalization identified strong evidence of a shared genetic signal at the rs653178 locus on chromosome 12 (PP.H4 = 0.994). Conclusions: This study provides genetic evidence supporting a causal role for eosinophil-related traits in hypothyroidism susceptibility. The consistency of the findings across complementary Mendelian randomization approaches, independent replication, multivariable analyses, and colocalization strengthens the evidence that eosinophil-related immune mechanisms contribute to hypothyroidism susceptibility.

Title: Coordinated remodeling of NAD⁺ metabolic networks across the lifespan of Caenorhabditis elegans
Authors: Alshaheeb, A. A.; Yahia, M. S.; Argento, I. A.; Sadler, J. J.; Spence, A. M.; Johnson, S. V.; Ritter, E. R.; Munoz, I.; Dennis, K. N.; Breidor, B. C.; Olayiwola, E.; Laremore, T. N.; McReynolds, M. R.
Abstract: Changes in the metabolic network that sustain NAD+ during aging remain poorly understood. Analysis of steady state levels is insufficient to reveal whether biosynthetic or consumption pathways are perturbed or preserved. Here, we address this gap in understanding by integrating metabolomics, proteomics, gene-expression profiling, and stable-isotope tracing across the Caenorhabditis elegans adult lifespan. NAD abundance increases with age despite reductions in selected biosynthetic components. Tracing reveals reduced mid-adult incorporation of nicotinamide and nicotinic acid into NAD, alongside declining nicotinamide riboside abundance and loss of detectable nicotinic acid-derived labeling into this precursor. Early mitochondrial Complex I remodeling accompanies sustained changes in redox and energetic indices. Disruption of NAD-consuming or salvage enzymes reduces reproduction and lifespan, whereas precursor supplementation provides no longevity benefit under the conditions tested. Together, these findings reveal that NAD accumulation can coexist with extensive metabolic remodeling, establishing the importance of evaluating network dynamics beyond cofactor abundance.

Title: Daphniphyllum macropodum genome assembly and multiplexed screening unveils alkaloid modifying enzymes
Authors: Swamidatta, S. H.; Radzikowska, B. A.; Taylor, D. J.; Smit, S. J.; Waddell, L. J. N.; Langer, S.; Larson, T. R.; Unsworth, W. P.; Lichman, B. R.
Abstract: Daphniphyllum macropodum, a small shrub or tree native to East Asia, produces bioactive polycyclic alkaloids of remarkable complexity and variety, making them long-standing, attractive targets for chemical synthesis. However, the biosynthetic origins of Daphniphyllum alkaloids remain unknown, and no pathway-associated enzymes have been identified to date. Here, we report the chromosome-level genome assembly of D. macropodum, representing the first genome assembly for the Daphniphyllaceae, a family in the Saxifragales woody clade. To discover alkaloid-modifying enzymes, we developed a highly combinatorial, multiplexed screening approach which enabled testing multiple enzyme candidates with multiple substrates in a single reaction. Deconvolution and characterisation identified two cytochrome P450 enzymes that catalyse the hydroxylation of the yuzurimine-type alkaloid daphhimalenine B. Specifically, CYP82C230 functions as a daphhimalenine B 2-hydroxylase to yield the natural product yuzurimine C, whereas its paralog, CYP82C231, acts as a daphhimalenine B 13-hydroxylase generating a novel alkaloid we have named yuzurimine F. These are the first reports of an enzymatic modification of a Daphniphyllum alkaloid. Collectively, this work advances our understanding of D. macropodum biology and represents the first steps towards elucidating the complex Daphniphyllum alkaloid biosynthetic pathway.

Title: Visually guided analysis of single cell proteomics data with SCP-Viz
Authors: Ruiz, S.; Braswell, C.; Orsburn, B.
Abstract: Single cell proteomics (SCP) is a specialized, but expanding, field of research today. One of many challenges slowing SCP adoption is the inherent instability of the proteome and the changes that can occur before getting cells to a lab for preparation and analysis. Additionally, all current interpretation tools require experienced bioinformaticians to make the step from data to interpretation. Here, we present a visual toolkit that can accept SCP data from any instrument or common data processing algorithm. To demonstrate the capabilities of this tool we apply it to the analysis of dried digests of single human cancer cells following long room temperature storage. Remarkably, proteomic depth of the dried and stored samples analyzed is higher than the original analysis of these same digests on a similar system directly following isolation. Critically, when comparing control and drug treated cells, both the protein abundance and post-translationally modified peptides appear similar in both fresh and stored digests of these single cells. These findings are highly encouraging and, taken together, may help decrease the barriers for entry and collaboration for the field of SCP globally.

Title: The crystal structure of the human SIPA1L2 PDZ domain reveals an atypically short, metazoan-conserved β2 β3 loop
Authors: Klos, T.; Zambo, B.; McEwen, A. G.; Morlet, B.; Gogl, G.; Schmidt, H.
Abstract: Signal - induced proliferation-associated 1-like protein 2 (SIPA1L2) is a large neuronal Rap GTPase-activating protein implicated in dynein-dependent retrograde transport of BDNF-TrkB signaling endosomes and genetically linked to Parkinson's disease. It consists of a RapGAP domain, a PDZ domain, and a coiled-coil domain separated by intrinsically disordered regions. Its compact PDZ domain mediates protein-protein interaction by binding short PDZ-binding motifs (PBM) in target proteins. Here, the human SIPA1L2 PDZ domain (residues 943-1027) was crystallized and its structure determined by molecular replacement. The domain adopts the canonical PDZ fold of six beta-strands forming two antiparallel beta-sheets flanked by two alpha-helices. The beta 2 - beta 3 loop, located next to the PBM binding groove, is unusually short - eight residues, against a 14-residue human-PDZome consensus. A BLASTP- and AlphaFold3-based survey across Metazoa shows that, despite PDZ sequence identities falling to ~25 %, the fold and the short loop are structurally conserved (Calpha; RMSD 0.5 - 0.8 Angstrom), indicating that this is a genuine, evolutionarily constrained architectural feature of SIPA1L2-type PDZ domains. PBM binding was not observed in co-crystallization trials. Native holdup assays against a neuronal proteome identified no specific partners for the SIPA1L2 PDZ domain. The structure retains the canonical carboxylate-binding loop and a class-I-type histidine, so partner scarcity is not due to loss of the PBM binding apparatus. Impaired PBM binding seems to result from the combination of the unusually short beta 2 - beta 3 loop and an evolutionarily invariant His964 located at the beta 2 strand. The short loop might restrict the conformational dynamics of the beta 2 strand, thereby stabilizing His964 side-chain conformations that encroach on the PBM binding groove. The structure thus defines SIPA1L2 as a structurally canonical yet apparently orphan PDZ domain.

Title: Location of maximum bending stress in tapered hollow plants: A case study on Moso bamboo (Phyllostachys edulis)
Authors: Chalermsin, C. L.; Tsugawa, S.; Sato, M.
Abstract: Many slender plants, such as trees and bamboo, have naturally tapered, axially graded forms to withstand wind loads; however, while trees feature solid cross-sections, bamboo culms are hollow. Although tapered hollow stems improve mechanical efficiency, the location at which the maximum bending stress develops remains unclear. As failure in such structures is driven by the bending-induced stress state, identifying this location is essential for understanding their structural capacities. This study aimed to (1) identify the location of the maximum bending stress of a tapered hollow beam made from an axially functionally graded material under various load profiles, (2) verify the consistency between linear and large deflection analyses, (3) investigate the effect of taper ratio on this location, and (4) apply the analysis to Moso bamboo (Phyllostachys edulis) as a case study. Governing nonlinear equations were derived for uniformly distributed load, inverse triangular load, triangular load, and point load; the equations were solved using a large deflection analysis. A linear analysis was also conducted and compared with the nonlinear results. The results showed that the linear analysis is sufficient for predicting the location of the maximum stress under distributed loading; however, under concentrated loading, it is accurate only at low loads. A more tapered geometry shifted the maximum stress toward the tip. In Moso bamboo, the maximum stress is located in the upper region of the culms, providing insights into the natural structural design of tapered hollow plants and a foundation for the design of bio-inspired tapered hollow components.

Title: MetaboRx: R Shiny application for quality assessment and preprocessing of mass spectrometry-based metabolomics data
Authors: Guppy, B. K.; Merrill, R. A.; Brown, R. F.; Apak Evans, T. I.; Taylor, E. B.
Abstract: Introduction Metabolomics datasets offer deep insights into biological systems, yet the multi-step analytical workflow, from sample preparation through instrumental analysis, introduces unwanted variation. This variation, including signal drift and batch effects can confound true biological signals. Although rigorous quality control (QC) and data preprocessing are prerequisites for downstream analysis, existing workflows are often fragmented, time-consuming, and inaccessible to non-experts. Objectives To develop a user-friendly software tool for rapid quality assessment and rigorous preprocessing of metabolomics feature tables. Methods MetaboRx is an R Shiny application that integrates orthogonal quality metrics into a single workflow, enabling systematic and transparent evaluation of metabolomics data before and after preprocessing. The application identifies formatting errors and analytically unreliable features and provides flexible preprocessing and visualization options. Results MetaboRx is freely available at https://github.com/ETaylorLab/MetaboRx. Using a semi-targeted LC-MS metabolomics dataset from mouse plasma, perturbed with simulated low-quality data, we demonstrate how MetaboRx facilitates detection of data quality problems, reduces unwanted variation, and prepares data for downstream analysis. Conclusion MetaboRx streamlines metabolomics data quality assessment and preprocessing through an interactive and integrated workflow. The application may improve consistency and reproducibility in metabolomics studies by supporting informed preprocessing decisions and transparent reporting of QC outcomes prior to downstream analysis.

Title: TS-Zarr: a cloud-optimized Zarr layout for viewing and analyzing biomedical time series
Authors: Shah, R.; Garai, S.; De Freitas, D. D.; Truong, V. Q.; Ganglberger, W.; Paron, T.; Westover, M. B.; Sinha, N.; Wagenaar, J.
Abstract: Background: Biomedical time series are recorded at high sampling rates for hours to days across tens to hundreds of channels. Each recording occupies gigabytes to terabytes of storage. FAIR data sharing requirements often place recordings in cloud storage. Visual analysis requires downsampling windows wider than a few seconds to the pixel width of the screen. Visualization tools therefore either read a local copy of the recording or query a dedicated resampling server in front of the data. Findings: We present TS-Zarr, a Zarr v3 layout for time series data. It stores the samples of each channel alongside a pyramid of summary statistics at progressively coarser levels. Zarr on cloud storage offers low-latency, high-throughput parallel reads. The layout lets a reader fetch only the channels and windows it needs. These targeted reads scale better than the same reads from HDF5 and EDF. Precomputed levels trade additional storage and error-bound signal transformation for faster and more scalable visual analysis that moves from the whole recording to narrow windows. As users grow and windows widen, precomputed reads from cloud storage scale beyond the point at which a resampling server fails. Conclusions: Precomputed levels let researchers visualize a recording without downloading a local copy or querying a dedicated resampling server. The time to read a view remains bounded as the window under view widens. Zarr on cloud storage also provides efficient, highly parallelizable, targeted reads of raw sample data for analysis.

Title: EvoRx: Machine Learning-Based Prediction of Antibiotic Resistance in Escherichia coli Using Genomic Features
Authors: Arora, A.; Natarajan, E.
Abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) complicates bacterial infection management, motivating genomic approaches to predicting antibiotic susceptibility. This study assessed the predictive performance and generalisability of machine-learning models using resistance-associated genomic features from Escherichia coli. Publicly available genomic and phenotypic records yielded 446 genomes, 252 binary genomic features and 1,935 susceptibility observations across nine antibiotics. Logistic Regression, Random Forest and XGBoost classifiers were compared using validation ROC-AUC, followed by evaluation on held-out test subsets. Additional analyses examined identical genomic feature profiles across partitions, performance across source publications and feature redundancy. Ampicillin and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole achieved held-out accuracies of 93.98% and 93.59%, ROC-AUC values of 0.912 and 0.954, and resistant-isolate recall of 95.16% and 94.55%, respectively. In contrast, ceftazidime achieved 88.52% accuracy and 0.940 ROC-AUC but identified only 22.22% of resistant isolates. Seventy-four held-out observations shared identical 252-feature profiles with training isolates; all were correctly classified. After excluding overlapping observations without retraining, ROC-AUC decreased from 0.912 to 0.848 for ampicillin and from 0.954 to 0.901 for trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole. Exploratory cross-publication evaluations showed variable performance, with shared multilocus sequence types in 16 of 18 comparisons. Reducing genomic features did not materially alter validation performance in the two antibiotics examined. These findings indicate that genomic predictors can discriminate resistance phenotypes, but aggregate accuracy may obscure poor resistant-isolate detection. The findings also distinguish performance on conventionally held-out isolates from performance on previously unseen resistance-feature profiles, an important consideration when bacterial population structure and correlated determinants substantially influence model evaluation. Independent phylogenetic and prospective validation remains necessary before clinical use.

Title: VINCIT: A virus-incorporated biomaterial niche enables spatially controlled in vivo CAR T cell engineering
Authors: Goodier, K. D.; Zhu, Y.; Wei, C.; Jiang, Z.; Jiang, Y.; Lu, X.; Chen, S.; Greco, A.; Yu, D.; Liu, X.; Choy, J.; Su, Y.; Ma, J.; Lin, J.; Kong, J.; Wang, E.; Luong, D.; Wilson, D. S.; Doloff, J. C.; Schneck, J.; Konig, M. F.; Mao, H.-Q.
Abstract: In vivo generation of chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T cells could bypass the complex manufacturing required for conventional cell therapies, but systemic gene delivery remains limited by off target exposure and inefficient access to target immune cells. Here, we develop VINCIT (Virus Incorporated Niche for Cellular ImmunoTherapy), an injectable nanofiber hydrogel composite that establishes a localized immune-engineering niche for CAR T cell generation in vivo. VINCIT spatially retains viral vectors while recruiting endogenous immune cells, enabling local transduction of T cells, after which the engineered T cells enter the circulation. VINCIT spatially confines transgene expression compared with intravenous viral delivery and markedly enhances T cell transduction compared with subcutaneously injected free virus. VINCIT is compatible with both adeno-associated and lentiviral vectors, and CAR T cells generated in vivo exhibit antigen-specific effector responses and mediate CD19+ B cell depletion. In a humanized mouse model of lymphoma, a single VINCIT administration produces sustained tumor control and extends median survival from 32 to 110 days. Mechanistically, efficient CAR T cell generation requires coordinated interactions among multiple immune populations, with neutrophil depletion markedly reducing cellular recruitment and subsequent T cell programming. These findings establish a localized biomaterial niche for spatially controlled in vivo immune cell engineering.

Title: Short-Duration Fluid Shear Stress Enhances LPS-Driven Macrophage Pro-Inflammatory Response in a Magnitude-Dependent Manner
Authors: Shokrani, P.; Dillon, R.; Prendeville, H.; Dolan, E. B.
Abstract: Macrophages are mechanosensitive cells that integrate physical and biochemical cues to shape inflammatory responses. Mechanical stimuli such as stretch, strain, and matrix stiffness have been extensively studied; however, the effects of fluid shear stress (FSS) on macrophage function remain relatively poorly understood. In this study, we investigated how mild-magnitude, short-duration FSS applied alone or in combination with Lipopolysaccharide (LPS), affects bone marrow-derived macrophages (BMDM) phenotype and function. FSS alone had no effect on naive macrophages, and lower magnitude shear stress did not produce any significant effects under any condition. However, when macrophages were exposed to 0.8 Pa FSS prior to LPS stimulation, tumour necrosis factor (TNF) secretion was significantly increased, and IL-10 production decreased compared with static controls. This magnitude-dependent priming effect was also sequence-specific, as FSS applied after LPS stimulation did not produce any significant changes. These findings demonstrate that mild FSS can mechanically prime macrophages to amplify the inflammatory response but only above a threshold magnitude and when applied before biochemical stimulation. Our results highlight the importance of both shear magnitude and stimulation order in determining macrophage mechanosensitivity, with implications for understanding immune cell behaviour in mechanically dynamic microenvironments and how inflammation can be affected by the mechanical forces in vivo. Keywords: Mechanosensation; fluid shear stress; lipopolysaccharide; inflammation.

Title: Systematic mapping of protease-substrate specificity through geometric graph learning
