Authors: Guo, X.; Bi, Y.; Ran, Z.; Pan, T.; Sun, H.; Hao, Y.; Jia, R.; Wang, C.; Zhang, Q.; Kurgan, L.; Song, J.; Li, F.
Abstract: Protease-substrate specificity is central to cellular regulation and disease pathogenesis, and accurately modelling its structural determinants remains challenging. Substrate recognition is governed by spatial constraints and higher-order relationships that extend beyond local sequence motifs. Most computational approaches rely predominantly on motif-centric or sequence-based representations, limiting their ability to capture the geometric and relational structure underlying enzymatic specificity. Here, we introduce OmniCleave, a structure-aware geometric graph learning framework for modelling protease-substrate specificity at scale. OmniCleave is trained on 57,278 structure-informed protease-substrate pairs derived from 9,651 substrates spanning over 100 proteases across six distinct families. The framework integrates multi-scale structural graphs with higher-order protease relational topology, explicitly encoding spatial context and inter-protease dependencies within a unified geometric representation. This formulation moves beyond local pattern recognition and enables transferable modelling across six protease families. Across large-scale benchmarks, the framework consistently outperforms existing approaches and reveals interpretable geometric determinants underlying substrate recognition. Experimental validation confirms three previously unannotated caspase-3 substrates and 21 cleavage sites predicted by OmniCleave, supporting the biological relevance of the learned representations. Together, OmniCleave provides a scalable geometric framework for modelling protease-substrate specificity, with practical utility for systematic analysis of protease biology.

Title: Saturation mutagenesis and NMR of a fold switch reveal position-dependent deep learning performance
Authors: Felbinger, N.; Carillo, K. J.; Chen, Y.; Orban, J.; Pierce, B.
Abstract: A predictive understanding of the properties of fold-switching or metamorphic proteins can provide insights into protein dynamics and energetics, and enable the design of complex protein functions and molecular machines. Recently developed deep learning modeling tools, including AlphaFold, have led to dramatic increases in structural modeling accuracy, but their performance for prediction of fold switching or point mutant effects is unclear. Here we used NMR to measure all substitutions at three key positions of the GA/GB fold switch that differentially adopt -helical (3), {beta}-grasp (4{beta}+), or unfolded states, generating a quantitative experimental benchmark for mutation-level fold switching. Using this dataset to assess and compare a panel of deep learning and physics-based modeling and design algorithms, we identified variable and position-dependent performance across methods. Some AlphaFold2-based algorithms were able to predict mutant effects at individual sites, indicating partial sensitivity to physical effects of residue substitutions. Additional comparisons of predictions with experimentally measured stability changes further highlighted position-dependent success and general challenges for predictive algorithms. Together, this study provides a rigorous new benchmark for mutation-induced fold switching and reveals the capabilities and limitations of current deep learning models, establishing a foundational baseline for facilitating the next generation of prediction tools.

Title: Resistome-based machine learning source attribution of a superbug
Authors: Mendez, C.; Vargas-Peralta, D.; Rendon, L. A.; Castillo-Ramirez, S.
Abstract: Many bacterial human pathogens infect not only humans but also other species, and source attribution has been very useful for studying transmission among the different sources. Yet, critical pathogens such as Acinetobacter baumannii have not been studied using source attribution approaches. Here, we conducted machine source attribution using the resistome of almost 1200 A. baumannii genomes from four sources: humans, companion animals , soil, and white storks. Of note, no other study has used the resistome as input data before. First, we selected the best model among 168 parameter combinations, which was Random Forest, with 5-fold cross-validation and chi2 for feature selection. The model shows a reasonably good accuracy with an F1 weighted score = 0.744, yet class accuracy was dependent on the source. Whereas for companion animals and humans, 93% and 86% of the predictions were correct, respectively; the other two categories (soil and white stork) show correct predictions below 50%. Yet, a core phylogeny and ST assignment reveal that the wrong predictions are associated with multi-host lineages. Finally, we identify the most important ARGs contributing to each class prediction and, in the case of companion animals, tetgenes, which confer resistance to tetracycline, were among the top contributors. Our study shows the resistome's potential for developing models to predict source associations. More broadly, this study shows how integrating machine learning and phylogenomics can help us understand multi-host transmission dynamics.

Title: Simulated microgravity induces aging phenotypes in human organoids
Authors: Mu, W.-C.; Baechle, J.; Schneider, K.; Fuentealba, M.; Wu, F.; Manwaring-Mueller, M.; Bracey, N.; Chebykin, A.; Saini, A.; Park, J.; Kim, J.; Winer, D. A.; Sayed, N.; Noishiki, C. A.; Gale, A. I.; Mason, C.; Davis, M. M.; Furman, D.
Abstract: Simulated microgravity provides a controlled perturbation for testing how loss of mechanical load affects human tissues. After 24 hours in rotating-wall vessels, neural, cardiac and tonsil organoids developed tissue-specific transcriptional responses that overlapped published spaceflight datasets, accompanied by higher transcriptomic-age estimates in neural, cardiac, and tonsil models, altered cardiac-organoid contraction dynamics and modified tonsil-organoid antiviral gene-expression signatures. These findings establish a multi-organoid framework for studying acute responses to gravitational unloading.

Title: Extracellular vesicles from alternatively activated macrophages remodel the injured hepatic niche and promote repair
Authors: Addison, M. L.; Kilpatrick, A. M.; Candela, M. E.; Ashmore-Harris, C.; Cartwright, J.; Aird, R. E.; Man, T.-Y.; Ching, K.; Kesidou, D.; Cholewa-Waclaw, J.; Humphries, C.; Wagstaff, L.; Dear, J. W.; Forbes, S. J.
Abstract: Alternatively activated macrophages (AAMs) are in clinical development for acute liver injury, but their mechanisms of action remain incompletely understood. AAM therapy remodels the injured hepatic niche, promoting reparative macrophage states, suppressing inflammatory myeloid programmes and restoring hepatocyte metabolic and biosynthetic programmes. We identify extracellular vesicles released by AAMs (AAM-EVs) as essential mediators of AAM therapeutic activity. AAM-EVs enhance macrophage phagocytosis and induce reparative transcriptional and proteomic responses, including increased TREM2 abundance. Following administration in established APAP injury, AAM-EVs reduce necrosis and neutrophilic inflammation, and promote hepatocellular regeneration, and we observe preferential and rapid association of AAM-EVs with hepatic macrophages alongside reparative phenotypic shift. Moreover, pharmacological inhibition of EV release attenuates parent AAM efficacy and TREM2 macrophage accumulation, while EVs derived from Dicer-deficient AAMs exhibit reduced therapeutic activity, implicating miRNA-associated mechanisms. Comparative single-nucleus transcriptomics reveals overlapping but distinct macrophage and hepatocyte responses to AAMs and AAM-EVs. Together, these findings identify EV-mediated communication as an important mechanism of macrophage-induced liver repair and support the development of AAM-EVs as a cell-free therapeutic strategy.

Title: Polymer type and surface functionalization determine the impact of nanoplastics on neural crest cell adhesion, migration, proliferation, and apoptosis in primary cultures.
Authors: Dufour, S.; Fodil, R.; Relaix, F.
Abstract: Nanoplastics (NP) constitutes a pervasive source of environmental pollution that contaminates all ecosystems, the atmosphere and freshwater. They are absorbed by living organisms and cross biological barriers, with increasing evidence pointing to their harmful effects both at cellular levels and in whole organisms. The impacts of NPs vary not only depending on their size and concentration, but also on the cell type, the polymer composition and surface charge, requiring a comprehensive understanding of the responses of a wide range of cells to these parameters. Because neural crest cells (NCC) are highly proliferative and migratory embryonic progenitors that contribute to a wide range of tissues, they provide a relevant model for investigating the impact of environmental pollutants on developmental cell behaviors. Using a well-established primary NCC culture system, we show that polypropylene (PP) and polyethylene (PE) NPs are more detrimental than polystyrene (PS) NPs to NCC survival and proliferation in a dose-dependent manner. These effects were particularly pronounced for amine-functionalized NPs, which increased NCC apoptosis compared with carboxylate-functionalized NPs. In addition, amine-functionalized PP and PE NPs shortened NCC production period and strongly decrease cell adhesion and migration through alterations of substrate adhesions. Our results indicate that NPs disrupt key biological processes of NCCs, depending on the polymer type and surface functionalization and might contribute to the pathogenesis of structures derived from the NCCs.

Title: Isolate relatedness is more strongly associated with host and geography compared with phenotypic variation in a broad host range pathogen
Authors: Sharma, A.; Groves, C. L.; O'Donnell, S.; Webster, R. W.; Lopez-Nicora, H. D.; Willbur, J. F.; Smith, D. L.; Gluck-Thaler, E.
Abstract: Determining the drivers of diversity in plant pathogen populations is a critical for developing effective management strategies. Sclerotinia sclerotiorum, a cosmopolitan fungus infecting over 400 plant species, causes considerable yield and economic losses worldwide. However, longstanding questions remain about the association between genetic and phenotypic variation in this pathogen, leaving the drivers of its diversification unresolved. Here, we characterized the diversity of S. sclerotiorum isolates from the United States in a global context and tested the hypothesis that phylogenetic relatedness structures phenotypic variation among isolates. Genome-wide variant analysis resolved US isolates into several distinct lineages, with short within-lineage branch lengths consistent with recent common ancestry or clonal propagation. Population structure analysis confirmed two major global clusters, one composed predominantly of Australian isolates and the other largely of isolates from the rest of the world, including the US. Notably, several US isolates grouped within the Australian cluster, suggesting historical intercontinental movement of this pathogen. Contrary to our expectations, isolate relatedness was more strongly associated with data such as host, geographic origin, and year of collection compared with morphological variation, suggesting that phenotypic variation segregates independently of phylogenetic structure. Instead, the distribution of phenotypic variation primarily reflected two trade-offs: rapid radial growth with shorter sclerotial development versus slower growth with prolonged sclerotial development, and the production of many small sclerotia versus fewer larger ones. Together, our results shed light on the complex relationships between phenotypic, ecological, and phylogenetic variation and bring us one step closer to predicting how diversity is structured in natural populations of a global fungal pathogen.

Title: Hidden but Expanding Sampling Bias Distorts Prokaryotic Genome Collections
Authors: Götsch, H.; Baumdicker, F.
Abstract: Public genome collections underpin our understanding of bacterial diversity and the distribution of traits such as antibiotic resistance, and increasingly serve as training data for genomic foundation models. Their growing size promises an increasingly complete view of microbial genetic variation. However, these collections combine studies with different sampling priorities, often overrepresenting subgroups of closely related strains of particular interest. The resulting bias reduces effective information, and its consequences for diversity estimates and the value of further sequencing remain insufficiently quantified. Here we show that accounting for this escalating sampling bias is essential for accurate gene frequency estimates and hints at greater genomic diversity than current data suggest. We propose to detect and reduce sampling bias based on phylogenetic relationships compared to expectations under random sampling, which, in contrast to dereplication and data reduction methods, preserves fine-scale diversity in large samples. Applied to 402 prokaryotic species in the NCBI genome database, our method PhyloThin indicates that the effective number of samples is 41% lower than the actual number but retains more than twice as many genomes as dereplication. Sampling bias varies substantially among species, showing that genome counts alone provide an incomplete measure of how well a species has already been characterized. PhyloThin thus turns biased, expanding genome collections into more representative samples for studying genome evolution and population genetic inference with implications for training genomic foundation models, pathogen surveillance, and the discovery of novel genetic functions.

Title: Dynamics of somatic L1 retrotransposition in the human brain
Authors: Demirci, I.; Larsson, A. J. M.; Paterlini, M.; Dumitru, I.; Hagemann-Jensen, M.; Alkass, K.; Druid, H.; Ziegenhain, C.; Michaelsson, J.; Mold, J. E.; Sandberg, R.; Frisen, J.
Abstract: The sole source of genomic diversity in the human brain caused by autonomous retrotransposition is facilitated by the long interspersed nuclear element-1 (L1). However, assessing the rate, timing and source elements of this event has been challenging due to the lack of technologies that capture of L1s at sufficient scale in single cells. Here, we introduce LUSTRE, a single-cell assay that enables mapping L1 sites without whole-genome amplification, and profile ~17,600 neurons from the dentate gyrus, cortex, cerebellum of the adult human brain. We report the presence of somatic L1s that define related lineages and conservatively estimate a validation-adjusted rate of 0.1-0.3 somatic events per neuron. Our analyses further indicate two distinct waves of retrotransposition during development and combined with the variability in their polyA tract lengths across single nuclei, suggest the formation of lineage hierarchies marked by new somatic retrotransposition events and cell divisions. Mapping the origin of L1s through 3'-transduction events identify the rare source L1s that are responsible for the majority of retrotransposition events. These results uncover the dynamics of L1-driven somatic mosaicism and establish L1s as endogenous recorders of cellular and lineage history in human tissues.

Title: Bivalent, Copper-Mediated Amyloid-β Binding Disruptsthe Prion Protein's Neuroprotective Conformation
Authors: Smart, A.; Pavlovici, F.; Singewald, K.; Marshak, C.; Carollo, C.; Kaplan, S.; Millhauser, G. L.
Abstract: Emerging evidence shows that the cellular prion protein (PrPC) is a major receptor for Amyloid-{beta} (A{beta}) and that this aberrant interaction may influence the progression of Alzheimer's disease (AD). However, the molecular basis of this interaction remains poorly understood. Both proteins strongly bind Cu2+, and we previously discovered that PrPC, A{beta}30, and Cu2+ form a ternary complex at equimolar ratios. Here, using electron paramagnetic resonance (EPR) and nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectroscopy with isotopically labeled proteins, we characterize the stoichiometry, stability, and molecular interactions of this ternary complex. We show that the complex forms preferentially at substoichiometric to equimolar Cu2+ concentrations yet remains stable at high Cu2+ ratios. The formation of the ternary complex is bivalent, requiring the previously identified A{beta}-binding domain on PrPC (residues 95-110) along with mutual Cu2+ coordination to the N-terminal octapeptide repeat domain in PrPC. Line broadening observed in A{beta}30 NMR experiments identifies its negatively charged N-terminal residues and central hydrophobic core (residues 17-21) as the primary PrPC binding sites. Through histidine mutation studies, we determine A{beta}30 coordinates Cu2+ primarily through His14. Critically, the ternary complex formation displaces Cu2+ from a specific His residue on the C-terminal domain of PrPC, disrupting the neuroprotective cis interdomain interaction that otherwise regulates the toxic effector N-terminal domain. Using segmentally isotopically 15N-labeled PrPC, we show that while the cis interaction is not fully eliminated by interaction with A{beta}, it becomes a disfavored conformational state. Together, these findings demonstrate how Cu2+ reinforces the PrPC-A{beta} interaction, in turn destabilizing PrPC's neuroprotective fold, offering a molecular mechanism for A{beta} accumulation at - and potential trafficking across - the plasma membrane.

Title: Ancestral sequence reconstruction enables functional expression of archaeal thermostable tungsten-containing aldehyde:ferredoxin oxidoreductases in E. coli
Authors: Boes, D. M.; Wang, Y.; De Wit, P.; Schmitz, R. A.; Vina, J.; Mateljak, I.; Hollmann, F.; Hagedoorn, P. L.
Abstract: Tungsten-containing enzymes offer important opportunities in industrial biocatalysis, e.g. to convert carboxylic acids into aldehydes without requiring co-substrates ATP and NADPH. These W-enzymes operate at low reduction potentials compared to the more ubiquitous Mo-enzymes, enabling unique reactions. Their application is limited by the lack of functional expression in commonly used heterologous host organisms. Here, we show that variants of Pyrococcus furiosus aldehyde:ferredoxin oxidoreductase (PfAOR) obtained using ancestral sequence reconstruction can be functionally expressed in E. coli with an activity of 0.86 U/mg towards crotonaldehyde at 60 {degrees}C, which is a 50-fold higher activity compared to the recombinant extant enzyme. The ancestral enzymes, named ThermoAOR3 and ThermoAOR4, carrying 61 and 84 mutations respectively, were purified using a single-step affinity purification, showed a kcat of 0.95 and 0.86 s-1 at 60 {degrees}C, respectively, and have Km values comparable to native PfAOR. ThermoAOR3 contained a redox active [4Fe-4S] cluster like native PfAOR. Furthermore, it contained 10-15% of the expected pterin cofactor, W and Fe, which indicates the enzyme production can still be improved. Altogether, we demonstrate the first heterologous expression of a functionally active W-AOR using a widely used bacterial host, which represents a breakthrough enabling exploration of these enzymes for industrial biocatalysis.

Title: Dynamic nanocomplexes of antibiotics and biofilm-degrading enzymes overcome biofilm tolerance to treat Pseudomonas aeruginosa infections
Authors: Yourdkhani, A.; Brittain, N. Y.; Nwagwu, C.; Lee, J. H.; Cao, J.; Jamshid-Nezhad, S.; Finbloom, J. A.
Abstract: Pseudomonas aeruginosa biofilms limit antibiotic penetration and protect embedded bacteria, making established infections difficult to treat. To combat the biofilm, administering tobramycin (Tob) with deoxyribonuclease I (DNase) could pair antimicrobial action with biofilm matrix degradation, but their distinct physicochemical properties hinder co-delivery and transport into the biofilm core. Taking advantage of the acidic biofilm microenvironment, we developed pH-responsive nanocomplexes (NCs) that expand, favoring local retention of the NCs and their cargo. We used stepwise electrostatic precomplexation to co-load Tob and DNase into the NCs, then electrostatically added a PEG-bearing polymer to their surface to improve NC distribution within biofilms, forming PEG-NCs. Across established biofilms of three P. aeruginosa strains, these dynamic NCs overcame biofilm-associated tolerance toward tobramycin and produced the most consistent reductions in bacterial burden and biomass. Formulation-function analyses coupled with biofilm imaging suggested complementary contributions from PEG and active DNase components. In an established murine abscess model, a single intra-abscess PEG-NC injection reduced bacterial burden by approximately 2 log-fold and improved abscess healing, whereas dose-matched Tob and Tob+DNase controls did not significantly improve infection outcomes. Overall, dynamic NCs mediate the co-delivery of biofilm matrix disruptors with antibiotics to improve treatment of established biofilm infections.

Title: Compound-specific DNA adduct profiling with nanopore sequencing and IonStats
Authors: Koski, Y.; Patel, D.; Kakko von Koch, N.; Jouhten, P.; Aaltonen, L.; Palin, K.; Sahu, B.; Pitkanen, E.
Abstract: Covalently bound DNA adducts are mutation precursors that contribute to aging and diseases such as cancer. Accurate detection of adducts in the genome will shed light on tumorigenesis. However, commonly used detection methods are unable to pinpoint the exact genomic locations of adducts. Long-read nanopore sequencing has the potential to accurately detect multiple types of DNA adducts at single-nucleotide precision. In this study, we developed a novel statistical toolkit, IonStats, to profile DNA adducts in nanopore sequencing data. With IonStats, we investigated the effects of the adduct-inducing genotoxic compounds aristolochic acid II and melphalan on nanopore sequencing and found both shared and compound-specific perturbations in base quality scores, ionic current profiles, and translocation dynamics. Notably, these treatments profoundly altered nanopore readouts and led to substantial sequence-specific read interruptions. Our study shows that nanopore sequencing can be effectively employed to detect and characterize DNA adducts, paving the way for high-resolution, high-throughput profiling of DNA damage and the exposome.

Title: CATEomics: model selection and ensembling for heterogeneous treatment effect estimation from high-dimensional omics data
Authors: Furuta, T.; Himori, K.; Zhang, B.; Kitani, A.; Matsui, Y.
Abstract: CATEomics addresses the lack of a standardized and reproducible process for choosing among conditional average treatment effect (CATE) estimators in high-dimensional omics studies, where their estimation errors cannot be evaluated directly from observed outcomes. The R package accepts a SummarizedExperiment, applies common preprocessing and data partitions across R and Python estimators, compares their out-of-fold estimates using proxy losses, supports model selection and ensembling, and returns the resulting CATE estimates to the original object for downstream omics analysis. Availability and implementation: CATEomics is implemented in R and is freely available under the MIT license at https://github.com/matsui-lab/CATEomics. The software version described here (v0.99.0) is archived on Zenodo at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24189754. A vignette illustrates the complete workflow from a SummarizedExperiment to downstream analysis.

Title: Functional specialization of TAF4b governs early prophase I entry and recombination frequency in Brassica rapa
Authors: Majka, J.; Lv, Z.; Nguyen, T. D.; Doll, R.; Schoenenbach, J.; Mason, A. S.
Abstract: While the core transcription factor TAF4b regulates meiotic transcription and recombination in the diploid model Arabidopsis thaliana, its functional specialization and evolutionary dynamics remain poorly understood in paleopolyploid genomes. Here, we investigated how a unique, single-copy TAF4b gene on chromosome A7 modulates early meiotic progression and reproductive success in the paleopolyploid crop Brassica rapa. By characterizing multiple independent taf4b TILLING mutant lines through an integrated pipeline of whole-genome background sequencing, stage-specific anther transcriptomics (RNA-seq), yeast two-hybrid assays, and quantitative cytogenetics, we show that TAF4b has evolved an exclusive, non-redundant, and meiosis-enriched role despite the presence of duplicated somatic TAF4 loci. Disruption of TAF4b universally reduced class I crossover frequency, critically depleted HEI10 crossover-designation foci, and triggered univalent formation leading to severe fertility loss. Our stage-specific RNA-seq profiling and structural modeling demonstrate that this phenotype is driven by a precise transcriptomic dysregulation strictly restricted to the narrow interphase/leptotene transition. Crucially, this early transcriptomic imbalance disrupts the expression stoichiometry of core axis, synapsis, and recombination regulators, including ASY1, REC8, SWI1, and BRCA2B, leading to prolonged ASY1 retention and defective physical chromosome behavior. In conclusion, we demonstrate that TAF4b acts as a stage-specific upstream gatekeeper of the early prophase I expression program in B. rapa. These findings establish a direct link between core transcriptional gating, downstream chromosome dynamics, and meiotic stability following evolutionary genome duplication.

Title: CAS-X: A Probabilistic Multi-Tissue eQTL Framework for Prioritizing Candidate Effector Genes at Type 2 Diabetes Risk Loci
Authors: Uddin, M. M.; Khan, S. M. Z. A.; BommaYadagiri, K.
Abstract: The genetic etiology of Type 2 Diabetes (T2D) involves regulatory mechanisms operating across multiple metabolic tissues. However, candidate effector gene prioritization can be limited by approaches that focus predominantly on pancreatic transcriptomics. To address this limitation, we developed CAS-X, a computational multi-tissue functional genomics framework for prioritizing candidate effector genes at T2D susceptibility loci. CAS-X integrates fine-mapped Posterior Inclusion Probabilities (PIP) and allelic fold changes (aFC) across five tissues: pancreas, skeletal muscle, subcutaneous adipose, visceral adipose, and whole blood. In the reported analysis, multi-tissue integration identified 28 candidate genes meeting the selected prioritization threshold, compared with 12 under the pancreas-only baseline, representing a 133.3% increase in candidate coverage. Prioritized candidates included JAZF1, FTO, GRB14, and CDKN2B. Framework robustness was examined through Leave-One-Tissue-Out sensitivity analysis and comparisons with non-metabolic GTEx Brain Cortex controls. Pathway enrichment analysis highlighted associations with insulin resistance, adipocytokine signaling, and lipolysis regulation. The analysis also incorporated phenome-wide associations and computational assessments of therapeutic tractability. CAS-X provides a computational approach for integrating regulatory evidence across metabolic tissues to support candidate effector gene prioritization in T2D research.

Title: Target-enrichment sequencing reveals intergenotypic reassortment of infectious salmon anaemia virus in Atlantic Canada
Authors: Zhao, M.; O'Brien, J.; Hawkins, L.; Da Silva Filipe, A.; Smollett, K.; Soares, S.; Ness, M.; Solheim, M. A.; Steine, N.; Karlsen, M.; Hill, S. C.
Abstract: Infectious salmon anaemia virus (ISAV) causes severe disease and substantial economic losses in farmed Atlantic salmon (Salmo salar). The virus has an eight-segment, negative-sense single-stranded RNA (ssRNA) genome and is divided into European and North American genotypes. Despite their co-circulation in locations such as the Atlantic coast of Canada, reassortment between these genotypes has never been observed. However, routine diagnostic and sequence-based surveillance often target individual genome segments and may therefore fail to identify reassortant viruses or accurately resolve their genomic ancestry. In this study, we developed a probe panel targeting both genotypes and applied Oxford Nanopore sequencing to 37 ISAV-positive samples collected from 14 farm sites in the Bay of Fundy, New Brunswick, Canada. Twenty-seven samples yielded 29 consensus genomes, including separate viral consensuses recovered from two mixed infections. Segment-specific phylogenies identified 24 viruses with a previously unreported intergenotypic genomic constellation comprising a European-genotype segment 3 and North American-genotype segments 1, 2 and 4 - 8. Their consistent monophyletic clustering across segment-specific phylogenies supports a single ancestral reassortment event followed by onward circulation of the reassortant lineage. A time-scaled phylogeny of segment 3 estimated the posterior mean time to the most recent common ancestor (tMRCA) of the sampled reassortant cluster as September 2016 (95% HPD: March 2013-June 2019), indicating that this segment 3 lineage pre-dated its first sampling in 2021. Five additional viruses represented several distinct EU-genotype lineages. To our knowledge, this is the first documented reassortment between the European and North American ISAV genotypes. These findings identify an intergenotypic reassortant lineage detected across multiple farms in the Bay of Fundy and demonstrate the value of whole-genome sequencing for detecting reassortment, mixed infections and epidemiologically relevant viral diversity.

Title: CIRCA learns identifiable cell- and niche-level programs and their interactions with tissue pathology from spatial transcriptomics
Authors: Lovelace, T. C.; Tung, C.-H.; Enduru, N.; Zhao, Z.
Abstract: Interactions among cells and their local microenvironments shape tissue organization and function, while their dysregulation can contribute to disease. In Alzheimer's disease (AD), the complex responses of glial cells and neurons to amyloid-{beta} pathology can both mitigate and exacerbate neuronal injury. Spatial transcriptomics enables investigation of these relationships in situ, but recovering interpretable transcriptional programs and their interactions from spatial transcriptomics remains challenging, in part because conventional nonlinear models are non-identifiable. Here we present CIRCA (Causal Interaction Representation for Cellular Architectures), a self-supervised causal representation learning framework that jointly learns identifiable cell- and neighborhood-level transcriptional programs and the directed interactions among them under explicit assumptions. It can also be extended to incorporate additional modalities such as pathology. Benchmarked against five existing methods across seven cell-resolution datasets, CIRCA achieved the highest biological accuracy in six and the highest overall score in all five multi-section datasets, while recovering higher-order anatomical organization. In an AD mouse model, incorporating amyloid-{beta} pathology revealed four region-specific plaque niches enriched for microglia. Plaque-associated microglia shared a core disease-associated response whose strength varied by region, and AD genetic risk was preferentially enriched in hippocampal and cortical plaque-associated microglia. Reproducible latent factors linked to cell-level amyloid burden separated phagocytic from inflammatory microglial programs. Applied to a human colorectal cancer dataset, CIRCA resolved patient-specific tumor niches, conserved stromal remodeling niches, and distinct macrophage states, highlighting its versatility. Together, these results establish CIRCA as a methodological advance over existing approaches, enabling deeper insights into tissue organization and the molecular dependencies linking cells to their local environments.

Title: Evaluation depth reshapes method rankings in proteomic co-abundance network inference
Authors: Aliyari, S.; Bagherlou, N.; Salehi, Z.
Abstract: Network inference from quantitative proteomics is usually benchmarked at a single, arbitrarily chosen number of top-ranked edges, so the influence of evaluation depth has not, to our knowledge, been systematically tested. We compared five strategies (random forest with bootstrap selection-frequency filtering, WGCNA, GENIE3, Spearman correlation and context likelihood of relatedness) across seven proteomic datasets from four quantification platforms, using harmonised preprocessing and Precision@K, the fraction of a method's K top-ranked protein pairs present in a pooled reference of curated protein associations (STRING, BioGRID and CORUM). Method rankings changed with depth. In all six datasets that allow an equal-depth comparison, the leading method at K = 50 differed from the leader at K = 2,000, and 18 of 24 pairwise comparisons involving the filtered random forest reversed somewhere along the depth range, although seven of these reversals rested on differences of at most 0.02 in precision and each network was inferred only once. No method dominated. Relative to the same random forest without filtering, the selection-frequency filter was associated with small differences (+0.006 to +0.036 in Precision@500 in six of six equal-depth datasets; mixed at shallower depths) that cannot be separated from its 20- to 50-fold greater number of fitted trees. Prospective testing on independent datasets gave one qualified replication, one non-replication and one non-evaluable dataset. We recommend reporting precision trajectories across depths rather than single-threshold comparisons.

Title: Breedbase: An Integrated Breeding Informatics System with Statistical Analysis and Decision-Support Tools
Authors: Tecle, I. Y.; Tantikanjan, T.; Simoes, C.; Birkett, C.; Hulse-Kemp, A.; Jannink, J.-L.; Karaikal, S. K.; Corak, K.; Lockrow, A.; Manching, H.; Maza, B.; Menda, N.; Nyaga, C.; Peteti, P.; Powell, A.; Preble, R.; Rabbi, I. Y.; Thieme, M.; Waring, D.; Zierer, W.; Mueller, L. A.
Abstract: Breeding programs are becoming increasingly data-intensive, digital and collaborative. One-stop digital breeding ecosystems, in which data storage, field workflow tools, statistical analysis and breeding decision-support tools are seamlessly integrated, are increasingly important. Breedbase (https://breedbase.org) is one of the few open-source platforms that integrate these functionalities within a single system. It provides tools for phenotypic data quality control, descriptive, inferential and predictive statistical analyses. Integrated into the database are tools for single-trial analysis of variance (ANOVA), linear mixed modeling, stability analysis, correlation analysis, principal component analysis, k-means and hierarchical clustering, kinship and inbreeding analysis, genome-wide association study (GWAS), and genomic prediction. Input data and outputs from these analysis tools are visualized in interactive plots and are also available in text files for downloading and sharing. By persisting analysis datasets in the database and applying standardized and automated data preprocessing and analysis workflows, Breedbase is designed to improve efficiency, help maintain data integrity, and support reproducible analyses that can be readily shared among collaborators. Breedbase is open-source software, containerized using Docker, and available for self-hosting or cloud hosting and management by the Mueller lab.

Title: SPIDER: Contextualizing Biomedical Knowledge for Evidence-Grounded Scientific Reasoning
Authors: Liu, M.; Zhao, W.; Chen, J.; Quan, X.; Wang, X.; Feng, J.; Zhou, X.; Han, J.; Zhang, Y.; Wang, Y.; Zhang, X.; Xie, W.
Abstract: Aggregated relations in biomedical knowledge graphs can obscure evidence and study conditions, complicating the distinction between scientific disagreement and contextual differences. Here we introduce SPIDER, a multi-agent framework grounding biomedical relations in literature evidence and extracting study conditions for interpretation. Applied to a graph integrating 48 databases and ontologies, SPIDER analyzed 1.95 million PubMed abstracts, adding 2.31 million previously unrepresented, literature-supported entity pairs to construct SPIDER-KG. Daily updates incorporate relations and evidence from newly indexed PubMed records. Across 89,937 evidence-supported comparisons of potentially incompatible relations, SPIDER classified 79.0% as contextual differences, and 6.1% as genuine disagreement, achieving 80.3% macro-F1 averaged across both categories against expert annotations. On SPIDER-Bench and four biomedical reasoning benchmarks, SPIDER-KG improved large language models' interpretation of evidence-supported biomedical relationships. Retrospective analysis of newly reported gene--disease relationships further demonstrated how evidence-linked knowledge can contextualize emerging discoveries. SPIDER-KG provides a reusable, incrementally extensible evidence layer for biomedical reasoning.

Title: HARICOT: De Novo Assembly of Raw Nanopore Signals using Fuzzy de Bruijn Graphs
Authors: McConnell, U.; Ngo, Q.; Firtina, C.
Abstract: Nanopore sequencing enables reading long nucleotide sequences by measuring characteristic changes in ionic current as molecules pass through a nanopore. These current measurements, known as raw signals, can be analyzed without translating them into bases (i.e., without basecalling), which provides fast and resource-efficient genome analysis. Prior work, Rawsamble, enables finding overlaps between raw nanopore signals, without basecalling them, and generating assemblies from these overlaps with off-the-shelf assemblers such as miniasm. Constructing assemblies directly from raw signals can substantially reduce redundancy and fragmentation in signal datasets, which is useful for many downstream tasks such as constructing non-redundant and accurate basecalled reads from assembled signals. However, existing overlap-based signal assembly strategies suffer from limited scalability and resolution mainly due to using off-the-shelf assemblers (e.g., miniasm) that are designed for basecalled sequences. While scalability and performance limitations can be addressed by existing de Bruijn graph approaches to assembly, their reliance on exact matches makes these methods too sensitive to the inherently noisy raw nanopore signals. To improve assembly of raw signals using de Bruijn graph approaches, we present HARICOT, a mechanism that constructs assemblies from raw nanopore signals by utilizing fuzzy de Bruijn graphs and Hough-transform-based overlap detection to robustly tolerate errors and noise in raw nanopore signals. Our evaluations on various genomes of different sizes show that HARICOT significantly improves assembly contiguity and quality compared to Rawsamble, helping close the gap to popular assembly tools such as Flye or wtdbg2 operating on nucleotide sequences. At the same time, performance remains comparable to these assemblers, without requiring additional basecalling. We discuss that assembling raw nanopore signals before basecalling enables future work in various ways such as building these de Bruijn graphs in a streaming way and assembly-aware basecalling techniques that can basecall assembly graphs for accurate and redundancy-resolved basecalling. HARICOT is available at https://github.com/STORMgroup/HARICOT . We also provide the scripts to fully reproduce our results on our GitHub page.

Title: A Deep Operator Network to Predict Thermal Dose on Brain Tumors in MRI-Guided Laser Induced Thermal Therapy: with Synthetic Data
Authors: Lu, Y.; Krucoff, M. O.
Abstract: Background: MRI-guided laser interstitial thermal therapy (LITT) provides minimally invasive option for surgical treatment of recurrent brain tumors. While patient-specific prediction of thermal dose distributions would improve treatment planning, no quantitative methods currently exist for this purpose. Although conventional numerical solvers are being widely investigated, these methods are computationally expensive and often limited by accuracy and reliability. Purpose: Here we propose DeepoLITT, a rapid and accurate model to predict quantitatively heat propagation in LITT procedures. This study represents the first phase of the investigation which focuses on training and validating synthetic datasets to test model,s accuracy, robustness, and computational efficiency. Methods: We built DeepoLITT on a branch-trunk neural network architecture, where the first branch extracts feature from tumor images, the second branch encodes laser parameters (power, duration, and probe orientation), and the trunk models the mapping from spatial coordinates to the resulting temperature field. To train and test the model, we generated synthetic datasets with different noise levels (0~20%) to mimic LITT procedures with two distinct laser probe types (FullFire and SideFire [Monteris, Inc.]) by a FEM (finite element method) solver. The dataset consisted of 400 samples, of which 90% were used for training and validation and 10% for testing. To evaluate spatial similarity of predicted thermal dose distribution against the ground truth, we employed Dice Similarity Coefficient (DSC) and Hausdorff Distance (HD) computed on CEM43 (Cumulative Equivalent Minutes at 43 {degrees}C) isodose contours at thresholds of 2, 10, and 60 minutes. Finally, we evaluated the model,s inference speed with a representative image grid. Results: For the FullFire laser probe, the DeepoLITT model achieved temperature prediction error with average values ranging from 1.16{+/-}0.40% to 2.92{+/-}0.25%, and peak values ranging from 4.26{+/-}1.31% to 14.94{+/-}0.43% as data noise increased from 0% to 20%. For the SideFire laser probe, the model achieved temperature prediction error with average values ranging from 3.79{+/-}0.53% to 5.13{+/-}1.00% and peak values ranging from 15.18{+/-}7.15% to 20.75{+/-}2.84%. For thermal dose assessment, at the noise-free level for the FullFire laser probe, the model exhibited strong spatial agreement with FEM references, yielding DSCs of 0.96{+/-}0.02, 0.97{+/-}0.21, and 0.96{+/-}0.21 with corresponding HDs of 0.09{+/-}0.08 mm, 0.07{+/-}0.07 mm, and 0.06{+/-}0.08 mm at 2-, 10-, and 60-minute CEM43 thresholds. For the SideFire laser probe, the model achieved DSCs of 0.96{+/-}0.02, 0.97{+/-}0.21, and 0.96{+/-}0.21, with corresponding HDs of 0.20{+/-}0.31mm, 0.11{+/-}0.30 mm, and 0.15{+/-}0.31 mm, respectively. As the noise level increases, these DSC values show a decreasing trend, and the HD values increase. In terms of computational efficiency, the DeepoLITT model inferences temperature maps with 0.04{+/-}0.05 seconds per 3D sample ([31 x 31 x 3] grid), compared to 24.32{+/-}2.12 seconds required by the FEM solver. Conclusions: The study with synthetic data demonstrates the proposed model is an accurate and rapid method in predicting thermal dose. After testing clinical data, the method has high feasibility to be deployed in real clinical environment.

Title: Drastic improvement in MHC class I epitope prediction through training data augmentation, generative adversarial network modeling of selfness, and consideration of homology to class II epitopes.
Authors: Oh, S.; Hong, S.-E.; Kim, H.-S.; Paik, S.
Abstract: Accurate identification of immunogenic neoantigens is critical for personalized cancer vaccines but remains hindered by the high false-positive rates of current predictors. Here, we present DeepOmicsNeo, a modular deep learning framework that harmonizes three biological determinants of immunogenicity. The first module, DeepOmicsNeo-Binding, overcomes data scarcity in non-9mer peptide-Class I Major Histocompatibility Complex (MHC) binding prediction via a novel augmentation strategy that synthesizes pseudo-binders and non-binders by editing non-anchor residues, outperforming its competitors. The second module, DeepOmicsNeo-Selfness, addresses the paucity of negative training data for immunogenicity prediction by utilizing a Generative Adversarial Network trained on around 60 million human self-peptides. This unsupervised approach quantifies selfness to detect immunogenic peptides and the resulting score correlated with IFN-{gamma} secretion by T-cells. The third module, DeepOmicsNeo-H2, exploits the central-region homology between known HLA Class-I and Class-II restricted epitopes. The integrated model, DeepOmicsNeo-Immunogenicity, outperforms state-of-the-art predictors on the TESLA, HiTIDE, and TiTANIAN benchmark datasets.[2.1] Top20 precision, the most important benchmark for clinical utility in personalized cancer vaccine design, was drastically improved over other predictors. Together, these findings indicate that jointly modeling the three complementary features captures biologically meaningful determinants of immunogenicity, supporting DeepOmicsNeo as a robust computational framework for neoantigen prioritization in personalized cancer immunotherapy.

Title: GRABS: a content-addressed antibody-antigen binding-affinity dataset with predicted structures and a leak-free benchmark
Authors: Martins, L. d. M.; Zanetti Salles, P. P.; Meidanis, J.
Abstract: Machine-learning prediction of antibody-antigen binding affinity depends as much on the training data as on the model, yet public affinity measurements are scattered across databases with incompatible formats, mix genuine dissociation constants with censored or predicted values, and concentrate most of their label mass on a few heavily mutated targets. We present GRABS (Geometric Resource for Antibody Binding Studies), a curated, content-addressed, structure-ready dataset that consolidates nine public sources, of which the seven with redistributable licenses yield 4,380 canonical antibody-antigen records} (median-collapsed from 4,761 raw measurements), each with an experimentally measured dissociation constant (Kd), paired heavy and light variable regions (VH, VL), and an antigen sequence, covering 2,015 distinct antigen sequences. Every structure, graph, and feature is addressed by a content key, md5(VH+VL+antigen)[:10], and verified non-circularly: each graph's node features are decoded back to sequence and re-hashed, matching the content key for 4,282/4,282 (100%) structure-backed records. This integrity is load-bearing: an alignment ablation shows that a previously-reported strong cross-target result (R2 {approx} 0.415) was a misalignment-mediated source/batch leak that content-key regeneration dissolves. On the resulting leak-free, antigen-cluster-grouped benchmark, cross-target ranking of variants of a held-out antigen collapses to the noise floor (within-held-out-antigen Spearman {rho} {approx} 0 for every model family: sequence, structure, and folding-confidence), with structure giving no advantage, a rigorously leakage-controlled quantification of the limited reach of current methods. GRABS ships model-ready artifacts (Boltz-2 predicted complexes, per-residue ESM-2 embeddings, geometric graphs, feature vectors) with antigen-stratified splits, and is intended for leakage-free benchmarking and within-target affinity ranking (measure-then-rank), not zero-shot prediction for antigens absent from training.

Title: Pioneering Hybrid Genome Assemblies of Fusarium graminearum and Fusarium avenaceum from Indian Wheat: Insights into Virulence Frameworks and Genome Evolution
Authors: Choppadandi, G.; KJ, Y.; Navathe, S.
Abstract: Fusarium head blight (FHB), primarily caused by various species of Fusarium, is a destructive disease of wheat that reduces yield and contaminates grain with mycotoxins. The present study reports high-quality hybrid genome assemblies for two Indian wheat isolates, Fusarium graminearum strain TNW1 and Fusarium avenaceum strain DMW8, representing the first genome-scale comparative study of FHB associated Fusarium isolates infectious on wheat from India. Both Indian isolates retained conserved Fusarium secondary metabolite clusters, including aurofusarin, chrysogine, clavaric acid, koraiol, orcinol/orsellinic acid, and oxyjavanicin, while exhibiting distinct species-associated biosynthetic profiles. TNW1 contained zearalenone and DON-related biosynthetic clusters, whereas DMW8 contained beauvericin and other species -associated clusters, highlighting differences in predicted biosynthetic potential between the two Fusarium species. Notably, both genomes showed relatively low transposable-element (TE) content compared with their respective species groups, with TEs occupying 0.96% of the TNW1 genome and 1.55% of the DMW8 genome. RIP-associated genomic coverage was also comparatively low, at 20.01% and 22.38%, respectively. TE insertion analysis identified predominantly reference-associated insertions, with two candidate non-reference insertions detected in DMW8. Gene-family analyses revealed greater duplication and expansion contraction dynamics in DMW8 than in TNW1. Together, these findings highlight differences in predicted genomic features, secondary metabolite biosynthetic potential, and gene family composition between the two Indian isolates, providing genomic resources for future investigations of Fusarium biology and wheat pathogen interactions.

Title: Systematic prediction of genetic variance in a line development program
Authors: Bernardo, R.
Abstract: To date, predicting the genetic variance (VG) in biparental crosses has been unreliable. My objective was to determine if predicting VG via tabular analysis, which was developed assuming free recombination and having known VG in founder crosses, is effective even if these unrealistic assumptions are unmet. With line X being developed from the P1/P2 cross, the VG in X/Y was predicted as VX/Y = {lambda}1VP1/Y + {lambda}2VP2/Y, where {lambda}1 was the parental contribution of P1 to X and {lambda}2 was the parental contribution of P2 to X. Simulations involved four founder lines with biallelic marker loci and multiple alleles at quantitative trait loci. The VG in each founder cross was estimated from simulated phenotypic values of N lines under varying heritability (h2). Non-founder lines were developed successively from the founders. Among the 774 non-founder crosses, the mean correlation between the true VG and predicted VG ranged from 0.49 (N = 50 and h2 = 0.20) to 0.70 (N = 400 to 1000 and h2 [≥] 0.50). The mean regression of predicted VG on true VG was 0.51-0.52. Having N = 100-200 lines was sufficient for estimating VG. Free recombination increased the regression of predicted VG on true VG to 0.87 and the correlation between the two to 0.64-0.93. Overall, the results suggested that tabular analysis is currently the most effective method for predicting VG. Further research is needed on combining VG estimates in both founder and non-founder crosses when conducting tabular analysis in a breeding program.

Title: Multimodal Structural and Regulatory Architecture of Coding and Non-Coding Variants Across the Orofacial Clefting TP63-IRF6-GRHL3 Network
Authors: Vono, F. M.; Santos, V. G.; Toledo, A. N. d.
Abstract: Pathogenic variation across the TP63-IRF6-GRHL3 transcriptional network causes syndromic and nonsyndromic orofacial clefts (OFCs), yet scalar sequence predictors collapse distinct failure modes and leave isoform-specific coding variants, splice-altering indels, and distal enhancer alleles unresolved. Here, we integrate 29 AlphaFold 3 (AF3) assemblies (10 wild-type, 19 mutant), thermodynamic stability ({Delta}{Delta}G) calculations, and AlphaGenome regulatory modeling across clinical, saturation-mutagenesis, and reporter benchmarks. In strict leave-one-gene-out (LOGO) coding benchmarks, replacing paralog crystal templates with full-length human AF3 structures improves IRF6 classification (biophysical AUROC rising from 0.7844 to 0.8967; {Delta}{Delta}G from 0.6461 to 0.8516) and resolves canonical isoform gaps in the 602-residue MANE Select GRHL3 homodimer. Projecting IRF6 missense variants onto a two-dimensional stability-versus-interface phase plane separates dominant-negative popliteal pterygium syndrome (PPS) poisons from haploinsufficient Van der Woude syndrome (VWS1) alleles (VWS1-versus-PPS Quadrant I odds ratio [OR] = 0.0263 [reciprocal OR = 38.0], p = 4.652 x 10-3) and distinguishes DNA-contact poisons from dimer-unfolding alleles across 12 zebrafish in vivo assays. Atomistic base-readout contacts in the AF3 TP63-MCS9.7 tetramer mirror loss-of-function profiles in MaveDB ({rho} = 0.6048, p = 6.52 x 10-4) and AlphaGenome keratinocyte DNase predictions ({rho} = 0.6040, p = 6.65 x 10-4). Across non-coding benchmarks, AlphaGenome splicing tracks reach an AUROC of 0.9876 while prioritizing cryptic splice variants of uncertain significance, and epithelial chromatin tracks capture enhancer grammar, plasmid-cloning artifacts, and context-dependent ARHGAP29, FOXE1, and local 8q24 chromatin effects within AlphaGenome's 1.049-Mb horizon.

Title: Comparative metagenomics reveals diversity and metabolic heterogeneity of sediment microbes from the Great Barrier Reef
Authors: Ishida, H.; Robbins, S. J.; Bell, S. C.; Lim, J. Y.; Terzin, M.; Webster, N.; Bourne, D. G.; Laffy, P. W.; Hugenholtz, P.; Yeoh, Y. K.; Chan, C. X.
Abstract: Microbial communities in coral reefs are highly connected through benthic-pelagic coupling. Pelagic and host-associated microbiomes have recently been characterised via genome-resolved metagenomics. However, similar characterisation of sediment communities has lagged behind due to their higher complexity. Here, using short- and long-read shotgun sequence data, we characterised sediment microbial communities of Australia's Great Barrier Reef. From 191 samples across 48 broadly distributed sites, we recovered 2,698 prokaryotic metagenome-assembled genomes (MAGs) representing 1,201 species-level clusters, most of which are novel. Compared against their sympatric counterparts in seawater, sediment MAGs exhibited greater phylogenetic diversity and flexibility in metabolic potential, implicating diverse respiration strategies and cycling of nitrogen, sulphur, and hydrogen. They also encode more abundant and novel biosynthetic capabilities, likely reflecting competition and adaptation to intermittent fluctuations in nutrient regimes, and between oxic and anoxic conditions. Our results provide foundational genomic resources for reef sediment microbes, uncovering biodiversity and function that together with planktonic microbes shape the ecological success and stability of coral reef ecosystems.

Title: MARRI: Mechanism-Aware Learning of RNA-RNA Interactions with Foundation Models
Authors: Wang, B.; Luo, H.; Meng, Z.; Chen, G.; Wang, X.; Chen, Y.; Song, J.; Loscalzo, J.; Xu, H.
Abstract: RNA-RNA interactions (RRIs) are central to post-transcriptional regulation, yet their prediction requires accounting for structural accessibility and intermolecular base pairing beyond sequence complementarity. Pretrained RNA foundation models provide representations of individual RNAs, but translating these representations into interaction predictions requires mechanistic knowledge of interaction recognition. Here, we introduce MARRI, a mechanism-aware multimodal framework that couples pretrained representations with domain knowledge by embedding learned opening penalties and hybridization gains into bidirectional cross-RNA attention. MARRI improves ROC--AUC and PR--AUC over the strongest baseline by 12.20\% and 10.25\%, respectively, and maintains strong discrimination for unseen RNA partnerships and interaction regions. Perturbation and repeat-context analyses identify prediction-relevant sequence regions. Integrating MARRI-derived interaction propensities with disease-associated expression profiles links molecular prediction to systems-level models of disease progression and network remodeling. MARRI thus illustrates a knowledge-guided strategy for coupling molecular foundation models with domain knowledge to support grounded prediction, interpretation and systems-level hypothesis generation.

Title: LipidRT: leveraging retention time coherence for robust lipid annotation in reversed-phase LC-MS-based lipidomics
Authors: Regal-Marques, C.; Alcoriza-Balaguer, M. I.; Cermakova, H.; Roca, M.; Juan-Vidal, O.; Carretero, J.; Gradillas, A.; Barbas, C.; Garcia-Canaveras, J. C.; Lahoz, A.
Abstract: MS/MS data alone is often insufficient for confident lipid identification, while existing retention time (RT)-based methods, despite their promise, have limited applicability. We present LipidRT, an R-based Shiny application that uses RT coherence to validate, refine and expand lipid annotations in untargeted RPLC-HRMS lipidomics in a dataset-specific, software-agnostic manner. By exploiting conserved chromatographic elution relationships as structural constraints and excluding RT-inconsistent annotations from model fitting, LipidRT improves annotation confidence, coverage and consistency while minimizing manual curation.

Title: spicyR enables robust, well-powered co-localisation tests in large spatial omics cohorts
Authors: Dohadwalla, S.; Rao, S.; Ameen, F.; Willie, E.; Ormerod, J. T.; Patrick, E.
Abstract: Spatial omics technologies can now profile finely resolved cell populations in patient tissue at scale, offering a way to link their arrangement to outcomes. Yet images often differ in size, shape and cell content, and existing tests between patient groups mistake these differences for co-localisation or weight every image equally. We present spicyR v2, which avoids both problems with a fast, permutation-free test that accounts for these differences and weights each image by how precisely it measures co-localisation. In simulations and 74 analyses of 42 public datasets, it controlled false discoveries, had more power than spicyR v1 and was robust to tears, holes and differences in cell number that misled other methods. These analyses also revealed that many studies relating co-localisation to clinical outcomes are underpowered, and spicyR v2 can estimate the number of patients a new study needs. spicyR v2 analyses 100 million cells in minutes, making robust, well-powered tests of co-localisation practical for large spatial omics cohorts.

Title: Quantifying Homology and Length Bias in Antimicrobial Peptide Prediction
Authors: Paul, B. K.; Dip, S. A.; Shehu, A.; Moni, M. A.; Zhang, L.
Abstract: Bacteria are becoming resistant to existing antibiotics faster than new ones are found. Antimicrobial peptides are a promising alternative, but laboratory testing is slow and costly. Candidates are therefore ranked first by a classifier, and published classifiers report near-perfect accuracy. Two controls are missing from the benchmarks behind those numbers. Training and test peptides are not separated by sequence homology. The negative class is not matched to the positive class by length. We propose a controlled evaluation protocol that imposes both, plus a sample-size control that separates matching from the data it removes. We apply it to a four-model ensemble of our own and ten baselines on a benchmark of 16,168 sequences, holding the models fixed. A classifier given nothing but peptide length separates the benchmark far above chance. Homology control costs 0.067 MCC and length matching a further 0.115, taking the reported score from 0.834 to 0.661. Over ten redrawn partitions the length term holds while the homology term shrinks, so length is the effect that survives. The protocol also reorders the methods, and a frozen ESM-2 embedding overtakes the ensemble. Three published benchmarks show the same pattern. We recommend a minimum reporting standard that makes such losses visible.

Title: Learning spatial cellular state through 3D reconstruction of the cell
Authors: Lee, Y. J.; Anad, K.; Min, S.; Lugo-Martinez, J.
Abstract: Subcellular-resolution spatial transcriptomics localizes individual RNA transcripts within cells with high-precision. Existing methods for identifying spatially organized cell populations rely on cellular niches defined by neighboring cells, leaving open whether such populations can be identified from individual-cell representations alone. Moreover, representations that jointly capture transcript identity and three-dimensional (3D) spatial organization have not been systematically learned or biologically evaluated. Here we present a representation learning framework that models each cell as a gene-annotated point cloud of transcripts and trains a rotation-equivariant neural network to reconstruct 3D cell shape, yielding spatially informed transcript embeddings. We further aggregate these embeddings into a cell-state representation that summarizes transcript-level spatial patterns. Our framework outperforms existing point-cloud-based 3D reconstruction methods on cell-shape reconstruction. In MERFISH human uterine cancer, combining the learned embeddings with gene expression improved prediction of CD45RO protein intensity over both gene expression alone and niche-based embeddings. Applied to MERFISH human liver cancer and Xenium human lung datasets, our framework identified distinct spatial patterns between cell populations, including spatially organized subpopulations marked by disease-associated gene expression and patterns associated with pathological tissue structures. Together, these results show that learning transcript representations through 3D cell reconstruction provides a novel approach to capture cell-state heterogeneity and biologically relevant spatial organization in subcellular spatial transcriptomics.

Title: Benchmarking four large language models on generating and selecting hypotheses that match published findings in 50 studies of ageing biology
Authors: Poteshkin, Y.; Udodov, E.; Batin, M.
Abstract: Objective We asked how often hypotheses generated by large language models for 50 research tasks matched the withheld finding of the published study, and whether model forecasts could identify the matching hypotheses. Methods We built tasks from 50 peer-reviewed studies in ageing biology published after the models' stated training cutoffs; each task gave the background and a research question and withheld the study's finding (the reference finding). GPT-6 Astra, Grok 4.5, Claude Opus 5.5, and Gemini 4 Argon each generated five hypotheses per task by three methods: a single request, a multistep pipeline, and the Omega Point method without literature search (2997 hypotheses). A hypothesis matched the reference finding if at least two of three judge models from other developers scored it at least 3 (primary threshold) or at least 4 (strict threshold) on a 0 to 5 scale; refusals counted as non-matches. A selection rule, chosen from 112 variants evaluated on the Grok 4.5 hypotheses, kept only the hypotheses for which all four predictor models forecast experimental confirmation; the predictors never saw the published finding. The controls were recorded random answers and each generator's first-listed hypothesis. Confidence intervals (95% CIs) were calculated by cluster bootstrap over tasks. Results Of the hypotheses generated by a single request, 13.2% to 18.0% matched the reference finding, compared with 11.2% to 18.8% for the multistep pipeline and 2.8% to 7.6% for the Omega Point method. With a single request, the hypothesis listed first matched in 37.5% of cases (75/200), and the hypotheses in positions 2 to 5 matched in 10.1% (81/800). Among the hypotheses selected unanimously, the match rate was 73.7% (14/19) for Grok 4.5, 47.4% (9/19) for Gemini 4 Argon, and 63.6% (14/22) for Claude Opus 5.5, compared with 12.1% to 17.9% for the random control and 37.5% to 40.0% for the first-listed hypotheses. The selected lists captured 27.3% to 35.0% of all matching hypotheses. Pooled across the three sets, the match rate among selected hypotheses exceeded that among first-listed hypotheses by 23.2 percentage points (pp; 95% CI [13.0, 32.6]). When Gemini 4 Argon re-extracted the reference findings, the match rate among selected hypotheses was 59.6% (34/57), compared with 61.4% (35/57) against the original reference findings for the same tasks. In a manual audit with the generator, judge scores, and selection status hidden, our classifications agreed with the judges' at the primary threshold in 81/100 cases (Cohen's kappa 0.62). Agreement was 89.7% after weighting the sample strata by their size in the corpus. We classified 19 of 30 sampled selected hypotheses as matches, and the judges classified 20 of 30. Conclusions In the evaluated sets, unanimous selection by the four predictors increased the match rate among selected hypotheses; the resulting match rate depended on the matching threshold. Generators listed a matching hypothesis first more often than in later positions, and 50 of the 60 selected hypotheses were listed first. The advantage over the first-listed hypotheses and over the best single predictor at equal list length was statistically significant for the Grok and Opus hypotheses but not for the Gemini hypotheses, and the pairwise differences of the advantage between generators were not statistically significant (p >= 0.16 after Holm correction). We selected the rule using the Grok hypotheses and evaluated it on the Gemini and Opus hypotheses for the same 50 tasks; it has not been tested on new tasks.

Title: CD44-DT regulates p21-dependent senescence via interacting with AR-PCNA complex, revealing a therapeutic vulnerability to chimeric ncRNA-mediated AR degradation in prostate cancer
Authors: Hakiminia, F.; Kallenbach, J.; Schindler, K.; Atri Roozbahani, G.; Rahnis, N.; Baniahmad, A.; Asadi, M. H.
Abstract: Aberrant androgen receptor (AR) signaling driven by androgens plays a critical role in prostate cancer (PCa) progression. Interestingly, bipolar androgen therapy (BAT), a novel therapeutic strategy with cycles between near-castrate and supraphysiological androgen levels (SAL), suppresses PCa growth. SAL induces cellular senescence in various PCa models mediated by the AR, activation of AKT signaling and hypophosphorylation of pRb. Here, we show that SAL upregulates the lncRNA CD44-DT, the CD44 divergent transcript, in PCa cells linking CD44-DT to AR signaling. Knockdown and overexpression datasets suggest that CD44-DT supresses SAL-induced senescence as a negative feed-back loop. Transcriptome, ATAC-seq, and ChIP-seq analyses of PCa cells reveal that AR is recruited to the first intron of CD44 gene locus. Transcriptome analyses of the knockdown suggests that members of AP-1 family act in concert with AR as an upstream activator of CD44-DT. Accordingly, inhibition of the AP-1 complex by a small molecule inhibitor results in downregulation of CD44-DT expression, enhanced SAL-induced senescence and reduced proliferation. Mechanistically, CD44-DT physically interacts with PCNA and AR. This interaction facilitates p21 tumor suppressor degradation, permits cyclin-CDK activation, retinoblastoma (Rb) hyperphosphorylation activation of the AKT-p70S6K pathway. These findings suggest that CD44-DT is part of AR signaling and acts as a novel onco-lncRNA that is upregulated by AR. To validate the role of AR, we engineered a chimeric ncRNA capable degrading the AR as a novel type of RNA-PROTAC. Accordingly, this RNA-based AR-degrader downregulates CD44-DT confirming AR regulation of CD44-DT. Interestingly, the RNA-PROTAC potently induces apoptosis. Thus, the data suggest that CD44-DT is a novel direct AR target gene that modulates PCNA and p21 protein stability identifying a novel negative feed-back loop at the crossroad between proliferation and senescence indicating CD44-DT as a potential therapeutic target for PCa.

Title: Doublecortin like kinase 1 (DCLK1) interacts with BRG1 chromatin remodeler and regulates neuronal activity-induced gene activation
Authors: Luo, Y.; Kim, B.; Haghighinajafabadi, N.; Westover, K. D.; Wu, J.
Abstract: SWI/SNF-like BAF ATP-dependent chromatin remodeling complexes play important roles in neural development and plasticity by regulating neural gene expression, especially in response to neuronal stimulations. Previously, we have shown that BRG1, the core subunit of BAF, undergoes neuronal activity-induced phosphorylation, which is important for the expression of a group of activity regulated genes (ARGs). Proteomic analyses identified Doublecortin like kinase 1 (DCLK1) as a novel BRG1 interacting protein. Neuronal depolarization induces nuclear enrichment of DCLK1 and increases interactions between BRG1 and DCLK1. We showed that the DCLK1 kinase domain and BRG1 C-terminal fragments are sufficient to mediate their interaction. Thus, DCLK1 is a candidate kinase responsible for BRG1 phosphorylation in response to neuronal activation. Using DCLK1 specific inhibitors and kinase inactive mutations, we showed that DCLK1, in a kinase activity dependent manner, promotes BRG1 phosphorylation and ARG activation. Thus, we identified a novel interacting kinase of BAF chromatin remodeling complex that regulates ARG expression. Because abnormal expression and mutations of both BAF complexes and DCLK1 are associated with neural disorders and cancer, our study provides molecular insights into their functions in these diseases.

Title: An open-source semi-automated workflow for multi-omics sample extraction
Authors: Hall, D. R.; Trejo, J. B.; Bredeweg, E. L.; Tate, K. L.; Eder, J. G.; Lalli, P. M.; Piehowski, P.; Liu, T.; Shishkov, O.; DeSousa, K.; Gritsenko, M. A.
Abstract: Multiomics analysis relies on extracting metabolites lipids and proteins from a single sample A widely used method for this is Metabolomics Proteomics and Lipidomics Extraction MPLEx a triphasic chloroform methanol water extraction but it is manually intensive and depends on skilled operators working around a fragile protein layer Here we present OpenMPLEx a semi automated MPLEx workflow for low cost open source Opentrons liquid handlers A minor change in chemistry pellets the protein so that a robot can collect the aqueous and organic phases from above We compared the automated workflow with two manual MPLEx protocols by liquid chromatography mass spectrometry LC MS based proteomics lipidomics and metabolomics The methods were roughly equivalent and measured similar differences between growth media We then scaled the workflow to 96 well plates and tested it on an 80 sample Pseudomonas putida experiment One operator took all 80 samples from cell pellets to LC MS data in a working week with about 3 h of hands on time rather than days at the bench and quantified about 3 900 protein groups All scripts labware definitions and print files are open source so that other laboratories can adapt the workflow

Title: Single-dose neonatal gene therapy preserves motor coordination and extends survival of Polg-deficient mice
Authors: Zanin, S.; Moriceau, S.; Afram, E.; Perez-Cartier, M. T.; Gaborit, C.; Simon Sola, M.; Kneeland, S. C.; Murray, S. A.; Munnich, A.; Ruzzenente, B.; Metodiev, M. D.
Abstract: POLG mutations are the most common single nuclear gene cause of mitochondrial disease. POLG disease spans a spectrum of clinical presentations with variable age of onset and severity. Early-onset disease is often severe and fatal (e.g., Alpers syndrome, myocerebrohepatopathy), while late-onset disease can be relatively mild (e.g., progressive external ophthalmoplegia). POLG disease is incurable, with few symptomatic treatments available, none of which can prevent its progression. Gene replacement therapy has the potential to halt or prevent POLG disease, but its development has been hindered by the large size of the POLG cDNA and the scarcity of suitable mouse models. Here, we developed a bespoke Polg knockout (KO) mouse model by inactivating the Polg locus in parvalbumin-expressing neurons (e.g., Purkinje cells) and fast-twitch skeletal muscle fibers. KO mice developed progressive motor coordination deficits, respiratory chain deficiency in Purkinje cells and skeletal muscle, and died prematurely. We also developed nine AAV-based gene therapy vectors and confirmed their ability to deliver and express the human POL{gamma}A protein in different mouse tissues. A single high-dose administration of either of two lead candidates into Polg KO neonates preserved respiratory chain activity in Purkinje cells and skeletal muscle, delayed the onset of motor coordination deficits, and extended lifespan. Thus, our work provides preclinical proof of concept for gene replacement therapy for POLG disease, establishing the feasibility of this approach and laying the foundation for further development in the field.

Title: Convergent Genomic Signatures of Selection in Thar: Genetic trade-offs for desert survival
Authors: Rathod, S. M.; Jain, R.; Mukerji, M.
Abstract: Background: Desert environments provide a setting for natural biological experiments to cope up with simultaneous stressors of extreme temperatures, aridity, UV exposure, and limited food resources. Biological adaptations that support living in such an environment could become liabilities when the environment and lifestyle change due to gene-environment mismatch. We explored whether genetically and culturally diverse endogamous native populations of the Thar exhibit convergent signatures of selection to desert conditions and whether the selected loci have implications in traits and disease susceptibilities relevant to non-native transitions. Results: We report 348 high-confidence variants across 45 candidate genes from a study on 176 individuals from eight genetically distinct Thar populations. These genes identified from humans and other desert inhabitants display convergent evolution with multiple selection scans (PBSn1, Tajima`s D, iHS, and XPEHH) in diverse Thar populations. Prominent genes include ZNF385D, SGCZ, SARDH, SLC12A3, etc. Selected variants essential in the desert environment were associated with complex traits like lipid metabolism, hypertension, renal and cardiovascular diseases, and addiction in GWAS and PheWAS. Noteworthy, in a syntenic locus, eQTLs in SARDH, which modulates DBH implicated in addiction, suggest a potential link with survival advantage in an uncertain desert environment. Likewise, a selected variant (rs7204044) in SLC12A3, implicated in hypertension in non-desert populations, seems to be a key to water-salt homeostasis in desert natives. Conclusions: These findings suggest that variants linked to adaptive traits in desert conditions could be linked to maladaptation in an altered environment. This has potential health consequences in climatic and lifestyle transitions among native inhabitants.

Title: SAM-Dependent Precursor Peptide Engagement by Darobactin Maturase DarE
Authors: Zhu, W.
Abstract: Radical S-adenosylmethionine (SAM) enzymes that synthesize structurally constrained ribosomally synthesized and post-translationally modified peptides (RiPPs) with therapeutic potential mostly do so by employing a dedicated RiPP recognition element (RRE). With the growing number of RRE-free maturases discovered, how these enzymes engage their substrates remains largely unexplored. In this work, we mapped substrate-enzyme interactions in DarE, an RRE-free radical SAM enzyme that installs the C-C and C-O-C crosslinks of the antibiotic darobactin during the first step of darobactin biosynthesis. Using anaerobic hydrogen-deuterium exchange mass spectrometry (HDX-MS), we simultaneously resolved specific regions within the enzyme and its precursor peptide substrate, DarA, across five complex states. The N-terminal extension and part of the TIM-barrel domain of DarE, along with the leader region of DarA, become protected, revealing the peptide-engagement interface. Additional protection emerged only in the presence of SAM, identifying SAM as a key contributor to precursor-peptide engagement in an RRE-free RiPP maturase. Electron paramagnetic resonance spectroscopy further demonstrated precursor peptide-dependent perturbations of the chemical environment of the iron-sulfur clusters. These findings suggest that SAM-dependent peptide engagement, mediated in part by the N-terminal extension of the radical SAM enzyme, provides an alternative mechanism for precursor-peptide recognition in RRE-free RiPP maturases. Our work also demonstrates the utility of anaerobic HDX-MS for characterizing protein-peptide-small molecule interactions in oxygen-sensitive metalloenzymes.

Title: Glycoform Distributions and Heparan Sulfate Binding of Intact SARS-CoV-2 Spike Variants by DIA-ECCR Native Mass Spectrometry
Authors: Xu, Z.; Du, C.; Olmedillas, E.; Saphire, E. O.; Wysocki, V.
Abstract: Glycosylation influences the structure, immunogenicity, and evolutionary selection of the SARS CoV 2 spike protein (S), but its extensive heterogeneity has hindered characterization of intact glycoform distributions. Here, we illustrate a data-independent analysis - electron capture charge reduction (DIA-ECCR) native mass spectrometry workflow for direct analysis of intact spike glycoforms across multiple variants. DIA-ECCR resolves variant-dependent differences in glycoform distributions and higher mass subpopulations. Monte Carlo simulations based on published site-specific bottom-up glycoproteomic data reproduce the central mass of the D614G experimental distribution and support a connection between intact and bottom-up measurements, while the broader experimental distributions and a second Gamma subpopulation indicate heterogeneity not captured by the simulations Mass photometry and charge detection mass spectrometry provide orthogonal measurements consistent with the DIA-ECCR results. DIA-ECCR also resolves mass shifts associated with binding of truncated heparan sulfate, demonstrating analysis of a heterogeneous protein:ligand complex. Together, these results outline a practical workflow that combines DIA-ECCR with native mass spectrometry (nMS) for characterizing intact glycoform distributions and ligand binding in highly heterogeneous glycoprotein assemblies, with potential applications in antigen characterization, vaccine design, and biopharmaceutical quality control.

Title: Crystal structure of the first de novo designed phosphotriesterase ZAPP-1
Authors: Woodbury, S. M.; Kim, D.; Mendoza, J.; Kang, A.; Nguyen, H.; Bera, A. K.; Baker, D.
Abstract: Designing a de novo phosphotriesterase requires scaffolding a dinuclear metal center bound by six catalytic residues, including a post-translationally carbamylated lysine, in a pocket that must also bind a small, flexible organophosphate and orient it for hydrolysis. We recently met this challenge using RFdiffusion3 to design the first de novo phosphotriesterases, and biochemically characterized our first hit, ZAPP-1 [1]. Here we report two crystal structures of ZAPP-1 at 1.42 and 2.28 [A] resolution. The crystal structures are nearly identical to the design model scaffold (C RMSD = 0.69, 0.71, and 0.99 [A] for three copies across two independent crystals), and the higher-resolution crystal assembles the dinuclear Zn(II) site in the designed pocket with carbamylated K16. The catalytic residues are near the designed geometry but demonstrate flexibility across the structures, albeit mostly rotameric (C{beta} RMSD [≤] 0.8 [A] for both copies in form 1). AlphaFold3 predicts the designed catalytic conformation with substrate bound and the observed crystallographic deviations without it, suggesting an induced-fit mechanism upon substrate binding.
