Together with prior biochemical characterization, there is strong evidence that ZAPP-1 functions as designed, validating the high precision achievable with our RFdiffusion3 design pipeline, but the structures suggest that future design should better preorganize the active site. The ability to design experimentally accurate and increasingly sophisticated enzymes directly from the computer should enable a new future of programmable catalysis and chemistry.

Title: Multi-Layer Functional Metabolomics Reveals Chemical Interactions Between the Plant-Associated Bacterium Serratia marcescens and Phytophthora
Authors: Herrera Rosero, D.; Geibel, C.; Waqas, M.; Gross, H.; Mordhorst, S.; Petras, D.
Abstract: Oomycete pathogens of the genus Phytophthora cause devastating crop losses worldwide, highlighting the need for novel biocontrol agents. Here, we developed a multi-layer functional metabolomics workflow that incorporates an LC-MS/MS-based metal infusion assay in combination with microfractionation-based bioassays against Phytophthora infestans and metal-binding assays to map bioactivity from Serratia marcescens extracts. MS/MS analysis and feature-based molecular networking supported the annotation of activity-associated metabolites, including prodigiosin, serratiochelins, and an uncharacterized putative serratiochelin analog designated serratiochelin G. Complementary chrome azurol S assays and post-column iron infusion provided evidence of iron-binding properties. Comparative genomic analysis and L-lysine supplementation supported a proposed biosynthetic origin of serratiochelin G involving cadaverine incorporation. This workflow enables metabolite prioritization by integrating non-targeted LC-MS/MS with chromatographically resolved bioactivity and complementary functional assays.

Title: Mechanistic Insights into ADAR1-p110 Nuclear Import: A Dual-Interface Interaction with Transportin-1
Authors: Chin, D. H. R.; Zhou, J.; Luo, Y.; Hong, D.; Tan, Y. B.; Chen, P. L.; Luo, D.
Abstract: The human ADAR1 exists as two isoforms: the predominantly cytoplasmic-localized p150, recognized for its role in suppression of aberrant immune activation, and the predominantly nuclear-localized p110 (missing the N terminal Z domain), whose biological functions remain less understood but are thought to rely heavily on its subcellular localization. Despite its structural similarity to the Z domain unique to ADAR1-p150, the functional significance of the Z{beta} domain shared by both isoforms remains unclear. Here, we identify an additional mechanism contributing to the nuclear import of ADAR1-p110 through a dual-interface interaction with transportin-1 (TNPO1), involving both the Z{beta} and dsRBD3 domains of ADAR1. Using cryo-electron microscopy, we show that Z{beta} engages TNPO1 at its canonical cargo-binding groove, while dsRBD3 binds at a peripheral site overlapping the RanGTP binding interface. Structure-guided mutagenesis and biochemical analyses support the contribution of Z{beta} to TNPO1 recognition. Disruption of the interaction between ADAR1 Z{beta} domain and TNPO1 alters the nucleocytoplasmic distribution of ADAR1-p110, resulting in increased cytoplasmic accumulation despite the retention of the previously characterized dsRBD3-associated nuclear localization signal. Furthermore, cytoplasmic redistribution of ADAR1-p110 mutants is accompanied by global suppression of cytosolic innate immune signaling pathways and reduced expression of interferon-stimulated genes. Together, these findings identify ADAR1 Z{beta} as an additional TNPO1-recognition element synergizing with dsRBD3 that contributes to ADAR1-p110 nuclear localization and highlight the relationship between its subcellular distribution and immune regulatory activity.

Title: Toward Standardized Fucoidan Extractions from Brown Algae: Optimization of Under-Addressed Parameters to Maximize Yield and Purity
Authors: Carstens-Kass, J.; Dedow, L. K.; Braybrook, S. A.
Abstract: Brown algal cell walls contain unique polysaccharides called fucoidans, which exhibit complex structural diversity and have applications across a range of industries. For these applications, fucoidan extraction methods should maximize yield while minimizing co-extracted impurities. However, extraction protocols vary widely, and their effects on yield and purity are rarely investigated. Thus, standardized and optimized fucoidan extraction methods are needed. Here, we aimed to identify optimal parameters for selected steps of a fucoidan extraction protocol. Starting with a commonly used protocol, we experimentally investigated three steps critical to yield and purity: (1) alcohol-insoluble residue preparation, (2) alginate removal, and (3) ion removal by dialysis. Our results show that sequential washes with 70% and 100% ethanol removed proteins, lipids, polyphenols, and pigments during alcohol-insoluble residue preparation without sacrificing fucoidan yield. We also demonstrate that extraction in calcium chloride solution reduces alginate-associated epitopes, while extraction in water does not. Finally, we show that dialysis with a membrane having a high molecular weight cut-off (12.4 kDa) results in fucoidan loss. Together, these findings inform specific recommendations for these three steps and provide a foundation for more standardized fucoidan extraction methods. Greater standardization could improve comparability across studies while facilitating the production of higher-yielding, purer fucoidan extracts for future research and downstream applications.

Title: ProlateNet: Sampling-rate transfer of convolutional networks with a weights-only certificate for physiological signals
Authors: Cui, H.; Zhu, Y.; Li, B.; Huang, S.; Xu, T.
Abstract: A central goal of physiological signal analysis is to train a model once and deploy it across recording systems. However, these systems sample EEG and ECG at different rates, and a network trained at one rate loses accuracy at the others. Continuous-kernel networks were built to solve this problem, but published ones still fail at unseen rates, and no existing method can certify a trained model before deployment. In this study, we propose ProlateNet, which builds kernels from prolate spheroidal wave functions to suppress aliasing across sampling rates and certifies a trained model from its weights alone. Across fourteen first-layer designs trained at one rate on three public EEG and ECG datasets, the published continuous-kernel layers FlexConv and sampling-frequency-independent (SFI) convolution show mean worst drops of 0.18 and 0.35 macro-F1 on SEED. ProlateNet is the only design that is stable and accurate on all three datasets with an error bound fixed before training, and its mean worst drop is at most 0.003. Without target-rate recordings, its certificate ranks the continuous-kernel designs on SEED by measured transfer with Spearman {rho} = 0.92, against 0.68 for energy above the training Nyquist frequency. Overall, ProlateNet shows that controlling aliasing enables convolutional networks to transfer across sampling rates and provides principled guidance for building physiological signal models that are trained once and deployed across recording systems.

Title: Biochemical selection on conserved glycans yield a cross-species AAV capsid for efficient panretinal intravitreal delivery
Authors: Wang, J.-H.; Cui, M.; Zhao, W.; Giguere, D.; Yang, Y.; Su, Q.; He, R.; Xie, J.; Xie, Q.; Ke, X.; Seddon, J. M.; Punzo, C.; Gao, G.
Abstract: Inherited retinal diseases are leading candidates for gene therapy, but photoreceptor-directed adeno-associated virus (AAV) vectors still require subretinal injection, which treats only part of the retina and carries surgical risk. Intravitreal delivery is simple and panretinal, yet inner-retinal barriers block most capsids, and capsids selected in one species rarely translate. Mapping retinal glycans across seven mammals, we found heparan sulfate (HS) marking the inner limiting membrane and terminal N-acetylglucosamine (GlcNAc) enriched on photoreceptor segments. These invariants defined a two-part design principle, attenuated HS binding with strong terminal GlcNAc engagement, implemented as a sequential in vitro selection, Conserved Receptor-Selection Technology (CReST). Its lead GlcNAc-selected capsid, AAV2.IvtB, increased retinal transgene expression 6.5-fold over AAV2.7m8 in mice and photoreceptor transduction 2.5-fold in pigs, acting through terminal GlcNAc engagement. It partially preserved photoreceptors in rd10 mice and suppressed laser-induced choroidal neovascularization. CReST is a receptor-guided, animal-free route to capsids with a defined, conserved mechanism.

Title: Force Volume Atomic Force Microscopy of THP-1 and Primary Mouse Macrophages Reveals that the Mechanical Signature of Macrophage Polarization is Model-Dependent
Authors: Cantero, B.; Cano, M.; Aiassa, L.; Codano, C.; Strawbridge, S.; Rizzello, L.; Battaglia, G.; Gomila, G.; Calo, A.
Abstract: Macrophages are immune cells with a rich morphological variety and markedly different biological functions when differentiated into M0 (non-activated) macrophages or polarized into M1 (pro-inflammatory) and M2 (anti-inflammatory) phenotypes. Atomic force microscopy (AFM) studies have recently associated a mechanical dimension with macrophage polarization. Herein, the elastic properties of the three phenotypes are measured and compared by force volume AFM in two less explored models: THP-1-derived macrophages (cell line) and mouse bone marrow-derived macrophages (BMDMs, primary cells). High-indentation measurements (indentation higher than 2 micrometers) with colloidal probes capture the full cell deformation, and a recently derived spherical model with bottom effect correction provides quantitative values of the Youngs modulus (E) that account for substrate effects and cell height with the correct probe geometry. THP-1-derived macrophages show significant mechanical differences, with EM1 higher than EM2 and EM0, whereas BMDMs show no significant differences between phenotypes. Furthermore, BMDM-derived M0 and M2 macrophages show 1.5 to 2 times higher E than the corresponding THP-1 phenotypes. The elasticity of cells with different shapes is also evaluated to account for the heterogeneous macrophage morphology found in all samples. These results indicate that the mechanical signature of macrophage polarization is model-dependent.

Title: Membrane Biofouling and Plasmid Conformation Shape the Retention of Antibiotic Resistance Gene-Carrying Plasmids during Ultrafiltration
Authors: Chen, W.; Serrano, F. R.; Kallies, R.; Müller, S.; Musat, N.; Schattenberg, F.; Schmidt, M.; Seifert, H.; Wang, G.; Worrich, A.
Abstract: Antimicrobial resistance poses a growing threat to human and environmental health, and wastewater treatment plants are important pathways for the release of antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs). Although ultrafiltration (UF) membranes effectively retain antibiotic-resistant bacteria, their capacity to remove extracellular ARGs remains less understood. Extracellular plasmids are concerning because they persist following cell lysis and may contribute to horizontal gene transfer. Unlike intact bacterial cells, these flexible DNA molecules may pass through membrane barriers. Here, we investigated the removal of extracellular plasmids carrying ARGs using a 100 kDa molecular weight cut-off (MWCO) UF membrane, focusing on biofouling, plasmid size, and conformation. Initial filtration experiments achieved removal efficiency (RE) above 99.9% for antibiotic-resistant bacteria and plasmids, and produced a pronounced biofouling layer. For the pre-fouled membrane, mass balances showed increased adsorption and permeation of plasmids, with RE declining from approximately 99% to below 95% over consecutive runs. Microscopy indicated plasmid deposition in biofouled regions. Additionally, plasmid size showed no consistent relationship with RE, while conformation had a pronounced effect, with supercoiled plasmids being retained more efficiently (98.8-99.6%) than their linear counterparts (82.4-92.4%). These findings demonstrate that plasmid retention by UF is influenced by both membrane conditions and DNA conformation, which nominal membrane pore size alone cannot capture. The high RE highlights the potential of UF as a tertiary treatment, while emphasizing the need to account for biofouling and DNA structural diversity when evaluating strategies to reduce extracellular ARG discharge from wastewater treatment plants.

Title: nf-core/pairgenomealign: a scalable pipeline for pairwise whole-genome alignment
Authors: Plessy, C.; Mahdi, M.; Fujita, T.; Frith, M. C.; Luscombe, N. M.
Abstract: Genome assemblies are accumulating rapidly across the Tree of Life, creating a growing need for reproducible and scalable methods for whole-genome comparison. We developed nf-core/pairgenomealign, a Nextflow workflow that automates pairwise genome alignment using the LAST software suite and produces standard alignment, visualisation, and summary outputs. The pipeline supports a wide range of evolutionary distances, runs reproducibly across local, cloud, and high-performance computing environments, and exports alignments in formats including MAF, BAM, BCF, and CRAM. We repurposed the compact format used for sequencing reads to combine the alignments of many genomes to the same target into a single file, which genome browsers display directly and from which multiple sequence alignments of any region can be extracted. Benchmarking against established genome aligners shows competitive performance with tunable trade-offs between speed and sensitivity, while applications to comparative genomics and assembly quality control illustrate its uses.

Title: Quantification of cannabidiolic acid in Cannabis sativa using a two-component allosteric protein biosensor
Authors: Guo, Z.; Luna-Flores, C.; Thomson, R. E. S.; Turland, C.; Grolman, D.; Alexandrov, K.; Behrendorff, J. B.
Abstract: Cannabidiol (CBD) is an important medicinal cannabinoid which accumulates in the Cannabis sativa plant as the precursor cannabidiolic acid (CBDA). Measurement of CBDA levels is important for crop valuation, harvest optimisation, and quality control. However, its quantification typically requires laboratory-based analytical methods that are not readily deployable at the point of need. Here, we report the development of an engineered protein biosensor for selective CBDA detection based on chemically induced dimerization of engineered nanobody domains. Here a cannabidiol-responsive nanobody pair was incorporated into a two-component beta-lactamase-based biosensor architecture, such that ligand binding ultimately results in reconstitution of beta-lactamase activity quantified in a simple colorimetric assay. The resulting sensor displayed high affinity for CBD (KD = 1.9 +/- 0.2 nM) and CBDA (KD = 32 +/- 4 nM). Structure analysis informed a single substitution mutation of ligand-binding nanobody to shift its selectivity in favour of CBDA. This minimal modification inverted sensor specificity, generating a CBDA-selective biosensor that showed no detectable activation either by CBD or the immediate biosynthetic precursor, cannabigerolic acid (CBGA). The engineered sensor exhibited nanomolar affinity for CBDA (KD = 21 +/- 2.4 nM), an 8.4-fold dynamic range, and a limit of detection of 0.5 nM. Sensor performance was validated using crude extracts from CBDA-producing biomass and achieved 95.6% agreement with LCMS-based quantification.

Title: A modular workflow for biomedical entity normalization across heterogeneous biological ontologies
Authors: Amil, A.; Chagoyen, M.
Abstract: Understanding the biological mechanisms underlying rare diseases requires integrating information about phenotypes, cell types, anatomical structures, and molecular functions and processes. Although some of this knowledge is available in structured resources, additional relationships remain dispersed across biomedical literature. Extracting and integrating this information requires normalizing heterogeneous biological entities against specialized ontologies. This motivated the development of a common biomedical named entity normalization (NEN) workflow and the evaluation of its performance across different entity types and ontologies. We developed a modular NEN workflow combining exact matching, lexical and semantic candidate retrieval, and reranking, without requiring ontology-specific training. Candidate retrieval integrates BM25, fuzzy matching, character n-gram similarity, and SapBERT. We evaluated the workflow across the Human Phenotype Ontology (HPO), Cell Ontology (CL), Uberon, and Gene Ontology (GO) using multiple benchmarks, separately assessing candidate retrieval, reranking accuracy, and overall normalization accuracy. We also investigated factors associated with retrieval difficulty and compared the workflow with CellExLink, a specialized cell-type normalization system. Retrieval performance varied across ontologies and benchmarks, with lexical and semantic methods providing complementary candidate coverage in some settings. Increasing candidate-set size improved retrieval recall but did not necessarily improve overall normalization accuracy, as larger candidate sets could reduce reranking performance. Retrieval difficulty was associated with mention characteristics and ontology categories. Our evaluation identifies the performance characteristics and limitations of a common normalization workflow across heterogeneous biological ontologies, highlighting the importance of assessing candidate retrieval and selection separately. The workflow provides a methodological foundation for extracting and integrating biological information from rare disease literature, with potential applicability to other biomedical information-extraction tasks requiring normalization against these ontologies.

Title: Visual Search and ASD: Basic vs. Superordinate Category Search
Authors: Abassi Abu Rukab, S.; Shulman, C.; Hochstein, S.
Abstract: We study visual search and categorization among individuals with Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) and a neuro-typical comparison group (NT). Individuals with ASD often exhibit distinct sensory processing patterns and may face challenges in efficiently detecting and categorizing visual stimuli. They may also process categories differently compared to NT groups, reflecting variations in typical sensory processing mechanisms. Based on our previous findings, this study employs visual search categorization tasks, testing reaction time and set-size slopes for different target categories. Participants included 26 individuals with ASD and 11 NT individuals, with similar mean ages and mean IQ Block Design subtest scores. They performed basic-level and superordinate-level visual search, as well as a categorization task. In the visual search task, participants identified targets within arrays of varying set sizes (4, 16, 36, 64). Face detection remained rapid across groups, and Basic-level search was similar in ASD and NT groups (mean set-size slopes: 48.7 and 45 ms/item, respectively). In contrast, superordinate search was much slower in ASD (99 ms/item) compared to NT (70.8 ms/item), reflecting increased cognitive demands. Object typicality influenced performance, with less typical items being slower to both categorize and detect. These findings suggest that basic-level processing is relatively preserved in ASD, whereas superordinate categorization imposes greater demands. The results highlight the role of typicality and support differences in perceptual and cognitive processing in ASD. Our findings contribute to better understanding visual cognition in autism and may inform strategies for improving conceptual generalization and visual learning.

Title: Branched-Chain α-Keto Acid Mitochondrial Uptake Regulates Fatty Acid Metabolism in Adipose Tissue
Authors: Wang, Y.; YUNXIA, L.; Liu, Z.; Li, M.; Su, L.; Lin, J.; Chua, G. L.; ren, s.; Tan, Y. s.; Chocholouskova, M.; Zhou, Q.; Dong, B.; Wong, C. M.-X.; Wong, Y.; Liu, G.; Wang, M.; Torta, F.; Sun, L.; Sun, H.; Silver, D. L.; Gao, C.; Zhang, X.
Abstract: Branched-chain amino acids (BCAAs) are essential amino acids and their homeostasis is tightly regulated by mostly mitochondrial localized catabolic activities where branched-chain -keto acids (BCKAs) are the first-step downstream products. BCAAs and BCKAs are both readily detected in circulation, necessitating targeted transporters for their uptake across cellular and mitochondrial membranes. Although mitochondrial transporter for BCAA uptake has been identified, the molecular entity for BCKAs mitochondrial uptake remains unknown. In adult mice, we measured circulating BCAA and BCKAs under feeding and fasting status, and found circulating BCKAs were markedly elevated during fasting while BCAAs levels remained constant. By integrating genetic association analysis in human and multi-tissue nutrient-responsive transcriptomic profiling in mice, we identified SLC25A35 as a candidate mitochondrial transporter highly associated with BCKA homeostasis. SLC25A35 expression was highly enriched in brown adipocytes. Genetic inactivation of SLC25A35 in mice specifically blunted BCKA mitochondria uptake and downstream catabolism without significant impact on BCAA homeostasis, as demonstrated by targeted metabolic profiling and isotope tracing in intact animals, in isolated primary adipocytes and in purified mitochondria. SLC25A35 expression directly promoted mitochondrial BCKA uptake, with a preference for KIC and KMV over KIV. Importantly, SLC25A35 mediated BCKA uptake and catabolism was independent from SLC25A44 mediated BCAA mitochondrial transport, and the BCKA specificity for SLC35A35 was further evaluated by structure-guided identification and mutagenesis based validation for conserved potential BCKA interacting residues in SLC25A35 transmembrane domains. Functionally, SLC25A35 expression enhanced lipogenesis by supporting fatty acid incorporation of BCKA-derived carbon and lipogenic gene expression, independent from mitochondrial production of PEP. During cold exposure, SLC25A35-deficient mice exhibited reduced mitochondrial respiratory activity in brown adipose tissue , depletion of short- and long-chain acylcarnitine species, and attenuated cold-responsive metabolic signalling. Together, these findings identify SLC25A35 as a nutrient-responsive mitochondrial BCKA transporter that reveal a previously unrecognized BCKA specific contribution to adipocyte lipid metabolism and thermogenic adaptation.

Title: Temporal Structure of Environmental Noise Controls the Localization and Tracking of Populations of Chemotactic Microorganisms
Authors: Arencibia, G.; Gutierrez, M. E.; Panetsos, F.
Abstract: Chemotactic microorganisms navigate fluctuating chemical landscapes by adjusting their motion in response to changes in locally sensed concentration. Consequently, population-level localization may depend not only on the magnitude of environmental fluctuations but also on their temporal structure. We investigate this dependence using a minimal agent-based model of noninteracting, Escherichia coli-inspired run-and-tumble swimmers in static and moving chemoattractant landscapes. We compare white, pink, Ornstein-Uhlenbeck, Brownian, and band-limited perturbations and examine how noise correlation time affects localization and tracking. Within the conditions studied, short-correlated fluctuations have relatively little effect, whereas slowly varying perturbations reduce retention, increase dispersion, and impair tracking. In the Ornstein-Uhlenbeck series, the strongest deterioration occurs when the noise correlation time approaches the characteristic run timescale. A low-frequency power fraction provides a useful empirical descriptor of these changes: localization data from different noise classes follow a similar trend when plotted against this quantity. Simulations with spatially localized advection further show that aggregate disruption depends on the placement of flow relative to the localization region. These findings link temporal noise structure and spatial transport to the robustness of population-level chemotactic organization in a minimal model.

Title: Fragment anchoring for metabolite annotation beyond whole-spectrum similarity
Authors: Park, Y. J.; Moon, J. H.; Suk, K. T.; Lee, D. Y.
Abstract: Many untargeted metabolomics features remain unannotated, and chemically related metabolites can have dissimilar tandem mass spectra. We present ANCHor, a framework for interpreting features of interest using shared fragment evidence. ANCHor selects fragments of a feature that recur among similar atlas spectra but are rare in background spectra, then evaluates matching experimental features using mass differences and transformation rules. Using 1,021 authentic standards as features of interest, ANCHor generated at least one anchor for 76.9%. We tested whether L-methionine anchors retain related spectra despite low overall similarity. Of 166 structurally related spectra, ANCHor retained 147, including 93 with modified cosine similarity <0.70 to L-methionine. In mycotoxin-treated hepatic spheroids, ANCHor prioritized putative transformation products, including low-similarity candidates. For library-unmatched fecal features in alcohol-associated liver disease, ANCHor found annotated references that guided identification of N1,N12-diacetylspermine, confirmed with an authentic standard, and supported a tryptophan-pyruvate product hypothesis with a reaction-generated reference. ANCHor thus supports testable structural hypotheses for library-unmatched features within atlas coverage.

Title: Breadth over Depth: Predictor-Agnostic Consensus for Improved Antibody--Antigen Structure Prediction
Authors: Ullanat, V.; Gupta, A.; Li, R.; Amengual-Rigo, P.; Furtmann, N.; Bryson, B. D.; Berger, B.
Abstract: Antibody-antigen structure prediction commonly relies on sampling a single co-folding predictor deeply and selecting its highest-confidence output using model-specific confidence scores. We introduce AbPoolRank, a predictor-agnostic structural selector that ranks mixed pools using cross-pose agreement, within-source reproducibility and interface geometry, without native confidence, predictor identities or predictor-specific parameters. On 103 cluster-disjoint, post-2021 antibody-antigen complexes from SAbDab2, three structures each from Boltz-2, Promera, Protenix-v2, ESMFold2-Fast and OpenDDE form a 15-structure pool that reaches 58.0% medium-or-better Success@1 (DockQ [≥] 0.49), exceeding confidence-based selection from every individual predictor sampled 100 times (26-52%). Existing ranking methods did not rescue deep single-predictor sampling or surpass our selector on mixed pools, with no method exceeding 51.5% on 100 structures from one co-folder and AbPoolRank matching the strongest single-structure methods while significantly outperforming consensus methods. AbPoolRank trained without one predictor lost at most 3.0 percentage points, and the frozen model accepted full MSA-conditioned ESMFold2, a sixth predictor absent from method development, without retraining or loss of accuracy. Diversification also improved the accuracy-compute frontier, with the 15-structure pool using 1.8-fold less aggregate GPU time than the most accurate single-predictor setting in our compute benchmark and 3.3-fold less than sampling that predictor 100 times. Together, these results show that shallow sampling across complementary co-folders, coupled with a confidence-free selector, provides an accurate and computationally efficient inference strategy for antibody-antigen structure prediction.

Title: An ancient transcription factor functions as a master regulator of primary cilia formation
Authors: Wang, W.; Zhang, X.; Qiu, Y.; Meng, X.; Cheng, S.; Chen, Y.; liu, S.; Chen, W.; Yi, J.; You, X.; Liu, H.; Xing, J.; Xu, C.; Jiang, H.; Wang, H.; Tian, G.; Hu, Z.
Abstract: How ancient transcription factors are repurposed during evolution to drive the functional diversification of conserved organelles remains a fundamental question in biology. Although highly conserved in basic morphology, eukaryotic cilia vary extensively in their sizes and functions. Previously, we showed that an evolutionarily ancient transcription factor, X chromosome-associated protein 5 (Xap5), controls motile ciliogenic transcriptional programs during mouse spermatogenesis (Wang et al., 2025). Here we show that Xap5 functions as a master regulator of primary ciliogenesis. In NIH/3T3 fibroblasts, Xap5 associates with the nuclear protein Non-POU domain-containing octamer-binding protein (Nono) to form a regulatory module that promotes Sox5 and Sox9 expression. Genetic ablation of Xap5 or Nono shortens primary cilia, and loss of Sox5 disrupts the downstream ciliogenic program, consistent with the established role of Sox9. In mIMCD-3 renal epithelial cells, Xap5 loss reduces both ciliation frequency and cilium length, whereas Sox5 and Sox9 respond in the opposite direction. Collectively, our results provide new insight into how an ancient transcription factor is repurposed through shared and context-specific downstream programs, and motivate testing whether altered Xap5-dependent gene regulation contributes to human ciliopathies.

Title: Oocyte ETC function and glycogen metabolism link maternal environment to offspring metabolism
Authors: Cooper, J.; Rautela, U.; Nguyen, K.; Gates, D.; Wolfrum, E.; Capan, C.; Lee, H.; Williams, D.; Okoye, C.; Nauta, K. M.; Senchuk, M.; Garcia, A.; Tay, J. W.; Sanchez-Avila, X.; Kelly, R. T.; Patel, M.; Sheldon, R.; Wojtovich, A. P.; Burton, N. O.
Abstract: Maternal exposure to environmental stressors can drive adaptive changes in offspring metabolism across diverse species and is linked to disease risk in humans. Such effects have most often been attributed to epigenetic mechanisms, but whether a mothers environment can also act on other mechanisms present in oocytes to alter offspring physiology remains unclear. Using a system in which C. elegans exposure to osmotic stress can drive a greater than 10-fold increase in offspring survival in response to future osmotic stress, we performed global proteomics profiling of dissected oocytes and discovered that maternal exposure to osmotic stress reduces the abundance of electron transport chain (ETC) proteins in oocytes. We further found that ETC function in oocytes promotes oocyte glycogen abundance. Metabolism of this oocyte-derived glycogen, in both oocytes and early embryos, antagonizes the phosphorylation of the AMP-kinase catalytic subunit AAK-2 at Threonine-243 in embryos. Lastly, we find that changes in AAK-2 activity in turn regulate the offsprings response to future osmotic stress, likely by converging on regulation of the ribosome with the integrated stress response (ISR) pathway. Collectively, our findings describe an intergenerational signaling cascade in which multiple maternal inputs, including maternal environments and maternal insulin signaling, converge on oocyte glycogen metabolism to trigger adaptive changes in offspring physiology via altering AMP-kinase activity in embryos. Notably, recent studies have similarly discovered the existence of insulin-regulated ETC and glycogen remodeling in fly, frog, and human oocytes. However, the function of this evolutionarily conserved phenomenon remains unclear. Our findings suggest that oocyte ETC/glycogen remodeling is regulated by a mothers environment and, at least in some contexts, links a mothers environment to adaptive changes in offspring physiology.

Title: Multireplicon plasmids show broad host distributions, high transfer potential, and are enriched in antimicrobial resistance genes
Authors: de Quinto, I.; Ramiro Martinez, P.; Silva Rosa, R.; Herencias, C.; Lanza, V. F.; Rodriguez-Beltran, J.
Abstract: Plasmids are DNA molecules that replicate independently of the bacterial chromosome and are typically associated with the spread of antimicrobial resistance (AMR) and virulence determinants, among other relevant traits. Complex genetic rearrangements (including plasmid fusion) can result in plasmids carrying two or more replication systems, known as multireplicon plasmids. Despite decades of study, we are still far from understanding how multireplicon plasmids arise, persist, and shape the evolution of AMR. Here, we analyzed 24,000 non-redundant plasmids across bacterial genera and found that more than 30% encoded multiple replicons. Compared with single-replicon plasmids, multireplicon plasmids were larger, enriched in antimicrobial, metal, and biocide resistance genes, virulence factors, and transfer-associated features, and observed across broader host taxonomic distributions. Some replicon pairs frequently co-occurred on multireplicon plasmids, whereas others were typically maintained on separate plasmids even when present within the same cell. Replicon pairs also showed non-random spatial organization, being preferentially located either in close proximity or at distant positions along the plasmid backbone. Their phylogenetic congruence varied substantially, suggesting that some replicon associations are evolutionarily transient, whereas others may be persistently co-inherited. Finally, we highlight the contribution of insertion sequences to multireplicon plasmid formation. Together, our work sheds light on the abundance, gene content, organization, and evolutionary dynamics of multireplicon plasmids and underscores their relevance to bacterial evolution and human health.

Title: Depolymerases unmask a conserved receptor to enable phage control of capsulated Acinetobacter baumannii
Authors: Kan, L.; Avellaneda-Franco, L.; Subedi, D.; Korneev, D.; Gillis, E.; Magnin-Bougma, I.; Carascal, M.; Devkota, S.; Kunwar, S.; Bhusal, R.; Hall, R. M.; Kenyon, J. J.; Gordillo Altamirano, F. L.; Peleg, A. Y.; Barr, J. J.
Abstract: We characterized bacteriophage Abs1 that infects clinical Acinetobacter baumannii isolates via the highly prevalent and conserved outer-membrane protein receptor, OprC. However, phage Abs1 is unable to infect capsulated A. baumannii strains as the capsule prevents phage access to its underlying receptor. To circumvent this, we combined phage Abs1 with recombinant depolymerases targeting the major A. baumannii capsule types. In a murine bacteremia model, this combination significantly reduced bacterial burden caused by diverse, capsulated A. baumannii strains.

Title: Predicting conformational changes induced by biomolecular interactions
Authors: Bae, Y.; Baek, J.; Choi, E.; Choi, J. H.; Han, H.; Jang, H.; Jeon, W.; Jo, J.; Kim, D.; Kim, H.; Kim, J. H.; Kim, J. H.; Kim, S.; Kim, T.; Kim, Y.; Lee, J.; Lee, J.; Moon, S.; Park, M.; Samuel, C.; Seo, H.; Seo, J.; Seo, S.; Shin, M.; Shin, Y.; Zhung, W.; Ahn, S.; Han, D.; Hwang, S. J.; Kim, H. M.; Kim, W. Y.; Lee, G. R.; Oh, B.-H.
Abstract: Biomolecular interactions trigger structural changes of protein complexes essential for cellular signaling, regulation, and drug action. Modern co-folding models can now generate detailed structures of multi-component complexes directly from sequence. However, recent evaluations reveal that they frequently fail to capture specific conformational states induced by a ligand or partner. Here, we show that explicitly modeling the structural transition from an unbound to a bound state, rather than generating the bound complex alone, better resolves these interaction-induced states. Our generative learning framework, K-Fold, transforms independently predicted unbound component priors into an assembled complex through an ultrafast diffusion bridge, operating entirely without multiple sequence alignments. By eliminating co-evolutionary dependencies, K-Fold accurately recovers non-coevolved interfaces in antibody-antigen and targeted-degrader complexes, as well as ligand-directed regulatory states in GPCRs and kinases. Furthermore, by coupling this diffusion bridge with diverse monomeric equilibrium ensembles, K-Fold provides a computationally tractable foundation for sampling complex multi-state landscapes without retraining. These results demonstrate that formulating molecular assembly as an explicit structural transition moves structure prediction beyond static geometries toward capturing biomolecular dynamics.

Title: Multi-omic guided iPSC dopaminergic differentiation leads to selective enrichment of PD-vulnerable SOX6+ midbrain neurons with motor recovery of PD models after transplantation
Authors: Garcia Swinburn, R.; Lyu, G.; Kreutzmann, J. C.; Xiong, A.; Kojima, R.; Abaurre, C.; Paslawski, W.; Schach, K.; Tremolanti, C.; Gellhaar, S.; Uhlen, P.; Castelo Branco, G.; Salto, C.; Dagliyan, O.; Svenningsson, P.; Arenas, E.
Abstract: Background Parkinson's disease (PD) is characterized by the progressive loss of midbrain dopaminergic (mDA) neurons, leading to severe debilitating motor impairment. Recent single-cell analyses have revealed that specific mDA subpopulations, such as SOX6 AGTR1 neurons, are most vulnerable to degeneration. Current human pluripotent stem cell differentiation protocols fail to selectively generate these subtypes. Methods Here, we describe a multiomic-guided strategy that enriches SOX6 mDA neurons by combining enhancing Sonic Hedgehog (SHH) agonism with prolonged Wnt activation. Initial brute force optimization of a protocol of a prior publication failed to obtain our desired outcome. Using longitudinal single-nuclei (sn) multiomic sequencing, we were able to localize differentiation chokeholds in our timeline and corrected by inducing Wnt more aggressively at the selected time point. After mDA progenitor optimization, we performed in vitro validation of downstream mDA differentiation by immunocytochemistry, detection of secreted dopamine by high-performance liquid chromatography and comparison of transcriptomics with publicly available post-mortem midbrain data. Once validated, engineered mDA progenitors were intrastriatally transplanted into hemiparkinsonian mice lesioned with 6-OHDA. Motor recovery was assessed longitudinally, and graft cellular composition was molecularly characterized using immunohistochemistry and snRNA sequencing. Finally, our sequencing dataset was used to validate transcriptional identities of grafted cells compared to postmortem midbrain data, as well as recognize lack of potential detrimental off-targets and pluripotency. Results Our multiomic approach accelerates floor plate specification, increases expression of mDA developmental markers, and substantially increases the yield of SOX6 mature mDA neurons compared to prior attempts. Following intrastriatal transplantation into hemiparkinsonian mice, these cells restored motor function in approximately 4 months and generated grafts containing mature, stably committed SOX6 A9-like neurons that mirror their endogenous human counterparts. Conclusions Our work establishes a differentiation platform for generating the PD-susceptible mDA subtype, providing a foundation for precision disease modelling and subtype-targeted cell replacement therapies.

Title: Engineering developmental transitions during human neurulation through modular integration of multimodal spatial cues
Authors: Hagiwara, M.; Nozaki, S.; Sugino, Y.; Mimura, T.; Ngo, Y. X.; Gonzalez Teshima, L. Y.; Koh, I.; Inoue, Y.; Matsuo, I.
Abstract: Reconstituting developmental transitions in vitro requires reproducing complex spatial cues that guide cellular self-organization. Here, we developed MoSAIC (Modular Spatial Assembly and Integration of Cues), a modular platform that reconstructs multimodal mechano-chemical spatial cues by decomposing complex culture operations and subsequently integrating them. Central to MoSAIC is a composite architecture combining rigid polycarbonate structures with soft extracellular matrix hydrogels, providing geometric precision and structural stability while permitting cellular self-organization and tissue deformation. Using human induced pluripotent stem cells, MoSAIC enabled independent control of tissue geometry, ECM localization, physical boundaries, and morphogen gradients, together with defined mechanical and chemical perturbations. Their integration guided a continuous ectodermal sheet through neural induction, bending, and bifurcation into neural and epidermal tissues, followed by polarized neural tube formation and dorsoventral patterning. The resulting tissue exhibited posterior identity, while non-genetic perturbations enabled interrogation of mechanisms governing neural tube closure.

Title: BGC Atlas v2: biosynthetic gene clusters with taxonomic and environmental context at scale
Authors: Bagci, C.; Talamas-Tanner, A.; Ziemert, N.
Abstract: Genomic and metagenomic studies have revealed that microbes have the capacity to produce an enormous diversity of secondary metabolites. These compounds play important roles in microbial interactions and are also a major source of medicines and other useful natural products, yet only a small fraction of this biosynthetic potential has been experimentally characterized. BGC Atlas was developed to explore this largely uncharacterized diversity by placing biosynthetic gene clusters (BGCs) into genomic and environmental context. Here, we present BGC Atlas v2, which expands the collection more than eightfold to more than 16 million predicted BGCs and extends it from metagenomic assemblies to metagenome-assembled genomes (MAGs), single-amplified genomes and isolate genomes. The new release provides taxonomic assignments for nearly all BGCs, harmonized environmental metadata, nested searches across biosynthetic, taxonomic, environmental and geographic properties, and protein-sequence searches against BGC-encoded genes. Its scale also reveals how much bacterial and archaeal biosynthetic diversity remains unexplored. By connecting pathways to related families, organisms and environments, BGC Atlas v2 supports natural-product discovery and investigations of prokaryotic biosynthetic diversity across taxa and ecosystems. BGC Atlas v2 is freely available at https://bgc-atlas.cs.uni-tuebingen.de.

Title: Lipid nanoparticle-delivered Cas13b ribonucleoproteins targeting survivin overcome gemcitabine resistance in pancreatic cancer
Authors: Castano-Esteban, D.; Lopez-Valls, M.; Santos, M.; Recuero, E.; Martin-Vallejo, L.; Pardo, D.; Luciani, P.; Somoza, A.; Sot, B.
Abstract: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) remains one of the deadliest cancers, largely due to its poor response to chemotherapy and the development of drug resistance. Survivin (BIRC5), an inhibitor of apoptosis frequently overexpressed in PDAC, contributes to tumor cell survival and gemcitabine resistance, making it an attractive therapeutic target. Here, we developed a lipid nanoparticle (LNP)-based platform for the delivery of preassembled spCas13b ribonucleoproteins (RNPs) to achieve transient and sequence-specific RNA silencing in pancreatic cancer cells. We optimized ionizable lipid formulations for Cas13b RNP encapsulation and identified a formulation achieving approximately 80% encapsulation efficiency, with sustained colloidal stability and gene-silencing activity during seven days of storage at 4{degrees}C. LNP-delivered Cas13b RNPs efficiently silenced endogenous BIRC5 in three pancreatic cancer cell lines, reducing survivin protein levels and inducing apoptosis. In gemcitabine-resistant PANC-1 cells, BIRC5 silencing synergistically enhanced the cytotoxic effect of gemcitabine in vitro. This therapeutic combination was further evaluated in a PANC-1 xenograft model, where only the combined administration of BIRC5-targeting Cas13b RNP-LNPs and gemcitabine significantly inhibited tumor growth, without apparent systemic toxicity. Intratumoral administration also restricted nanoparticle distribution to the injected tumors. These findings establish LNP-mediated delivery of Cas13b RNPs as a new strategy for transient RNA-targeted therapy and provide proof of concept for combining survivin silencing by Cas13b with chemotherapy to address gemcitabine resistance in pancreatic cancer.

Title: Surrogate Verifiers Shape Decisions in Closed-Loop Experimental Design
Authors: Merzbacher, C.; Goecke, J.; Cohen, J.; Patz, M.
Abstract: High throughput, automated screening has revolutionized biological experimentation and prompted predictions of AI-enabled "self-driving" labs. Deployed autonomous lab systems typically use a learned surrogate to predict new experimental candidates and rank which conditions deserve expensive follow-up. Determining whether a computational surrogate verifier can substitute for an experimental assay's ground truth requires an understanding of model accuracy, uncertainty, and extrapolation. In this work, we present surrogate verifiers trained on N=7,688 Lacticaseibacillus growth curves exploring a 10-dimensional media component experimental design space. We train surrogate models across six distinct families including polynomial, Gaussian-process, tree-ensemble, neural, and Monod-kinetic forms to predict maximum optical density (OD600). Surrogates ranked by the most commonly reported accuracy metrics (held-out R^2; MAE; RMSE) disagree sharply on which experiments to test next and the best achievable yield. We evaluate models in a Bayesian optimization loop and find that the model used as the active learning oracle matters more than the acquisition function or batch size. We apply conformal calibration to build a model-agnostic assessment criterion of uncertainty and model coverage. We end by evaluating model accuracy and calibration under transfer to an unseen related bacterial strain, and confirm on a prospective validation plate that the transferred verifier's intervals fail in the direction and region our retrospective analysis predicts. This work explores the surrogate verifier within the loop as a previously underexplored axis of closed-loop design and points towards best calibration practices.

Title: Flow Virometry-Based Profiling of Viral Population Diversity
Authors: Liu, T.; Berg, N.; Donahue, C. J.; Planitzer, S. D.; Santos-Peral, A.; Partlow, E. A.; Motsa, B. B.; Ivanovic, T.
Abstract: Viruses exhibit great phenotypic heterogeneity. Flow virometry enables high-throughput analysis of phenotypic diversity in viral populations, while flow-based sorting allows subpopulations to be isolated for separate characterization. Despite their advantages, flow virometry and sorting have not yet been widely adopted in virology partly because of limited protocols and underexplored applications. Here, we provide a practical guide for analyzing and quantifying virus particles from diverse families using flow virometry enhanced by fluorescence labeling. We further explore applications beyond basic and static characterization of virus populations. We demonstrate that flow virometry can report on interactions between virions and binding partners, as well as between virions. It provides a particle denominator that, combined with genome copy measurements, enables estimation of viral population ploidy. We also show how dynamic processes, such as viral membrane fusion, can be measured in real time. Finally, we demonstrate the feasibility of sorting virions based on their intrinsic properties, such as morphology, for downstream study. This practical guide provides a roadmap for wider implementation of flow virometry in virology, while the applications illustrated here demonstrate potential to address a variety of questions about virion properties, interactions, and dynamics at the single-particle level.

Title: Depth-partitioned oxidation of atmospheric hydrogen, carbon monoxide and methane in a glacier forefield soil
Authors: Herbert, J.; Dede, B.; Koschitz, L.; Sarbach, J.; Schroth, M. H.; Schoelmerich, M. C.
Abstract: Glacier forefields are model systems for pioneer ecosystem assembly under extreme oligotrophy. Their microbial communities carry widespread genomic potential to oxidize atmospheric trace gases, yet whether this potential is transcribed in situ, and by which lineages, remains largely untested. Here we combined depth-resolved profiling of hydrogen (H2), carbon monoxide (CO) and methane (CH4) at ten locations in the Wildstrubel glacier forefield, Swiss Alps, with mesocosm experiments, long-read metagenomics, and genome-resolved metatranscriptomics. Soils were consistent net sinks for atmospheric H2 and CH4, with fluxes ~2-fold and ~6-fold higher, respectively, in older than in younger terrain. H2 uptake was concentrated in the upper 20 cm, whereas CH4 uptake extended deeper. In the field, CO uptake was masked by apparent subsurface production, but in mesocosms lacking this source both CO and H2 were drawn below atmospheric concentrations. Although 57% of metagenome-assembled genomes encoded trace-gas oxidation enzymes, topsoil transcription was dominated by Group 1h [NiFe]-hydrogenases from a few Actinomycetota populations, in which the CO dehydrogenase coxL was transcribed 20- to 35-fold less. The second most transcribed marker was smoX, most closely related to C2-C6 alkane monooxygenases, suggesting the use of short-chain alkanes of possible subsurface origin. Mobile genetic elements were widely transcribed, matching host transcription, but a 104-kb plasmid-borne coxMSL operon was largely silent. Acetylene perturbation induced no detectable switching between trace-gas pathways. Together, these data suggest that trace-gas metabolism is partitioned across soil depth: atmospheric H2 scavenging dominates topsoil transcription, whereas methanotrophy and CO production occur deeper. Net surface fluxes, particularly for CO, therefore, underestimate gross trace-gas turnover.

Title: Not all plant-based diets are alike: intake of minimally processed plant foods is associated with gut microbial richness among vegetarians and vegans.
Authors: Mendez-Hurtado, A.; Coleto-Checa, D.; Alvarez, A.; Marcos-Pasero, H.; Calderon, A.; Maestri, A.; Perez-Cuervo, A.; Blanco-Rivero, A.; Lacruz-Pleguezuelos, B.; Cardenas-Roig, N.; Carrasco-Guijarro, L.; Martin-Segura, A.; Aguilar-Aguilar, E.; Marcos-Zambrano, L. J.
Abstract: Plant-based diets are usually defined by what they exclude, overlooking which plant foods are eaten and how processed they are. Here we examine whether this overlooked dimension is related to the gut microbiome. In a cross-sectional study of 172 omnivorous, lacto-ovo-vegetarian and vegan adults profiled by shotgun metagenomics, vegetarians and vegans harboured fewer gut species than omnivores. Within this group, however, each standard deviation increase in minimally processed plant-food intake was associated with 27 additional species (p = 0.001), independently of fibre intake, and richness in participants with the highest intake approached that of omnivores. No such association was seen among omnivores. Higher intake was also linked to more species previously associated with favourable cardiometabolic health and to better health-related quality of life. Dietary labels alone may therefore conceal meaningful variation in the gut microbiome, and characterising how plant foods are processed may help in understanding how plant-based diets relate to health.

Title: ER-vacuole tether Mdm1 coordinates lipid homeostasis to support autophagosome formation
Authors: Obaseki, E.; Adebayo, D.; Rahal, M.; Vale, G.; McDonald, J. G.; Hariri, H.
Abstract: Autophagosome formation requires cells to mobilize lipids for phagophore expansion and completion while maintaining lipid homeostasis during nutrient stress. How lipid intermediates are partitioned between membrane synthesis and neutral lipid storage under these conditions remains unclear. Here, we identify ER-vacuole tether Mdm1 as a regulator of starvation-induced autophagy in budding yeast. Loss of Mdm1 reduced autophagic flux despite preserved TORC1 responses to starvation and impaired autophagosome completion, as indicated by the accumulation of perivacuolar Atg8-positive structures and reduced protease protection. Lipidomic analyses revealed decreased phosphatidylinositol (PI) in whole cells and Atg8-enriched membrane fractions, accompanied by increased diacylglycerol (DAG) and storage lipids. Derepression of phospholipid synthesis through OPI1 deletion or inhibition of triacylglycerol synthesis restored autophagic flux. Remarkably, exogenous DAG also rescued autophagy despite elevated endogenous DAG in Mdm1-deficient cells. DAG supplementation increased PI abundance and improved protease protection, linking changes in lipid metabolism to autophagosome completion. Together, these findings implicate Mdm1 in coordinating membrane phospholipid homeostasis with neutral lipid metabolism and suggest that the metabolic availability of lipid intermediates contributes to efficient autophagosome formation during starvation.

Title: Site-Specific and Diet-Dependent Genetic Architecture of Trabecular Bone in Male BXD Recombinant Inbred Mice
Authors: Chanpaisaeng, K.; Reyes-Fernandez, P.; Dilkes, B.; Quinlan, V.; Fleet, J. C.
Abstract: Vertebral fracture risk is influenced by trabecular bone (Tb) microarchitecture, a phenotype that is regulated by genetic and environmental factors. We examined the genetic architecture of Tb microarchitecture in the fifth lumbar vertebra (L5) and its modification by dietary calcium (Ca). Male mice from 51 BXD recombinant inbred lines were fed adequate (0.5%) or low (0.25%) Ca diets from 4 to 12 weeks of age. Micro-computed tomography (CT) was used to assess seven L5 Tb phenotypes, and the response to Ca restriction (RCR) was calculated for each phenotype. Quantitative trait loci (QTL) were identified by composite interval mapping and compared with previously reported femoral Tb QTL from the same mice. Genetic background significantly influenced all L5 phenotypes and their responses to Ca restriction. We identified 127 QTL distributed across 61 loci. First, very few L5 QTL overlapped those previously identified in the femur, providing strong evidence for skeletal site-specific genetic regulation of Tb microarchitecture. Second, QTL detection was strongly dependent on dietary Ca, with only 4 of 33 loci identified under adequate Ca intake also detected under low Ca intake. Third, QTL controlling the RCR were largely distinct from those controlling L5 phenotypes under either dietary condition. Many loci affected multiple phenotypes, suggesting shared genetic regulation of Tb characteristics. Integration of genetic variation, expression QTL, and existing functional evidence identified plausible candidate genes at several high-priority loci. Together, these findings demonstrate that genetic regulation of Tb microarchitecture is both skeletal site-specific and diet-dependent, and that adaptation to dietary Ca restriction has a distinct genetic component.

Title: Cell-type-resolved methylation analysis using bulk long-read sequencing across human tissues
Authors: Chen, H.; Mead, E. A.; Zhang, Y.; Karvelas, N.; Chen, Z.; Thorn, E. L.; Fan, Y.; Ni, M.; Bethancourt, C.-N.; Cohen, D. A.; Fan-Huang, G.; Yan, Z.; Bouhassira, E.; Soualhi, S.; Kozlenkov, A.; Abdul-Ghafar, J.; Mzoughi, S.; Guccione, E.; Dracheva, S.; Cohen, L. J.; Brody, R.; Charney, A. W.; Wu, H.; Kohli, R. M.; Farrell, K. W.; Vijg, J.; Gabre, J. T.; Cohen, D. J.; Elahi, F. M.; Crary, J. F.; Fang, G.
Abstract: DNA methylation shapes cellular identity and changes with aging and disease, but most human methylomes come from bulk tissue, which mixes signal across many cell types. A methylation change at the bulk tissue level can reflect a change in cellular composition or an intrinsic shift within a cell type, and the two cannot be separated from bulk data. Single-cell and sorted-cell methods resolve cell types directly, but their cost and workflow complexity pose challenges to large studies. Long-read sequencing of single DNA molecules can directly detect DNA methylation on each read. We built COMET (Cell-of-Origin from METhylation), a framework that uses cell-type-specific methylation to assign individual long reads to cell types from standard bulk long-read sequencing. COMET detects changes in cell-type composition robustly even from shallow bulk long-read data, quantifies methylation level of repetitive DNA within each cell type, and, with deeper sequencing, resolves methylation differences between health and disease in individual cell types. We applied COMET to 140 human blood samples, 104 human brain samples and 59 human colon samples. In blood, we found epigenetic aging clock is primarily driven by shifts in cell-type composition, and that APOE4 carriers have myeloid-specific methylation changes. In brain, we found sex-biased change in cell-type composition with age, resolved methylation and hydroxymethylation separately within each cell type. In colon, we found a consistent expansion of fibroblasts in tumors relative to matched normal tissue, localized methylation loss at LINE-1 in fibroblast cells, and identified tumor- and cell-type-specific hypermethylation in epithelial cells at the promoters of known colorectal cancer genes. By resolving cell-type-specific methylation directly from bulk long-read data, this approach opens broad study of cell-type epigenetics across human tissues in aging and disease.

Title: Haplotype reconstruction in multi-generational diploid and tetraploid populations
Authors: Zheng, C.; Resende, M. F. R.; Munoz, P. R.; Endelman, J. B.
Abstract: Previously, we developed a statistical framework and software (PolyOrigin1) to reconstruct parental haplotypes of each offspring in connected tetraploid F1 populations. A key application of the technology is quantitative trait loci (QTL) mapping, via regression of phenotypes on posterior probabilities of parental origins. In this work, we extend the methodology and software (PolyOrigin2) to multi-generational populations (both diploid and tetraploid), which are common in breeding programs. The extension links parental origins across generations to estimate posterior probabilities of founder origins. Compared to PolyOrigin1, the main challenge is to phase intermediate individuals that are both parents and offspring, which is overcome by the Bayesian update rule. In addition, genotypic error models are extended to account for sequencing errors such as allelic bias and overdispersion in genotyping-by-sequencing (GBS). Extensive simulations were used to compare PolyOrigin2 with previous methods and to study the effects of such variables as sequencing errors and the number of progeny per parent. We further evaluated PolyOrigin2 using three real datasets: diploid potato with 23 founders and 7 generations, tetraploid potato with 10 founders and 3 generations, and tetraploid blueberry with 10 founders and 4 generations. The results show that PolyOrigin2 is accurate for haplotype phasing and reconstruction in diploid and tetraploid pedigrees and opens new opportunities for haplotype-based QTL mapping.

Title: Proteome-scale inference of transcription factor binding motifs from predicted protein-DNA structures
Authors: Iovino, B.; Bulaong, N.; Boahene, L.; Law, W.; Hammond, N.; Potts, M.; Alvarez, R.; DeRisi, J. L.; Pak, J.; Kim, Y. J.; Royer, L. A.
Abstract: Transcription factors (TFs) control development and cell identity by binding sequence-specific DNA motifs, yet the binding specificities of most TFs remain unknown because experimental binding assays do not scale. In zebrafish, only one-third of TFs have assigned motifs, nearly all inferred by homology from human or mouse experimental data. Here we present a proteome-scale computational screen that infers DNA-binding specificity from predicted protein-DNA structures. We use AlphaFold3 to model zebrafish TFs with candidate motif sequences derived from accessible chromatin, then use NA-MPNN to infer the DNA motifs from the most confident predictions. Across 210 TFs with experimentally characterized orthologs, predicted motifs match the known motif for 44%. Propagated through sequence clusters, these predictions form ZebraMotif, a motif database for all 2,543 zebrafish TFs. ZebraMotif covers 2.8 times as many TFs as CisBP's zebrafish collection and links accessible regulatory elements to candidate upstream regulators genome-wide. Because the approach requires only a proteome and a set of candidate motifs, it is applicable to any species lacking experimental binding data.

Title: Feasibility of methionine oxidation quantification in proteins through Raman and FT-IR spectroscopy
Authors: Höltkemeier, T.; Fischer, I.; Venerito, M.; Le-Minh, V.; Griaud, F.; Merkle, P.; Gritsch, M.; Sobczuk, A.; Bitar, M.; Krois, E.; Kubryk, P.; Bechtold-Peters, K.; Haisch, C.; Friess, W.
Abstract: The development of biopharmaceuticals poses unique challenges, with alterations of chemical integrity potentially impairing product efficacy and safety. Thus, oxidation-susceptibility of drug candidates is typically assessed by chromatographic methods, potentially coupled with mass spectrometry (LC-MS), which enable residue-specific oxidation monitoring but require high-resolution instrumentation, specialized expertise, and may introduce sample preparation artefacts. These constraints have raised interest in orthogonal, simple and fast methods to probe oxidation in native protein samples. Raman and Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy (FT-IR) have shown potential for detecting methionine oxidation, the most common oxidative protein liability. The aim of this work was to transfer the known quantification potential of cuvette-based Raman spectroscopy to Raman microscopy and evaluate its suitability for high-throughput screenings. Following several technical optimizations, this work shows that the detection of oxidation by Raman microscopy could only be confirmed for molecular methionine in solution and not for proteinogenic methionine. In contrast, liquid-cell FT-IR enabled solid quantitative read-outs of methionine oxidation in proteins. Under the investigated forced degradation conditions, the method showed good agreement to orthogonal LC-MS measurements utilizing the multi-attribute method (MAM). These findings position liquid-cell FT-IR as a potential rapid, low-volume screening tool for oxidation assessments in native protein samples, particularly during early-stage biopharmaceutical development.

Title: Body-wide microbial ecosystem reorganization across the cognitive impairment spectrum in Parkinsons disease
Authors: Arıkan, M.; Delice, B.; Yıldız, Z.; Kahraman Demir, T.; H. Yılmaz, N.; Sen, A.; Hanoglu, L.; Yildirim, S.
Abstract: Cognitive impairment (CI) is a major determinant of disability in Parkinsons disease (PD), yet how microbial alterations across multiple body sites accompany cognitive dysfunction remains poorly understood. We characterized microbial communities from five body sites (stool, saliva, tongue, nasal cavity, and axilla) in 150 participants spanning healthy controls, PD with mild cognitive impairment (PD-MCI), and PD dementia (PDD), generating 616 samples for 16S rRNA gene sequencing. Multi-Omics Factor Analysis v2 (MOFA2) identified a multisite microbial signature with prominent oral and gut contributions that varied across clinical groups (Factor 8; {beta} = -0.58, p < 0.0001). MintTea analysis identified stable multisite microbial assemblies associated with cognitive status, including a module distinguishing PD-MCI from PDD (in-sample AUROC = 0.810). Core microbiome analysis revealed a net reduction of 45 genus-site core memberships across four anatomical sites in cognitively impaired participants, including reduced prevalence of the butyrate-associated genus Roseburia. Multivariable models incorporating microbial signatures and demographic covariates explained an average of 35.4% of cognitive-outcome variance, with microbial features contributing an additional 8.0 percentage points beyond age, sex, and education. Procrustes analysis revealed a pronounced, non-linear pattern of weakening cross-site microbial community correspondence at the dementia stage. The Global Body-wide Organization Index remained relatively stable between HC (0.335) and PD-MCI (0.341) but declined to 0.257 in PDD, representing a 23% reduction relative to HC. Together, these findings identify disease-associated multisite microbial signatures and altered core-community composition across the PD cognitive impairment spectrum, supporting further investigation of multisite microbiome profiling for cognitive stratification.

Title: Single-cell analysis identifies concurrent type 2 and interferon programs in experimental eosinophilic esophagitis
Authors: Dsilva, A.; Handler, K.; Baron, T.; Itan, M.; Avlas, S.; Zan Bar, I.; Varol, C.; Rothenberg, M.; Arnold, I. C.; Munitz, A.
Abstract: Background & Aims: Eosinophilic esophagitis (EoE) is a chronic, type 2 cytokine-driven allergic disease of the esophagus. How the immune and structural cell landscape of the esophagus changes between healthy and inflamed tissue requires further investigation. Methods: CD45-enriched esophageal cells from naive and oxazolone (OXA)-challenged wild-type mice were profiled by single-cell RNA sequencing. A cytokine-gated gene expression score identified type 2 program-high cells. Findings were compared with published human esophageal datasets, validated histologically, and examined in Il13ra1-/- mice. Results: A total of 62,245 esophageal cells were analyzed. ILC2s accounted for most type 2 cytokine-expressing lymphocytes in naive mice, whereas Th2 cells accounted for approximately 80% following OXA challenge. ILC2s concurrently lost Il5, Il13 and Gata3 expression while retaining Areg. Resident memory-like CD8 T cells became the largest lymphoid population. Mast cells switched from a connective tissue-type to a mucosal-type and partly cycling state, which was confirmed by increased MCPT1 cells. Esophageal eosinophils displayed a signature resembling skin eosinophils of atopic dermatitis rather than gastrointestinal eosinophils. Il13ra1-/- mice were protected from epithelial proliferation, thickening and eosinophilia. An interferon-associated program characterized lymphoid, myeloid and structural compartments, and its epithelial component was conserved in human EoE. Conclusions: Th2 cells and mucosal-type mast cells are the dominant sources of type 2 cytokines in experimental EoE. This study further identifies a conserved interferon-associated program that accompanies the type 2 response in the immune and structural compartments of the esophagus and highlights it as a candidate contributor to EoE pathology.

Title: The virome of New Zealand fur seals reveals novel viral diversity and evidence of continued Canine distemper virus circulation
Authors: Waller, S. J.; White, B. A.; Wierenga, J. R.; Hall, A. A.; Thompson, M.; Wilson, A. D.; Taylor, H. S.; Weir, J. S.; Geoghegan, J. L.
Abstract: Canine distemper virus (CDV) has recently been detected in New Zealand fur seals (Arctocephalus forsteri), including retrospective samples from 2020 and outbreaks associated with substantial mortality in late 2024 and 2025. However, the geographic distribution of CDV and the broader viral diversity harboured by New Zealand fur seals remain poorly understood. Characterising the fur seal virome can provide insights into viral diversity, dispersal and the occurrence of viral co-infections, while assessing the distribution of CDV across colonies. We used metatranscriptomic sequencing to characterise the viromes of 178 live and recently deceased fur seals sampled from four large fur seal colonies (Kaik[o]ura, Dunedin, West Coast and Wairarapa). We investigated viral diversity, community composition and geographic structure using phylogenetic analyses to examine viral evolutionary relationships and CDV distribution. We identified 23 viral species, including 20 putatively novel species. Several were related to viruses previously identified in terrestrial mammals. One viral species was detected across geographically separated colonies, while several other closely related viruses were identified across colonies, with viral sharing most frequent between Kaik[o]ura and Wairarapa. Viral diversity was similar between live and recently deceased fur seals, while community composition showed geographic structuring. CDV was detected only in Kaik[o]ura, where the lineage associated with the 2024 outbreak remained in circulation. No CDV was detected in the other sampled colonies. This study reveals substantial previously undocumented viral diversity in New Zealand fur seals, improving our understanding of viral distribution and CDV circulation in marine mammal populations.

Title: Continuous karyotypic and cryptic structural fluctuations drive acral melanoma evolution
Authors: Smith, E. A.; Prokofyeva, A.; Zhao, J.; Hu, M.; Zitnay, R. G.; Becker, C. A.; Jiang, A. Z.; Deacon, D. C.; Nix, D. A.; Reeves, M. Q.; Clement, K.; Judson-Torres, R. L.
Abstract: Reliable chromosome segregation during mitosis is essential for high-fidelity mammalian cell division. Even human cancers burdened by whole genome duplication and aneuploidy generally retain sufficiently stable segregation to produce clonal populations of progeny. Cancer genomes are accordingly understood to evolve in punctuated bursts, in which catastrophic rearrangement is followed by clonal expansion of a stabilized karyotype. However, bulk genomic sequencing, the workhorse of cancer genetics for the past two decades, cannot resolve structural variability within tumor subpopulations. Here we identify a subset of cancers that exhibit continuous ultra-low fidelity chromosomal segregation, with single tumors harboring individual cells whose metaphase chromosome counts ranged from 25 to over 200. This remarkable phenotype is recurrent in multiple cancer types and most common in acral melanoma, where it is associated with dicentric chromosomes, translocations, and complex structural variants. Single-cell whole genome sequencing revealed ongoing structural variation and the genomic signature of microhomology-mediated break-induced replication (MMBIR), a backup DNA repair pathway that triggers chromoanasynthesis. These genomes therefore do not pass through isolated catastrophic events and settle into stable lineages but rather undergo continuous evolution of chromosome number and structure across generations, resulting in extreme intratumoral heterogeneity and a shifting repertoire of gene fusions. We anticipate these findings will serve as a starting point for classifying tumors by ongoing karyotypic and structural fluctuation and for testing whether this state confers selective dependence on backup repair pathways.

Title: Bioresorbable permanent-magnet beacons for tracking internal biomechanics during free movement
Authors: Nie, Z.; Lin, X.; Wan, J.; Xu, J.; Wu, K.; Wang, Y.; Zhang, C.; Yang, C.; Zhong, R.; Sun, N.; Man, W.; Huang, Y.; Zhang, S.; Wu, D.; Wang, Y.; Wang, Y.; Hong, M.; Sun, Y.; Hu, H.; Koo, J.; Han, M.
Abstract: Perioperative complications represent a global health burden that can be reduced through timely interventions guided by continuous physiological monitoring. Bioresorbable sensors excel through natural degradation without subsequent surgical extraction, but motion artefacts disrupt their accurate measurement. We synthesize bioresorbable permanent-magnet nanocomposites from aligned iron nanowires as implantable beacons. These beacons intrinsically generate magnetic fields responsive to biomechanical changes, thereby enabling wireless and chipless monitoring. An artificial-intelligence-enhanced wearable magnetic-field camera decodes these spatial maps into calibrated values that tolerate vigorous movement. The system achieves a displacement-equivalent mean absolute error of 2.74 m. Experiments in rat models demonstrate intracranial pressure tracking with clinical-grade accuracy during vigorous activities, and longitudinal monitoring of intracranial hypertension associated with ischaemic stroke during natural behaviours.

Title: Evaluation of sources of variability in a TEER (trans-epithelial/endothelial electrical resistance) system
Authors: Gutierrez, R.; Lund, S.; Reipa, V.; Petersen, E. J.
Abstract: Trans-epithelial/endothelial electrical resistance (TEER) measurements are a key nondestructive measurement of the barrier integrity of cells grown on inserts. To support the use of TEER measurements in bioassays, we have evaluated the sources of variability in a case study involving a chamber-based TEER system to assess a gut co-culture model. Data from 23 separate experiments, each lasting 22 d, were evaluated. Multiple lines of evidence suggested minimal variability within a run, a period during which several plates were analyzed sequentially. In contrast, run-to-run variability was substantially larger, even when two runs were performed several hours apart on the same day. Bayesian analysis of both KCl and blank insert data revealed that run-to-run variability was among the largest sources of variability, with relative uncertainty values of 3 % to 6 % of the mean value. Correlational analysis investigated whether deviations of KCl or blank insert TEER values within a run compared to long-term median values were correlated with deviations of the biculture gut model values within that same run from their long-term median values. Unexpectedly, the KCl values were not correlated, while the blank insert values had a weak correlation. We also evaluated the information gained from different control measurements. The findings from this study can influence how statistical analyses are performed on TEER results and can inform the design of robust TEER methods. For example, the approaches described here can be used to characterize variability within and among runs in TEER measurements for other methods.

Title: Revealing interactions between glutathione peroxidase 4 and phosphoinositides
Authors: Walters, S. H.; Park, B.; Signorelli, R. L.; Labrecque, C. L.; Musayev, F. N.; Van Lehn, R. C.; Fuglestad, B.
Abstract: Glutathione peroxidase 4 (GPx4) is the primary enzyme that reduces lipid hydroperoxides to prevent membrane oxidative damage and protecting against ferroptosis. GPx4 is known to engage with lipid headgroups through electrostatic interactions, positioning the substrate for reduction. This work reveals and characterizes binding of highly anionic phosphoinositides (PIP lipids) by GPx4. PIPs are vital lipids in human cells and are central to many signaling processes, particularly in cytosolic-facing membranes. Lipid overlay assays confirm interactions between GPx4 and phosphorylated PIPs, comparable to known anionic lipid binders. Protein NMR describes the interaction between GPx4 and PIPs within micelles. The greatest resonance shifting occurs with tris-phosphorylated PIP, suggesting that higher anionic charge leads to greater binding, a known driver of GPx4 substrate recognition. Preferred anionic interactions were also confirmed with titration and crystallographic structure analysis of D-myo-inositol 1,3,4,5-tetrakisphosphate (IP4). A headgroup-binding site on GPx4 is revealed to be proximal to the cationic membrane interaction site. In conjunction with molecular simulations, these results show that PIP lipid interactions allow full GPx4 membrane engagement and position the headgroup to allow the lipid tail to interact with the catalytic site. Understanding whether GPx4 preferentially interacts with PIPs will allow better understanding of the protective function of this essential enzyme and a mechanism that may protect essential lipid signaling pathways from oxidative damage.

Title: Targeting host eIF4A with zotatifin inhibits Bundibugyo virus and other filoviruses
Authors: Bogucka-Janczi, K.; Yurugi, H.; Biedenkopf, N.; Kraft, F.; Shtanko, O.; Magalhaes, V. G.; Ciesek, S.; Song, Z.; Ruggero, D.; Moyo, V.; Gumbo, T.; Rajalingam, K.
Abstract: Filoviruses, including Ebola and Marburg viruses, depend on host eIF4A helicase activity for replication. Zotatifin is a first in class, clinical stage eIF4A inhibitor that acts as a molecular glue, stabilizing the interaction between eIF4A and selected polypurine rich RNA sequences, thereby inhibiting RNA unwinding and ribosomal scanning. Here, we identify pronounced polypurine enrichment in the 5'untranslated regions (5'UTRs) of the seven major filoviral protein-coding genes NP, VP35, VP40, GP, VP30, VP24, and L across four virus species, including Bundibugyo virus (BDBV). Consistent with these findings, zotatifin inhibits the replication of Ebola, Marburg, Sudan, Tai Forest, and Bundibugyo viruses at low nanomolar concentrations. Zotatifin has been administered to humans in oncology and COVID19 clinical studies. Clinical pharmacokinetic pharmacodynamic (PKPD) modeling indicates that exposures resulting in inhibition of BDBV replication are achievable in humans at tolerated doses following subcutaneous administration. Together, these findings support the repurposing of zotatifin as a host directed antiviral candidate against BDBV and other filoviruses, with potential applications in preparedness for future outbreaks.

Title: B cell tolerance is dysregulated in people with complex regional pain syndrome: A high-dimensional immunophenotyping study
Authors: Mason, A. C.; Collin, F. A.; Karrasch, J. F.; Heng, B.; Anh, S. B.; Krishnamurthy, S.; O'Brien, J. A.; Huang, Y.; Wong, R.; Macefield, V. G.; Russo, M. A.; Christelis, N.; Georgius, P.; Reed, J. H.; Austin, P. J.
Abstract: Complex regional pain syndrome (CRPS) is a devastating chronic pain disorder that typically arises after distal limb trauma. It has a complex, multi-system pathophysiology that is not well understood, preventing the development of targeted therapies. Observations of self-reactive antibodies in CRPS patients that can elicit pain hypersensitivity in rodents have established an autoimmune contribution to the onset and maintenance of CRPS-like pain, although the mechanisms underlying this remain unclear. To understand the development of pathogenic autoantibody responses in CRPS, this study performed the first high-dimensional characterisation of B cell activity in a cohort of 42 CRPS patients and 42 matched healthy controls. Immunophenotyping of peripheral immune cell populations by mass cytometry identified altered frequencies of class-switched and double-negative memory B cell subsets in CRPS, and increased use of autoimmune-associated IGHV1-69 and IGHV4-34 gene-encoded heavy-chains within the class-switched B cell compartment. Additional proteomic and autoantibody assessments identified differences in serum protein and IgA autoantibody profiles that may lead to altered complement signalling and pro-inflammatory cytokine production in CRPS. Together, these findings represent evidence of dysregulated B cell self-tolerance in CRPS that could facilitate production of pathogenic autoantibodies in people with the condition.

Title: Trajectory fit alone does not identify causal edges: a white-box masked ODE benchmark for trans-omics digital twins of drug action mechanisms
Authors: Zhang, Z.; Jia, L.; Pan, Y.; Zhao, H.
Abstract: Dynamic multi-omics models infer drug mechanisms from trajectories, but trajectory accuracy alone cannot verify that learned regulatory edges are mechanistically correct.
