We asked to what extent fitting time-series dynamics identifies intervenable causal edges across observation and optimization budgets.We built white-box ordinary differential equations with candidate-edge masks for gene-expression, protein, signalling and metabolite dynamics, using a mouse-liver trans-omics topology and ground-truth semi-synthetic time series. Under noise-free,complete, densely sampled data, from-scratch training ranked edges near chance(edge-class area under the receiver-operating characteristic curve, 0.48-0.53); the unattainable oracle-initialized upper bound reached 0.94-0.99 on the same metric.Unobserved layers absorbed error. In ground-truth knockout tests, development-batch endpoint-sign accuracy was 67.9% for one-hop non-convergent targets but 33.3% for two-hop targets. Across tested practical budgets, fitting did not yield reliable edge recovery; trajectory fit alone therefore does not establish mechanistic identification. This benchmark supports mechanistic audits and exploratory per-prediction confidence grading in multi-omics models.

Title: Comparative Mitogenomics and Molecular Phylogeny of Agriculturally Significant Tephritid Fruit Fly Pests in Bangladesh
Authors: Rahman, S.; Shormi, F. A.
Abstract: Tephritid fruit flies of the tribe Dacini rank among the most economically destructive agricultural pests globally, with several species of Bactrocera Macquart and Zeugodacus Hendel causing severe losses to fruit and vegetable production across South and Southeast Asia. Bangladesh harbors several economically important dacine species, including Bactrocera dorsalis (Hendel), B. carambolae (Drew & Hancock), B. zonata (Saunders), B. correcta (Bezzi) and Zeugodacus cucurbitae (Coquillett). Here we present a comparative mitogenomic and phylogenetic framework based on 21 unique GenBank mitogenome records: 19 dacine ingroup records and two outgroups. The ingroup includes B. papayae, B. philippinensis and B. invadens, whose synonymy with B. dorsalis is disputed. All records contained 13 protein-coding genes (PCGs) and two rRNA genes. Genome size in the 14 taxa of subgenus Bactrocera ranged from 15,273 to 15,977 bp. Whole-genome AT content ranged from 66.6% in B. tsuneonis to 82.2% in Drosophila melanogaster, and the five focal pest species clustered at 72.9-73.6%. Maximum-likelihood analysis of a 13,600-site alignment (13 PCGs plus 12S and 16S rRNA; GTR+FO; IQ-TREE v1.6.11; 1,000 ultrafast bootstrap replicates, UFBoot) recovered the B. dorsalis complex (UFBoot = 100), within which pairwise distances were only 0.64-1.33%, and a B. correcta + B. zonata pair (UFBoot = 100). Nine taxa showed compositional heterogeneity and third codon positions were highly variable, so deeper nodes should be interpreted cautiously. As no Bangladeshi specimens were sequenced, this study is a curated reference baseline for molecular identification and pest surveillance, not a population-genomic analysis.

Title: Microbes use transporters to regulate the release of metabolites based on value
Authors: Sulheim, S.; Broli, G.; Doubleday, P. F.; Gillon, A.; Luneau, J. S.; Padmanabha, P.; Quinn, A.; Ulrich, E.; Vogel, M. A.; Zamboni, N.; Engel, P.; Mitri, S.
Abstract: Microbial interactions are shaped by the exchange of metabolites, ranging from intermediates in central carbon metabolism to amino acids, vitamins and fermentation by-products. While specific metabolic processes such as overflow metabolism are well documented, a general principle explaining the chemical diversity of metabolite release and the variation in individual release rates remains elusive. Here, using a combination of computational and experimental approaches on seven different microbes, we show that release rates are negatively correlated with the value of metabolites, and that this relationship explains more variability in release rates than other frequently associated factors. By measuring metabolite release from 67 E. coli mutants lacking individual transport genes, we find that transporters both cause and counteract net metabolite release. These findings suggest that metabolite release constitutes a fitness cost that microbes have evolved to reduce, while revealing the underlying transport mechanism. This unifying explanation reshapes our understanding of how microbial interactions emerge and persist.

Title: Identification of SAMD4B as a Centrosome-Associated Regulator of the Sonic Hedgehog Signaling Pathway
Authors: Bernatik, O.; Vyslouzil, D.; Paclikova, P.; Renzova, T.; Kovarikova, P.; Cajanek, L.
Abstract: Background: Many protein-protein interactions are required for the assembly and function of primary cilia, microtubule-based organelles critical for the Sonic hedgehog (Shh) signaling pathway and, in turn, for embryonic development and tissue homeostasis. However, our understanding of this complex process remains incomplete. Methods: To identify new regulators of primary cilia formation or function, we carried out proximity labeling experiments and compared interactomes under ciliogenesis-restrictive and permissive conditions. Using an unbiased strategy, we selected candidates that were tested functionally by siRNA-mediated depletion or gene editing, in combination with gene expression analysis and various microscopy techniques, using either vertebrate cell lines or zebrafish as model systems. Results: We demonstrate that one of our identified candidates, protein SAMD4B, is associated with the centrosome and is required for Shh signaling in NIH3T3 cells and eye development in zebrafish. Our data implicate defective ciliary recruitment of Shh pathway regulators ARL13B and SMO as a plausible mechanism underlying the SAMD4B-mediated regulation of Shh signaling. Conclusions: Together, our data identify a previously unrecognized link between SAMD4B, a protein known to be associated with cytoplasmic RNA condensates, and ciliary signaling.

Title: NeuroSim: a clinically informed multi-disorder EEG simulator with personalized pattern injection and AI-driven neurological modeling
Authors: Bunterngchit, C.; Aslam, S.; Sattar, A.; Rasool, A.; Wang, Y.
Abstract: Deep learning for electroencephalography (EEG) based neurodiagnostics is constrained by the limited availability of labeled clinical recordings. Datasets covering Alzheimers disease (AD), Parkinsons disease (PD), schizophrenia (SCZ), epilepsy (EPI), and frontotemporal dementia (FTD) are scarce, demographically narrow, and heterogeneous across acquisition sites, while privacy requirements restrict data sharing. Existing EEG simulators typically address a single disorder or trade biological interpretability for statistical fidelity. This study presents NeuroSim, a simulation framework that generates synthetic multichannel EEG with user-controlled injection of disease-specific patterns across five disorders and multiple severity levels. A physiologically motivated baseline generator produces band-limited rhythms, event-related potentials, artifacts, and hierarchical subject-level and trial-level variability. Disease patterns are introduced through region-specific and severity-specific spectral modulation that encodes established biomarkers, including posterior alpha suppression in AD, motor beta enhancement in PD, and spike-wave discharges in EPI. An interactive interface exposes montage, sampling rate, duration, artifacts, stimuli, affected regions, and severity, and exports signals with reproducible metadata. The simulated signals reproduced the expected biomarker directionality under spectral, topographic, and multivariate statistical analysis. A convolutional-attention classifier trained on simulated data reached 95.3 to 96.8 percent hold-out accuracy, and post hoc explainability analyses produced class-separable embeddings with attributions concentrated on pathophysiologically expected electrodes. Application of the analysis pipeline to recordings from the Temple University Hospital EEG Corpus confirmed compatibility with heterogeneous clinical data. In subject-level augmentation experiments on real clinical EEG, supplementing real training data with NeuroSim samples increased classification accuracy from 91.6 to 94.5 percent for AD versus healthy controls and from 90.9 to 94.0 percent for PD versus healthy controls, exceeding the improvement obtained with conventional signal-level augmentation. NeuroSim is released as open-source software to support augmentation, benchmarking, and explainable artificial intelligence in neurological diagnostics.

Title: Learning RNA secondary structure from chemical probing with MXfold2
Authors: Yamauchi, R.; Tsukiyama, S.; Sato, K.
Abstract: Training RNA secondary structure predictors is limited by scarce reference annotations, even as chemical probing produces abundant nucleotide-level measurements. These measurements inform pairing states without identifying base-pairing partners. Here we extend MXfold2, which combines neural and thermodynamic folding scores, to learn from probing profiles and predict RNA secondary structures from sequence alone. We introduce three training objectives. One learns from probing-assisted target structures. The other two use implicit maximum-likelihood estimation to pass surrogate gradients from reactivity-ranking and likelihood losses through discrete folding. Simulations, RNAgym measurements and external structural tests show improved chemical agreement and gains in exact base-pair prediction when chemical supervision is combined with structural pretraining and replay. Probing profiles can thus broaden the range of RNAs that inform sequence-only structure prediction, including RNA populations with few complete structure annotations.

Title: SNP2Cluster-Py: A pathogen-agnostic, context-aware framework for Core SNP and transmission-cluster analysis
Authors: Kwenda, S.; Christoffels, A.
Abstract: Whole-genome sequencing enables high-resolution identification of genetically related pathogen isolates, but genomic similarity alone does not establish epidemiologically meaningful transmission. We developed SNP2Cluster-Py, an open-source Python framework that separates context-aware Core SNP clustering from the subsequent application of epidemiological and temporal criteria. The software accepts a precomputed pairwise Core SNP-distance matrix and user-configured metadata and supports analysis of all eligible isolates in a single context, as well as sequence-type, geographical, epidemiological and ordered composite contexts. Within each context, authoritative Core clusters are defined as connected components of an SNP-threshold graph; K-means assignments and silhouette widths are retained as exploratory diagnostics only. We evaluated the workflow using 172 Klebsiella pneumoniae isolates from six neonatal-surveillance hospitals in South Africa, a focused 36-isolate single-hospital subset from the same surveillance dataset, and 168 Streptococcus pneumoniae carriage isolates from Ghana. In the full K. pneumoniae dataset, ST-only analysis assigned 141 isolates to Core SNP clusters, whereas Facility + ST analysis assigned 134, demonstrating how facility stratification can remove cross-facility genomic connections. In the single-hospital subset, both contexts assigned 30 of 36 isolates to five Core clusters, and Facility analysis retained 23 isolates in four temporally compatible clusters. In the pneumococcal dataset, ST-context analysis assigned 114 isolates to 38 Core clusters, which were characterised across sampling locations and time through Community analysis. SNP2Cluster-Py therefore provides a reproducible framework for adapting genomic clustering to specific surveillance questions while maintaining a clear distinction between genomic relatedness, analytically inferred transmission clusters and confirmed direct transmission. SNP2Cluster-Py v1.1.2 is available under the Apache License 2.0 through GitHub and Zenodo.

Title: CELL-X: A Single-Cell Transcriptomics Framework for Cell-Type and Disease-State Prioritization of Type 2 Diabetes Risk Genes
Authors: Uddin, M. M.; Khan, S. M. Z. A.; Bomma Yadagiri, K.
Abstract: Genome-wide association studies (GWAS) have identified hundreds of loci associated with Type 2 Diabetes (T2D), yet pinpointing specific causal genes and their relevant cellular contexts remains a critical bottleneck. To address this gap, we developed CELL-X, a novel computational framework systematically integrating fine-mapped genetic evidence with high-resolution single-cell transcriptomics and disease progression dynamics. Utilizing a custom out-of-memory processing engine, we analyzed an integrated human pancreatic islet atlas of 245,878 cells without forced data downsampling. We evaluated 37 genetically supported T2D candidate genes, quantifying cell-type relevance via a max-scaled Cell Relevance Score (CRS). Disease-associated transcriptional dynamics were subsequently incorporated using a Disease Relevance Score (DRS) based on heterogeneous expression shifts across normal, prediabetic, and T2D metabolic states. CELL-X successfully identified beta cells as the dominant disease-relevant cellular context and prioritized established causal genes, including SLC30A8, GLIS3, GCK, and TCF7L2. Validation against a 30-gene benchmark demonstrated exceptional target recovery and significant metabolic pathway enrichment. Furthermore, rigorous statistical null modeling confirmed this prioritization is driven by true biological variance rather than background transcriptomic noise. Ultimately, CELL-X provides a highly scalable, robust framework for generating biologically informed hypotheses in complex polygenic disease research.

Title: Charge-engineered nanohybrid coatings for microbial fouling resistance
Authors: Devadig, R.; Kandadai, V. A. S.; Jawaharraj, K.; Jasthi, B. K.; Gnimpieba, E.; Shagla, C.; Dalton, A.; McHugh, J.; Ajayan, P. M.; Tripathi, M.; Gadhamshetty, V.
Abstract: Microbial attachment is the gateway to biofouling and microbially influenced corrosion. Yet biocides and passive barrier coatings do not actively regulate the charged metal-microbe interface at which adhesion begins. Here we report a charge-engineered coating, a graphene thin-film nanohybrid (gTFN) on nickel (Ni) forming an asymmetric metal-graphene-metal junction, that suppresses cell attachment through interfacial charge redistribution rather than soluble toxicity. Against the model sulfate-reducing bacterium Oleidesulfovibrio alaskensis G20, gTFN combines an impermeable graphene scaffold, an immobilized low-leaching Ag cap and a serrated topology, reducing microbial surface coverage by 98%, increasing charge-transfer resistance 47-fold and lowering corrosion current 167-fold relative to Ni. Surface-potential mapping and density functional theory reveal interfacial dipoles that pattern the surface potential, while imaging shows graphene wrinkles channeling residual attachment. Transcriptomic profiling reveals downregulation of biofilm-associated and energy-metabolism genes. These results establish interfacial charge redistribution as an active antifouling and anticorrosion mechanism for controlling microbial biointerfaces.

Title: MetaEntropy: quantifying protein variability in complex viral mixtures via entropy
Authors: Jones, L. R.; Manrique, J. M.
Abstract: High-density sequence data has become commonplace in the study of complex viral mixtures from wastewater. Established algorithms are available for lineage deconvolution and labelling of clinically-elusive mutations. However, less attention has been paid to the quantification of translated amino acid diversity. We present MetaEntropy, a modular R package for assessing protein sequence variability and identifying sites under potential selection via Shannon entropy. MetaEntropy integrates utility functions for visualizing genome-wide and protein-specific variability, extracting nucleotide and amino acid mutation profiles, and identifying entropy hotspots. Despite being designed for wastewater surveillance, the package can also profile protein diversity from cross-sectional intra-patient data. However, it does not analyze population structure or quasispecies, for which several tools are available. By focusing on positional entropy, MetaEntropy bypasses the sequence constraints, computational overhead, and consensus-based variant loss typical of traditional haplotype reconstruction and multiple sequence alignment strategies. To balance sensitivity against neutral variation, the package evaluates entropy using a standard 20-class canonical amino acid scheme and a 7-class model based on traditional physicochemical properties. Calculated entropy values are normalized to a 0-1 scale, enabling direct comparisons of protein diversity across loci and sample strata. As proofs of concept, we employ MetaEntropy to detect well-known SARS-CoV-2 functional changes from wastewater data, and to explore tissue-specific heterogeneity in systemic infections. MetaEntropy is available from the Comprehensive R Archive Network (CRAN) at https://CRAN.R-project.org/.

Title: An Infected Cryopreserved Precision-Cut Lung Slice Model for Drug Susceptibility Testing in Pneumocystis murina Pneumonia
Authors: Pellegrino, M. R.; McLean, J. L.; Kottom, T.; Limper, A.
Abstract: Precision-cut lung slices (PCLS) preserve native three-dimensional lung architecture and cellular complexity, providing a valuable ex vivo platform for studying pulmonary host-pathogen interactions. However, existing PCLS infection models typically introduce microorganisms into previously uninfected tissue, while fresh PCLS prepared from infected lungs have limited experimental flexibility and scalability. To our knowledge, cryopreserved PCLS generated from lungs with an established in vivo pulmonary infection have not been described. Herein, we evaluated cryopreserved PCLS from mice with established Pneumocystis murina pneumonia (PCP) as an ex vivo platform for infection and therapeutic studies. PCLS were prepared from dexamethasone-immunosuppressed mice with established PCP, rested for 24 h, cryopreserved in a novel freezing medium for 12 days in liquid nitrogen, rapidly thawed, recovered for 24 h, and treated with pentamidine for 72 h. Viability was assessed in uninfected and PCP-infected PCLS before and after cryopreservation. Although post-thaw viability decreased in both groups, substantial viability was still retained, allowing further experimentation. qPCR showed that cryopreservation did not alter expression of the type I and type II alveolar epithelial markers podoplanin (Pdpn) and surfactant protein C (Sftpc) in either group. Importantly, pentamidine significantly reduced Pneumocystis mitochondrial small subunit (mtSSU) rRNA levels in thawed PCP-infected PCLS, demonstrating suitability for anti-Pneumocystis drug testing. These findings establish the first cryopreserved ex vivo PCP model using infected mouse PCLS, preserving endogenous fungal burden and infection-associated host responses while enabling flexible, scalable studies of Pneumocystis biology, host-pathogen interactions, therapeutic efficacy, and potentially other pulmonary infections.

Title: Beta-cell-derived urocortin-3 contributes to glucose-regulated somatostatin and glucagon secretion in the mouse pancreas
Authors: Vergara-Ucin, J.; Andersen, D. B.; di Giuseppe, G.; Mezza, T.; Rosenkilde, M.; Holst, J. J.
Abstract: Aims/Hypothesis. Glucagon secretion is impaired in both type 1 and type 2 diabetes. The mechanisms behind this dysregulation are incompletely understood. Urocortin-3 (UCN-3), a beta-cell-derived peptide, stimulates somatostatin (SST) secretion and may thereby regulate glucagon secretion. We investigated the mechanisms through which UCN-3 regulates pancreatic hormone secretion and examined the physiological contribution of endogenous UCN-3 to glucose-regulated hormone secretion. Methods. Pancreatic hormone secretion was studied using the isolated perfused mouse pancreas. The effects of exogenous and endogenous UCN-3 were investigated using selective antagonists of SST receptors (SSTR) and corticotropin-releasing hormone receptor 2 (CRHR2). In addition, the role of UCN-3 was examined in streptozotocin (STZ) treated mice. Results. Exogenous UCN-3stimulated somatostatin secretion and inhibited glucagon secretion in the mouse pancreas. Blockade of SSTRs completely abolished the glucagonostatic effect of UCN-3, demonstrating that inhibition of glucagon secretion is indirectly mediated through SST signaling. Moreover, CRHR2 antagonism prevented both UCN-3-induced SST secretion and inhibition of glucagon secretion, identifying CRHR2 as the key receptor mediating these effects. During acute glucose stimulation (3.5-10mM), CRHR2 antagonism reduced glucose-induced stimulation of SST and attenuated glucagon inhibition, indicating that endogenous UCN-3 participates in the acute islet response to hyperglycemia. However, during sustained hyperglycemia, CRHR2 antagonism reduced SST secretion without altering glucagon secretion. In STZ-treated mice, glucose-induced SST secretion was lost. Conclusions. Urocortin-3 regulated glucagon secretion indirectly through CRHR2-dependent stimulation of SST secretion. Endogenous UCN-3 contributes to the acute islet response to hyperglycemia, supporting a physiologically relevant beta-cell-to-delta-cell-to-alpha-cell paracrine axis in the mouse pancreas. This pathway is disrupted following beta-cell loss, suggesting a potential contribution to impaired islet hormone regulation in diabetes.

Title: Palmitic acid overload does not promote full-blown dysfunction in SGBS adipocytes which is reflected in their secretome
Authors: Angelini, S.; Stifani, G.; La Runa, G.; Cosenza, L. C.; Lodi, G.; Voltan, R.; Secchiero, P.; Castaldo, F.; Gessi, S.; Merighi, S.; Fernandez, M.; Bigot, A.; Wabitsch, M.; Cervellati, C.; Sanz, J. M.; Passaro, A.; Sergi, D.
Abstract: Background: Energy excess, and particularly long-chain saturated fatty acid (SFA) overload, are instrumental in promoting obesity and hampering metabolic health. However, SFA contribution to human adipocyte metabolic and endocrine dysfunction remains elusive. Nonetheless, we have already provided evidence that a 48-hour palmitic acid (PA) exposure is not sufficient to hamper Simpson-Golabi Behmel Syndrome (SGBS) adipocytes insulin signalling. Objective: This study aims at evaluating whether a 96-hour exposure to PA is able to disrupt SGBS adipocyte metabolic health and induce the release of a secretome capable of hampering insulin signalling in skeletal muscle cells. Methods: SGBS adipocytes were treated with either 1000 uM PA or bovine serum albumin (BSA) for 96 hours followed by the assessment of the NFkB signalling and the expression of genes associate with inflammation and adipocyte metabolic stress. Furthermore, adipocytes were labelled with BODIPY and lipid droplet as well as cell size semi-quantified using ImageJ. Insulin-induced phosphorylation of Akt and Akt substrate of 160 kDa (AS160) was assessed by Western Blot. The effect of PA on SGBS secretome was assessed by both ELISA as well as MILLIPLEX. Finally, human immortalised myotubes were co-cultured with BSA or PA-treated SGBS adipocytes for 24 hours followed by the assessment of insulin signalling at the Akt level. Results: PA did not activate the NFkB signalling pathway, but induced the expression of MCP-1 while tending to upregulate IL-6 mRNA levels. Despite 96-hour PA exposure leading to an increase in lipid droplet and cell size, this was not coupled with an impairment in insulin signalling. Nevertheless, this SFA promoted an increase in IL-6 and IL-8 secretion while tending to enhance the release of adiponectin by SGBS adipocytes. Finally, the secretome from PA-treated SGBS adipocyte did not impair insulin-induced phosphorylation of Akt relative to controls in myotubes. Conclusions: Thus, in the absence of the stromal vascular fraction, direct exposure of SGBS adipocytes to PA overload is not sufficient to elicit overt dysfunction. The absence of full-blown adipocyte dysfunction is reflected in the secretome of these cells which failed to disrupt skeletal muscle insulin signalling.

Title: Comparative transcriptomics reveals shared and context-dependent adaptations of bovine cells across culture systems for cultivated meat
Authors: Ribarski-Chorev, I.; Burghardt, M.; Tawil, S.; Gershkoviz, A.; Shpatz, D.; Schudy, G.; Beh Hamo, Y.; Gilad, Y.; Vainshtein, I.; Kfir, A.; Tuller, T.; Schlesinger, S.
Abstract: Developing cell-culture systems for cultivated meat requires understanding how candidate cells respond to prolonged expansion and different growth environments. However, the extent to which bovine cells share transcriptional adaptations across these conditions, or retain responses specific to their origin and cellular state, remains unclear. Here, we systematically profiled bovine umbilical cord (BUC)- and adipose tissue (BAT)-derived mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs) across different culture architectures, passage stages, and differentiation states, including immortalized BUC cells and satellite cells as a myogenic reference. We show that global transcriptomic variation is strongly associated with culture architecture, cell identity, and cellular state. Immortalization preserved several early-passage transcriptional features, particularly proliferation-related programs, while opposing selected changes associated with primary cell aging. Culture architecture induced distinct rather than uniform three-dimensional responses. Spheroid formation produced a pronounced transcriptional shift characterized by reduced proliferation-, chromatin-, and development-associated programs, alongside changes in extracellular-matrix organization, metabolism, and intracellular remodeling. Across primary umbilical cord-derived, adipose-derived, and myogenically induced umbilical cord-derived cells, scaffold-versus-plate comparisons revealed correlated but non-identical transcriptional responses. These involved changes in extracellular-matrix organization, adhesion, membrane trafficking, and developmental pathways, with endocytosis enriched across all three comparisons among the pathways examined. During myogenic induction, both satellite cells and BUC-derived cells exhibited muscle-related cytoskeletal and contractile programs, while scaffold culture further supported myogenic signatures in BUC-derived cells. These findings distinguish recurring culture-associated responses from transcriptional features tied to cell source and expansion history. They support evaluating cultivated-meat candidate cells in their intended culture systems, not solely under conventional plate conditions.

Title: SOUR Disentangles Heritable and Microenvironmental Contributions to Intratumoral Heterogeneity in Spatial Lineage Tracing Data
Authors: Weine, E.; Burt, D.; Abraham, K. J.; Colgan, W.; Weissman, J. S.; Irizarry, R. A.; Broderick, T.; Schraiber, J. G.
Abstract: Intratumoral heterogeneity is hypothesized to be a major contributor to treatment resistance, yet the processes that generate it remain only partially understood. New technologies enable measurement of gene expression in individual tumor cells while also determining where the cells are located within a tumor and how they are related through cell division. A central question for such data is how much gene expression differences reflect characteristics passed from parent cells to their descendants, rather than influences from their local surroundings. Distinguishing these influences is challenging because closely related cells often reside near one another. Existing methods examine the relationship between gene expression and each of these factors separately, and can therefore incorrectly attribute spatial effects to ancestry or inherited effects to spatial location. Here, we present SOUR, a statistical method that uses both cell ancestry and spatial location to estimate their respective contributions to differences in gene expression. Using simulated data and two spatial lineage tracing datasets, we demonstrate that SOUR can estimate the separate contributions of cell ancestry and spatial location to variation in gene expression, while substantially reducing the confounding observed with existing approaches.

Title: Curated annotations locate biological concepts in protein language models from layers to neurons
Authors: Hallee, L.; Gleghorn, J. P.
Abstract: Interpretability methods describe what a network has learned, yet their claims are rarely tested against model-independent ground truth. We argue that proteins are an ideal modality for interpretability since curators annotate functional sites residue by residue. Across three ESMC protein language models (300M-6B parameters), we show that conclusions depend on where models are read, how concepts are decoded, which units are examined, and how they are scored. Concepts become linearly readable along depth long before erasure impairs masked-token prediction, and 20-fold scaling shifts concept depth more than peak score. Most of a nonlinear probe's lead over a linear one reflects fitting and readout shape rather than nonlinear encoding. Over whole proteins, saturated metrics render feed-forward neurons indistinguishable from random rotations. At annotated residues, dual-signed neuron poles identify 2.5-5.4 times as many concepts as rotations without training, though sparse autoencoders identify more. Without held-out validation, however, shuffled annotations label nearly every latent, and causal reliance emerges in neuron groups rather than single poles. Reading selected intra-block states exposes binding and active sites that stream probes read poorly and lifts a simple probe 5% above the best published MCC on a leakage-controlled interaction benchmark. We recommend reading a model directly against annotation, scoring units where they fire with a measure that is not saturated, and training a dictionary only where it adds coverage.

Title: Systematic inference of biological relatedness across the global ancient DNA record
Authors: Huang, E. C.; Ringbauer, H.
Abstract: The rapidly expanding scale of ancient DNA data creates an increasing need for high-performance software methods. One area for such improvement is the inference of pairwise biological relatedness, a prominent aspect of many ancient DNA studies. We present fastpmr, a fast and memory-efficient method for biological relatedness inference based on the computation of pairwise mismatch rates. We demonstrate that fastpmr can achieve over 1000x speed-up over READv2, a widely used relatedness-inference method. We leverage this performance to investigate relatedness at the scale of the global ancient DNA record. Analyzing biological relatedness across all pairs in the Allen Ancient DNA Resource (n = 19,118 ancient and 23,089 total samples) recapitulates human evolutionary history and identifies previously unknown genetic duplicates and likely sample mix-ups, demonstrating fastpmr's utility for ancient DNA analysis and quality control at scale.

Title: Predictive modeling of photoactivation, diffusion and adsorption in cell - The case of the optogenetic CRY2-CIBN system
Authors: DELON, A.; WANG, I.; Grosjean, M.; Destaing, O.; Grichine, A.
Abstract: Strategies combining optogenetics and careful spatiotemporal control of photoactivation are highly promising to decipher the dynamical network of biochemical reactions taking place at the m scale in living cells. To improve the spatial resolution of such methods, the roles of various molecular processes, such as photochemical reactions, diffusion and interactions, need to be understood and quantifed. In this article we develop a minimal and realistic model to describe photoactivation, diffusion and surface-binding of optogenetic probes and validate it thanks to experimental results obtained with a CRY2-CIBN system. A theoretical description of optogenetic activation is implemented, based on the photophysics of CRY2 and on its binding kinetics to the membrane through light-dependent heterodimerization with its partner, CIBN. The cell cytosol is described as a closed reservoir of activable CRY2 molecules. Then, a series of photoactivation pulses of a focused laser beam are applied to activate CRY2 proteins, driving their relocalization to the CIBN molecules anchored at the plasma membrane. We examine both the recruitment rate and the spatial distribution of CRY2 molecules recruited after illumination with either propagative or evanescent light. We have estimated numerical values for the corresponding parameters and put into evidence the key role of the optical saturation of photoactivation. These findings establish a framework to further improve spatial control in optogenetic experiments.

Title: Polymer overlap and the organization of enzyme activity in crowded solutions
Authors: Cecic Vidos, J.; Migliorini, G.; Hamacek, J.; Piazza, F.
Abstract: Macromolecular crowding shapes biochemical reactions in subtle ways, yet a general framework connecting enzyme activity to the physical properties of polymeric crowders remains elusive. Here we show that polymer scaling concepts provide a common framework to organize the effects of crowding on enzyme activity. Using dextran as a model crowder and fluorescence measurements extending beyond the initial-rate regime, we measure the time course of product formation upon peptide hydrolysis by a representative protease. Time-dependent analysis with a reversible kinetic model yields an inferred equilibrium constant whose dependence on dextran concentration collapses onto a common exponential curve after rescaling by a molecular-weight-dependent concentration. We show that the latter displays the same scaling law as the overlap concentration expected for branched dextran, linking quantitatively the reaction response to a fundamental property of polymer solutions. The common behaviour breaks down for the largest dextran at concentrations well above this scale, identifying the limits of the common scaling behaviour. Altogether, these findings suggest that polymer overlap is a general organizing principle for interpreting biochemical kinetics in polymer-crowded solutions.

Title: Behavioral Plasticity and Dispersal of Free Swimming Coral Larvae via Vertical Tracking Microscopy
Authors: Ho, I.; Zhang, Q.; Foster, B.; Lopez-Nandam, E. H.; Vyas, P.; Matsuda, S.; Albright, R.; Prakash, M.
Abstract: Coral larvae disperse and seek suitable sites for settlement while undergoing rapid development, making this period central to reef connectivity, recruitment, and recovery. Yet how the accompanying changes in larval morphology, ciliary activity, and swimming behavior shape dispersal remains poorly understood. Here, using vertical tracking microscopy, we follow individual Acropora millepora larvae over hundreds of body lengths at successive developmental stages while resolving body morphology. We show a developmental progression from buoyant rise to upward- and downward-directed gravitactic swimming, followed by weaker gravitactic alignment at later stages, accompanied by body elongation and increasingly structured ciliary flows. Integrating these kinematics into a minimal, data-driven model, we separate buoyant drift from active swimming and estimate the propulsion costs of vertical migration and lateral spreading. Buoyancy supports early ascent without propulsion expenditure, while the model predicts lower costs of descent and lateral spreading at late developmental stages. Simulations in fluctuating flow, assuming no flow sensing, predict that directed swimming weakens when flow-induced rotation acts on timescales comparable to intrinsic heading relaxation. Together, these results reveal how development reorganizes the physical drivers of larval motion in ways that may support the transition from dispersal to settlement, providing a basis for incorporating developmental changes in swimming into models of coral larval dispersal.

Title: Immunometabolic IRG1-NLRC5 Axis Controls Inflammatory Cell Death
Authors: Pandian, N.; Sundaram, B.; Kumar, S. P.; Palacios, G.; Young, A. P.; Sarkar, R.; El Farran, C.; Kanneganti, T.-D.
Abstract: Innate immunity is the first defense against pathogens, sterile injury, and homeostatic perturbations. One key mechanism used by the innate immune system for host defense is inflammatory cell death, PANoptosis, which eliminates infected or damaged cells and releases cytokines and other danger signals that can further propagate the immune response. Given these inflammatory functions, PANoptosis must be tightly regulated to prevent excess inflammation and pathology. Cellular metabolism is a key regulator of innate immunity, yet how metabolic reprogramming regulates innate immune signaling to control cell death, inflammation, and disease remains poorly understood. Here, we identify the immune-responsive gene 1 (IRG1)-itaconate axis as a critical regulator of PANoptosis. Innate immune triggers robustly induced IRG1 expression, leading to itaconate accumulation and driving IRG1-dependent inflammatory cell death. Mechanistically, glutaminolysis fueled IRG1-dependent itaconate synthesis, and inhibition of glutamine metabolism reduced itaconate accumulation and blocked PANoptosis. Furthermore, NAD depletion, a known inducer of NLRC5-mediated PANoptosis that has been connected to hemolytic, infectious, and inflammatory conditions, acted upstream inducing IRG1 expression and promoting NLRC5-PANoptosome assembly. Together, these findings highlight IRG1 as a metabolic node linking innate immunity to PANoptosis, identifying IRG1 as a potential therapeutic target in hemolytic and inflammatory diseases.

Title: Antibody-Fcγ receptor-driven NOX2 activation during phagocytosis of tumor cells is suppressed by CD47, preventing CD8 T cell engagement and immunotherapeutic responses.
Authors: Sharma, P.; Olson, L. J.; Akter, S.; Leek, J. F.; Kerkvliet, J. G.; Kueter, H. M.; Fowkes, E. J. C.; Thiex, N. W.; Thirdborough, S. M.; Beers, S. A.; Cragg, M. W.; Hoppe, A. D.
Abstract: Antibody-dependent cellular phagocytosis (ADCP) contributes to the elimination of antibody-opsonized tumor cells and engagement of adaptive immunity. This process is inhibited by tumor-cell overexpression of CD47. Here, genome-wide CRISPR screens in macrophages identified the NADPH oxidase (NOX2 complex) and the CD47 receptor, SIRP, as regulators of phagosome acidification. Target-cell CD47 suppressed NOX2 generation of reactive oxygen species at antibody densities that support ADCP, revealing distinct CD47-dependent thresholds for ADCP and oxidant generation. CD47 removal from the target cell delayed phagosome acidification in wild-type macrophages, but not in NOX2-deficient macrophages. Consistent with a role for this pathway in antitumor immunity, tumor-opsonizing anti-Tyrp1 therapy allowed clearance of CD47-deficient B16F10 melanoma tumors in approximately 36% of wild-type mice but failed in NOX2-deficient mice. Tumor clearance required CD8 T cells and IFN{gamma}, but perforin was dispensable. CD4 T cell depletion markedly improved tumor clearance. These findings suggest a noncanonical role for CD8 T cells in supporting ADCP-mediated tumor control. Combining anti-Tyrp1 with a mouse-serum-albumin-IL-2 fusion (MSA-IL-2) or PD-1 blockade enabled superior clearance of CD47-deficient tumors in NOX2-deficient mice, but not wild-type mice. Rechallenge experiments distinguished primary tumor clearance from durable immunity, whereby NOX2-deficient mice treated with anti-Tyrp1 and PD-1 blockade lacked rechallenge protection despite high initial cure rates. Conversely, the addition of MSA-IL-2 supported durable protection in both wild-type and NOX2-deficient mice. These results indicate that tumor CD47 functions beyond a "don't-eat-me" signal by controlling NOX2 activity to positively and negatively regulate CD 8 T cell function. Significance CD47-SIRP suppresses NOX2 activation, regulating a critical feedback loop between ADCP and CD8 T cell activation during tumor-opsonizing antibody therapy, suggesting new strategies for cancer immunotherapy targeting tumor surface antigens.

Title: Comprehensive identification of bacterial and archaeal habitat associations using IndicPiper
Authors: Bueno de Mesquita, C. P.; Woodcroft, B. J.; Fierer, N.
Abstract: Taxa that are prevalent and abundant in a particular habitat more so than other habitats can be considered indicators of that habitat. In addition to providing basic natural history information, indicator taxa can be used to verify metadata assignments in large public databases, identify potential contamination, and assess contributions of different source populations to a sink population. Despite these potential applications, a comprehensive database of microbial indicator taxa for major habitats of interest does not yet exist. Here we present IndicPiper, a database and methodology that uses the Sandpiper database combined with indicator taxa analysis to identify the habitat associations of bacterial and archaeal genera. IndicPiper includes a clearly defined methodology and set of functions such that any user with a list of habitats of interest could run the functions and generate their own database. IndicPiper uses the Genome Taxonomy Database (GTDB) for taxonomy, and the provided database or custom databases can be used to analyze any prokaryotic sample-by-taxa abundance table, including those from shotgun metagenomic and 16S rRNA marker gene sequencing. After presenting the methodology and results, we then present three applications of IndicPiper on actual modern and ancient DNA sequencing datasets. We used IndicPiper to assess the contribution of different source habitats to Lake Tjornin sediments in Iceland over the past 2000 years, to paired indoor and outdoor dust samples from homes across the U.S, and to freshwater samples across the Willamette River watershed in Oregon, USA.

Title: MSGFLEX: An optimized end-to-end pipeline for proteomics and metaproteomics analysis built on MS-GF+ with a dedicated rescoring model XPECTRA
Authors: Relangi, T. R.; Hall, H. A.; Wright, A. T.
Abstract: Mass spectrometry-based proteomics workflows often face competing demands between identification sensitivity, false discovery rate (FDR) control, and computational scalability, particularly for metaproteomic datasets that require searching large and complex sequence databases. Here, we present MSGFLEX, an integrated end-to-end workflow that combines database searching, machine-learning based rescoring, and peptide-to-protein quantitative inference. MSGFLEX integrates three components: SPARX handles raw file conversion, and MS-GF+ database searching; XPECTRA is a cross-validated XGBoost ensemble that rescores peptide-spectrum matches by combining ensemble predictions with MS-GF+ search evidence through noisy-OR fusion model. QUANTIX provides protein quantification through multiple protein rollup strategies. Across four benchmarking datasets, XPECTRA consistently increased peptide and protein identifications relative to Percolator, MS2Rescore, and MSBooster. On a human gut metaproteome dataset, XPECTRA achieved the largest effect size among all methods evaluated (Cohen's d = 0.95; p < 0.0005). SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP)-based analysis indicated that XPECTRA learned consistent relationships from spectral and physicochemical features. Database partitioning does not introduce detectable bias in peptide identification or FDR estimation, while QUANTIX's DWrollup provides the most accurate recovery of known protein abundance changes in a ground-truth spike-in benchmark. Together, these results establish MSGFLEX as a scalable and interpretable framework for mass-spectrometry based proteomics and metaproteomics.

Title: A site-resolved post-translational modification framework for drug-response analysis
Authors: Zein, M. M.; Hassanien, A. E.
Abstract: Post-translational modifications (PTMs) regulate protein activity and treatment-associated signalling, providing functional information that can connect drug-response estimates with candidate pharmacodynamic measurements. Assessing this information requires a framework that determines its contribution beyond fixed molecular features while retaining the identity of the modified sites underlying model predictions. We developed the PTM Biological Dynamics Layer (PTM-BDL), which integrates typed PTM states with protein sequence, structure-derived and drug chemical features to predict log-transformed half-maximal inhibitory concentration and resistance while providing site-level interpretation through integrated gradients. Retrospective evaluation used source-derived and propagated PTM profiles across biologically distinct BCR-ABL, HDAC/EP300 and EGFR/ERBB2 settings, yielding internal areas under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROCs) between 0.785 and 0.946. Retraining demonstrated a consistent incremental contribution from PTM inputs in K562/CML, with a mean AUROC increase of 0.0268 and positive gains in all five folds, alongside more modest incremental gains in HeLa/HDAC and EGFR/ERBB2. Within K562/CML, CRKL Y207 and STAT5A Y694 retained the leading attribution ranks for their proteins across three seeds, while greater PTM attribution in dasatinib than in cytotoxic drug contexts identified a focused setting for pharmacodynamic investigation. These findings support context-dependent use of PTM information and connect predictive assessment with prioritisation of individual sites, providing a basis for targeted pharmacodynamic measurements and independent experimental validation.

Title: Phosphate selectivity in XPR1 is driven by direct multi-ion competition
Authors: Wallis, C.; Wang, X.; Zhang, Y.; Corry, B.
Abstract: Inorganic phosphate (Pi) is essential for numerous cellular processes, and its intracellular concentration must be tightly regulated. In mammals, phosphate efflux is mediated by the Xenotropic and Polytropic Retrovirus Receptor 1 (XPR1/SLC53A1), the only known mammalian Pi exporter. We and others have recently proposed that XPR1 functions like a Pi channel, with the protein preferentially conducting the H2PO4- species of Pi over HPO42-. While some studies suggest that XPR1 can conduct other anions, the molecular basis of XPR1 substrate selectivity remains unknown. Here, we use over 110 s of molecular dynamics simulations, together with free-energy calculations, to investigate substrate selectivity in XPR1. We show that H2PO4- (Pi1-) is preferentially conducted over HPO42- (Pi2-), and that Pi1- progressively outcompetes Cl- for occupancy of the transport pathway. Free-energy and ion-interaction analyses reveal that selectivity arises from two distinct mechanisms: favourable protein-Pi interactions and direct ion-ion interactions in the pore. This direct contact facilitates Pi1- displacement via the previously proposed knock-kiss-kick mechanism, whereas entry of Cl- is restricted due to the preference for water-mediated interactions. Simulations with additional anions show that XPR1 remains permissive to several monovalent species, including nitrate, bicarbonate and methanesulfonate, while poorly conducting the divalent anion sulfate. These findings suggest that XPR1 does not achieve phosphate selectivity through absolute exclusion of competing anions. Instead, preferential Pi transport emerges from substrate-specific interactions and competition between multiple ions within a relatively permissive permeation pathway, providing a molecular basis for substrate discrimination in XPR1.

Title: Cell-autonomous self-renewal
Authors: MacArthur, B.; Greulich, P.
Abstract: To self-renew, stem cells must precisely balance proliferation and differentiation. Typically, this is achieved under feedback from the niche; yet many stem cells also possess an intrinsic self-renewal program that allows them to do so autonomously, if required. However, because self-renewal implies a stable equilibrium -- in which the expected stem cell number neither increases nor decreases over time -- this seems to require fine-tuning to a critical point. Here, we show that this is not the case: self-renewal can, in principle, be easily achieved without the need for extrinsic instruction, feedback or fine-tuning, by a simple cell-autonomous capture-release dimerization cycle that makes use of partitioning errors at cell division to reliably establish asymmetric divisions and perfectly balance symmetric divisions. Such a cycle is seen in the interactions between early-2 factor (E2F) transcription factors cell cyle regulators and their pocket protein partners. Since E2Fs and PPs are also important cell-fate regulators we hypothesise that the E2F-PP cell cycle machinery formed a primordial template upon which self-renewal was first established and continues to be maintained.

Title: Resident liver macrophages buffer dietary and circulating cholesterol to maintain hepatocyte homeostasis
Authors: Hamilton, M.; Morshed, S. M.; Chlebowski, M.; Shiau, C. E.
Abstract: Cholesterol metabolism is viewed largely through the lens of hepatocytes, leaving the roles of other liver cells unclear. Using high-resolution live imaging and cholesterol tracing in intact zebrafish, complemented by genetic and clodronate-mediated macrophage depletion and single-cell analysis, we identify liver-resident macrophages (LMs) as cellular buffers of circulating and dietary cholesterol. LMs directly take up cholesterol, and their depletion redirects cholesterol to hepatocytes, which suppress cholesterol synthesis, increase bile-acid synthesis and efflux, and activate metabolic-stress and immune programs, including hepatokine lect2 induction. These responses are heightened by elevated dietary cholesterol and occur without overt inflammation or altered liver architecture. LMs partition cholesterol through abca1b-dependent export and cetp-mediated lipoprotein remodeling. Loss of abca1b causes cholesterol sequestration in LMs and reduced cholesterol-processing demand on hepatocytes, while LM depletion eliminates macrophage-derived cetp and reduces hepatocyte cetp. Together, these findings reveal the innate immune system as integral to normal metabolic physiology, with LMs buffering cholesterol to maintain hepatocyte homeostasis.

Title: Spatiotemporal Dynamics and Environmental Drivers of Maize Microbiome Structure across Diverse Agroecosystems in Georgia, USA
Authors: AMO, A. E.; Yang, C.; Johnson, M.; Kovar, L.; Wallace, J.
Abstract: The understanding of how microbial communities differ across soils, environments, plant tissues, and developmental stages is key to the improvement of crop productivity and resilience. Here, we conducted a statewide survey of maize (Zea mays L.) microbiomes across 35 fields at 16 locations in Georgia, USA, sampling soil, rhizosphere, root interior, and stalk interior at two developmental stages (600 and 1400 growing degree days, GDD). More than 38000 ASVs were produced after amplicon sequencing of 16S rRNA genes. The phyla shown to be dominant are Proteobacteria, Actinobacteriota, Chloroflexi, Planctomycetota, and Acidobacteriota. Based on alpha and beta diversity analyses, the below-ground compartments (soil and rhizosphere) revealed higher diversity and stronger spatial structuring when compared to the above-ground sample types, whereas root and stalk interior microbiomes revealed marked shifts across growth stages. Amino acid metabolism, secondary metabolite biosynthesis, and energy-related pathways predictions (via PICRUSt2) show stage-dependent enrichment. Network analyses show persistent keystone taxa (Proteobacteria and Actinobacteriota) mediating microbial stability, coupled with an increase in modularity and connectivity as we move from early to late growth stages. Some environmental variables, such as temperature, humidity, soil potassium, and soil sodium, showed significant correlation with microbial diversity indicative of a compartment-specific environmental sensitivity. Collectively, our results show that in maize, microbial community composition, interaction, and potential functionality are both impacted by developmental stages and environmental heterogeneity. This study provides a fundamental framework for understanding the microbiome dynamics in field-grown maize across various agroecological conditions. It equally provides ecological insights relevant to microbiome-informed crop management.

Title: Precision Fermentation Gets a New Player: Genome Assembly and Genetic Transformation of a Novel Strain, Pichia hangzhouana, for Precision Fermentation of Food Ingredients
Authors: Karimian, P.; Johnston, E.; Vafadarshamasbi, U.; Afshari, R.; Bachler, A.; Mead, O.; Boer, P.; Hands, P.; Hlaing, M. M.; McAuley, C. M.; Kasprzak, A.; Liu, J.-W.; Vanhercke, T.; Hartley, C. J.
Abstract: Precision fermentation leverages the metabolic pathways of microorganisms to produce valuable proteins and enzymes. Pichia hangzhouana, synonymous with Zygoascus hellenicus, is a non-conventional yeast with potential for food biotechnological applications. This study characterizes the CSIRO strain P. hangzhouana FRR5246, isolated from a tea beverage, to evaluate its suitability as a precision fermentation host for a variety of industrial, agricultural and food production applications. P. hangzhouana demonstrated robust growth across a range of carbon sources, with the highest optical density observed in media containing sucrose or sorbitol as sole carbon source. The yeast showed susceptibility to geneticin, hygromycin B, nourseothricin sulfate, and zeocin sulfate antibiotic agents. Successful genetic transformation was achieved, with the expression of a recombinant orange fluorescent protein (OFP) under the control of the native glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase (GAP1) promoter. The secretome exhibited strong antimicrobial activity against Escherichia coli and Staphylococcus aureus, indicating the presence of potent antimicrobial compounds. In addition, whole genome sequencing of P. hangzhouana FRR5246 provided genetic tools for recombinant expression of heterologous genes, insight into the genes, genetic architecture and regulatory mechanisms underlying phenotypic qualities, as well as confirming phylogenetic classification of this strain as clustering with the Dipodascomycetes, most closely related to species Zygoascus hellenicus. P. hangzhouana FRR5246 is a promising candidate for precision fermentation of food ingredients, capable of utilizing diverse carbon sources and producing recombinant proteins. In addition, production of antimicrobial compounds further enhances the potential for biotechnological exploitation. Future work will focus on optimizing growth conditions and exploring native inducible promoters for controlled gene expression.

Title: Caenorhabditis elegans HLH-30/TFEB has age-dependent effects on the transcriptome and is required for normal progeny number and larval survival under basal growth conditions
Authors: Zhong, R.; Wijaya, S. P.; Sinurat, R. A. O.; Her, S. D.; Ying, Q.; Richardson, C. E.
Abstract: Background: The transcription factor TFEB/HLH-30 is a well-established regulator of autophagy and lysosomal biogenesis during starvation and stress, and it plays important roles in development and homeostasis. Our previous work demonstrated that Caenorhabditis elegans HLH-30 also functions under basal physiological conditions in mature neurons, where it promotes the expansion of endo-lysosomal degradative capacity during early adulthood. These findings raised the question of whether HLH-30 promotes lysosomal gene expression more broadly during early adulthood, and, more generally, whether its basal transcriptional functions depend on animal age. To address these questions, we analyzed the impact of hlh-30 loss on the transcriptome at two larval stages, L1 and L4, and two adult ages, Day 3 and Day 6, in hermaphrodites grown under basal conditions. Results: We identified modest effects of hlh-30 loss on the transcriptome that varied by stage/age. Enrichment analyses of genes downregulated in hlh-30 mutants identified functions related to defense response at L1 and in adulthood, and to cuticle development in adulthood. On the other hand, a role for hlh-30 in the basal expression of autophagy genes was exclusively detected in L1 larvae. A subset of genes encoding cathepsins showed decreased expression in the adult hlh-30 mutant; however, our results indicate that HLH-30 is not broadly required for basal expression of most lysosome biogenesis genes in adulthood. We also detected a trend toward reduced expression of genes involved in germline function at the L4 stage, when spermatogenesis occurs, and found that loss of hlh-30 resulted in reduced sperm and progeny numbers. In addition, we found that hlh-30 is required for full progeny survival through larval development. Finally, we identified a gene with increased expression at all four stages in the hlh-30 mutant, the germline transcription factor-encoding ztf-28. Knockdown of ztf-28 partially suppressed the reductions in progeny number and survival, suggesting that its increased expression contributes to these phenotypes. Conclusions: This study reveals roles for HLH-30 in transcriptome regulation under basal growth conditions that vary in both magnitude and content by animal age. Further, it demonstrates a previously unappreciated requirement for HLH-30 in promoting progeny number and survival, broadening our understanding of the physiological roles of this conserved transcription factor.

Title: Mapping Senescence Landscapes in Metabolic Liver Disease Progression
Authors: Schmidt, E. L.; Williams, L.; Peters, S. T.; Salekeen, R.; Calixto Mancipe, N.; Laux, L.; DuFresne-To, M.; Henzler, C.; Ikramuddin, S.; Wang, J.; Meyer, T.; Johnson, S.; Aliferis, C.; Park, B. U.; Adeyi, O.; Kummerfeld, E.; Robbins, P. D.; Niedernhofer, L. J.; Nelson, A. C.
Abstract: Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) affects more than 30% of the population, often progressing from reversible steatosis to irreversible fibrosis and cirrhosis. Although cellular senescence is implicated in driving MASLD, the evidence in human tissue and the mechanism are lacking. Here, we apply spatial transcriptomics and scRNAseq to human liver samples spanning healthy to fibrotic disease to address these knowledge gaps. Using a combination of cell stress, cell cycle arrest, extracellular matrix (ECM) remodeling, and inflammatory genes, senescent microenvironments termed "SenSpots" were identified by Visium transcriptomics that predominantly localized to portal tracts and fibrotic septa across all specimens. Functional profiling revealed a fundamental phenotypic divergence: SenSpots in healthy liver displayed a physiological wound-healing and tissue-development program, whereas SenSpots in fibrotic tissue expressed genes related to inflammation, stress, and ECM-disassembly. Spatial deconvolution and network expansion analyses demonstrated that SenSpots act as epicenters for TGF-{beta}, NOTCH, complement, and ECM-reorganization signaling, which spreads into the surrounding tissue microenvironment as disease advances. Furthermore, scRNAseq data validated the Visium results and identified a previously unappreciated population of senescent Schwann cells in the diseased liver niche. These findings map the spatial origination and paracrine propagation of pathological senescence and identify senotypes associated with liver fibrosis.

Title: CorridorKit: Open-source software for geometric comparison of skull base surgical corridors
Authors: Bachu, A.; Rajesh, R.; Germanwala, A. V.
Abstract: CorridorKit is open-source research software for comparing rigid surgical access corridors in physical image coordinates. Its Python engine represents finite instruments, circular portals, target samples, and protected geometry, and keeps evaluated paths linked to their reached samples, insertion depths, and clearance states through command-line, desktop, and 3D Slicer interfaces. In a reproducible 413-sample phantom, two portals reached 94 and 267 samples, with 326 in their union. Numerical verification included 82 analytical angular comparisons and 4,720 voxel-distance queries. In a public sellar CT example, conditional target coverage rose from 0 to 533 of 536 voxels as the modeled sphenoidotomy opening radius increased from 4 to 8 mm.

Title: The key role of oxidation state and flake size in the ecotoxicological impact of industrial graphene oxide nanoflakes
Authors: Subrati, A.; Bigini, P.; De Luigi, A.; Natale, C.; Mehennaoui, K.; Houin, M.; Chary, A.; Serchi, T.; Venus, T.; Saorin, A.; Monopoli, M. P.; Zhang, X.; Zhao, K.; Alonso, B.; Estrela-Lopis, I.; Gao, C.; Zabeo, A.; Hristozov, D.; Moya, S.; Diomede, L.
Abstract: Graphene oxide (GO) is a widely used nanomaterial across various scientific and technological fields. Environmental exposure to GO and consequent ecotoxicological effects have been largely reported. Despite the significant efforts and illuminating conclusions, establishing fair pairwise correlations between material and toxicity descriptors remains challenging and controversial. Key drawbacks in GO ecotoxicological studies to date include a lack of standardized materials, poorly defined descriptors, and insufficient material variants. Here, we establish the first comprehensive framework to tackle the multidimensional ecotoxicology of GO. We perform thorough material characterization to derive descriptors that precisely define four key GO variants used in industrial scale-up, with differing flake granularity and oxidation extent. These GO variants are evaluated against toxicological endpoint descriptors across two animal models (Daphnia magna and Caenorhabditis elegans) and two plant models (rice and pepper). Our findings underscore the inherently multidimensional nature of GO toxicity by identifying key physicochemical properties associated with it. This study provides an unprecedented platform for parametrizing GO materials using material and toxicity descriptors to contribute to nanomaterial safety.

Title: Rapid enhancement of antibiotic resistance and divergent remodeling of gene expression in single cells of bacteria
Authors: Umetani, M.; Hashimoto, M.; Akiyoshi, S.; Okura, R.; Sakata, N.; Kotani, H.; Kussell, E.; Furusawa, C.; Wakamoto, Y.
Abstract: Exposing bacterial cell populations to antibiotics often results in the emergence of descendants with enhanced resistance. Phenotypic heterogeneity and global physiological responses are thought to contribute to resistance evolution. However, identifying the specific stages of drug exposure where phenotypic heterogeneity and physiological responses play critical roles remains elusive. Using long-term single-cell lineage tracking of an Escherichia coli resistance model, here we reveal that resistance-enhanced cells emerge rapidly within a few generations in a clonal bacterial cell population under chloramphenicol (Cp) exposure and stably transmit the enhanced resistance for hundreds of generations in the presence of Cp. High expression of a resistance protein was advantageous during the initial period of drug exposure, but conferred only a marginal fitness advantage during the period of resistance enhancement. Transcriptomic profiles of resistance-enhanced cell populations were lineage-specific, suggesting that multiple gene expression states can support enhanced resistance. Altogether, these results suggest that an interplay between initial phenotypic heterogeneity and divergent remodeling of gene expression drives the rapid acquisition of enhanced antibiotic resistance.

Title: A Novel Autoantibody against LAG-3 in Systemic Lupus Erythematosus
Authors: Muramoto, Y.; Shiokawa, M.; Maeda, Y.; Kuwada, T.; Nishikawa, Y.; Tsuruyama, T.; Maruno, T.; Yanaidani, T.; Sawada, K.; Hirata, A.; Chikugo, K.; Yokode, M.; Matsumoto, S.; Ota, S.; Matsumori, T.; Izawa, K.; Hiejima, E.; Akamine, K.; Mizuta, M.; Yoshida, H.; Fujita, M.; Nakashima, R.; Yoshifuji, H.; Chiba, T.; Takita, J.; Morinobu, A.; Seno, H.
Abstract: Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) is an autoimmune disease characterized by immune tolerance loss, although its pathogenesis remains incompletely understood. Immune checkpoint molecules maintain peripheral tolerance, and their dysregulation contributes to autoimmunity. Autoantibodies against lymphocyte activation gene-3 (LAG-3), an immune checkpoint molecule, were identified in a subset of patients with SLE. We enrolled 130 patients with SLE, 119 patients with other autoimmune diseases, and 32 healthy controls. The sera of patients with SLE were screened for antibodies against various immune checkpoint molecules to identify clinically relevant disease-specific autoantibodies against LAG-3. Functional assays were performed to assess the effect of anti-LAG-3 autoantibodies on the interaction between LAG-3 and major histocompatibility complex (MHC) class II. Pathogenic relevance was evaluated using genetic deletion and immunization-based mouse models. Anti-LAG-3 autoantibodies were detected in 52/130 patients with SLE (40.0%) but only 4 of 119 patients with other autoimmune diseases (3.4%). These autoantibodies were associated with lupus nephritis and higher disease activity. In mice, Lag3 deletion or human LAG-3 immunization induced lupus-like autoimmunity. These findings support the clinical relevance of anti-LAG-3 autoantibodies in SLE and implicate LAG-3 checkpoint disruption in lupus-like autoimmunity.

Title: Litter Microbiome Composition in Commercial Broiler Houses Under Contrasting Management: A Pilot Study
Authors: Olson, E. G.; Gajurel, G.; Ricke, S. C.; Hale, B.
Abstract: Litter management affects broiler health, performance, and environmental impact, yet the effects of litter-applied amendments on the resident microbiome remain poorly characterized, particularly under commercial conditions. This pilot study evaluated the litter microbiome of three commercial broiler houses under contrasting management regimens. Two houses received a postbiotic litter amendment combined with sodium bisulfate (NaHSO) at 40% of the standard rate for one or two consecutive flocks, while a control house received the standard NaHSO rate alone. Composite litter samples were collected following flock removal, and the V4 region of the 16S rRNA gene was sequenced to characterize prokaryotic community structure, diversity, and composition. Within-sample () diversity did not differ among houses (ANOVA, p > 0.05), whereas {beta} diversity differed across Bray-Curtis, Jaccard, and weighted and unweighted UniFrac distances (PERMANOVA, p < 0.05). Pairwise comparisons detected no differences between the two amended houses, whereas each differed from the control across all distance metrics except weighted UniFrac for the house amended during a single flock (PERMANOVA, q < 0.05 for significant comparisons). Core microbiome and differential abundance analyses identified consistent compositional shifts, including greater representation of Bifidobacterium and lower relative abundance of Staphylococcus in both amended houses. Each management regimen was represented by a single house, so these observations should be interpreted as house-level associations rather than definitive treatment effects. Nevertheless, the consistency of microbiome responses between amended houses suggests that the defined alternative management regimen may influence resident microbial community composition in a manner relevant to litter conditioning, warranting further evaluation in replicated factorial designs.

Title: Deletion of Furin Facilitates Efficient and Versatile Coronavirus Pseudotyped Particle Generation
Authors: Wang, P.; He, Y.; Wu, L.; Wilson, S. J.; Rihn, S. J.
Abstract: Coronaviruses bring threats to both humans and animals. To initiate successful infections, coronaviruses must first navigate entry into a host cell. Coronavirus spike-bearing pseudotyped particle systems are indispensable tools for studying coronavirus entry and evaluating neutralizing antibodies and entry inhibitors. However, pseudotyped particle titers can be low when packaged particles bear coronavirus spikes that contain the furin cleavage site, and this has been a limitation for pseudotyped particle production and applications. Here, we demonstrate that CRISPR/Cas9-mediated knockout of furin protease in HEK293T cells significantly enhances the production of functional pseudotyped particles bearing spikes containing the furin cleavage site, including those from SARS-CoV-2, MERS-CoV, and MHV-JHM. Moreover, deletion of endogenous furin in producer cells yields an effect equivalent to deletion of the furin cleavage site, but with broader application across different spike proteins, and without virus manipulation. This work establishes a simple and effective platform to improve coronavirus pseudotyped particle systems by eliminating furin-mediated pre-activation, enabling more efficient and reliable production for downstream applications.

Title: Genomic Characterization of a Typical Enteropathogenic Escherichia coli Isolate from an Egyptian Fruit Bat, Rousettus aegyptiacus from Coastal Kenya
Authors: Kamau, J.; Kimemia, B. B.; Abuom, D.; Agwanda, B.; Musila, L.; Odoyo, E.; Kivata, M. W.; Mbae, C.; Onguso, J.; Haynes, R.; Kellar, G.; Lutomiah, J.; Eads, J.; Eyase, F.
Abstract: Enteropathogenic Escherichia coli (EPEC) are responsible for significant morbidity and mortality cases among young children under the age of five, particularly in low- and middle-income countries. Atypical EPEC has frequently been reported from animal hosts, however, information on the occurrence and genomic characteristics of typical EPEC in wildlife reservoirs remains limited. This study characterized an Escherichia coli isolated from an Egyptian fruit bat (Rousettus aegyptiacus) sampled in coastal Kenya using whole-genome sequencing. Oral and rectal swabs were collected from 24 bats captured in Kikambala, Kilifi County, Kenya. Bacterial isolates were cultured, sequenced on the Illumina NextSeq 1000 platform, and analyzed using a bioinformatics workflow that included in silico taxonomic classification, serotyping and multilocus sequence typing, virulence gene profiling, antimicrobial resistance gene detection, plasmid identification, and core genome phylogenetic analysis. One isolate, KIKB-471-SWR-A (O128:H6; ST15625), was classified as typical EPEC. Genomic analysis confirmed the characteristic virulence architecture of typical EPEC. Despite numerous antimicrobial resistance-associated genes being detected, the isolate remained phenotypically susceptible to all antimicrobials tested. The isolate clustered within an EPEC lineage, closely associated with a human-derived EPEC strain, and genetically distinct from both commensal and laboratory E. coli reference strains. Despite no evidence of zoonotic transmission, the findings demonstrated that wildlife can harbor E. coli lineages possessing virulence determinants associated with human pathogenic EPEC strains, underscoring the importance of genomic surveillance at wildlife?human interfaces within a One Health framework to improve the understanding of ecology, evolution, and public health significance of diarrheagenic E. coli.

Title: Environmental heterogeneity and microbial community architecture shape N2O fluxes in intertidal coastal sediments
Authors: Dolivet-Marechal, M.; Palacin-Lizarbe, C.; Schwob, G.; Siljanen, H. M. P.; paul, D.; Delort, A.; Gervaix, J.; Creuze des Chatelliers, C.; Schmidt, S.; Cognat, M.; Sebag, D.; Taugourdeau, O.; Schubert, C.; Labourdette, N.; Bertrand, I.; Rossi, L. M. W.; Le Roux, X.; Richaume, A.; Florio, A.
Abstract: Seagrass meadows are key ''blue carbon ecosystems'', yet their contribution to nitrous oxide (N2O) emissions remains poorly constrained. We investigated environmental and microbial descriptors of N2O fluxes in intertidal sediments of Arcachon Bay, home to Europe's largest Zostera noltii meadow. At six sites, we measured in situ N2O fluxes in adjacent bare and vegetated sediments and characterized sediment properties, N2O-cycling genes using qPCR and targeted metagenomics, and microbial co-occurrence networks. Fluxes ranged from -3.7 to 8.4 mol N2O m-2 d-1. Spatial location was the strongest descriptor of flux variation, with inner-bay sites showing higher emissions associated with environmental conditions, carbon accumulation, pH, and microbial community characteristics. Vegetation effects were comparatively small and site-dependent. Metagenomic descriptors of N2O-cycling genes were more informative than qPCR-based descriptors. Taxa associated with nirS (Thiohalophilus), nirK (Planktotalea) and nosZ1 (Roseobacter) were identified as potential contributors to N2O production or reduction, respectively. These findings indicate that spatially structured environmental conditions and microbial community characteristics better describe N2O flux variation than seagrass presence alone. Measurements across tidal and seasonal cycles are needed to establish the temporal consistency of these patterns.

Title: Multi-Cohort Blood Transcriptomic Meta-Analysis of Active Pulmonary Tuberculosis: Reproducibility of a 50-Gene Interferon Signature and Benchmarking of a 4-Gene Classifier
Authors: Hassan, U.; Tahir, F.; Bibi, A.; Jamal, W.; Kanwal, T.
Abstract: Background: Most blood transcriptomic signatures for tuberculosis (TB) come from a single population or a single platform. Few have been built by meta-analysis and benchmarked against published signatures. Methods: We meta-analysed three UK blood transcriptomic datasets (two Illumina microarray, one RNA-seq; 247 samples: 87 active pulmonary TB (PTB), 160 healthy controls (HC)). GSE107991 reanalyses the Berry test set, and two discovery datasets overlap Sweeney's discovery data, so the datasets are not fully independent. Genes were retained if they replicated in all three studies (FDR < 0.05, same direction) and passed random-effects meta-analysis (|logFC| > 1.5, FDR < 0.01). Performance was estimated in GSE28623 (The Gambia, n = 83) and GSE56153 (Indonesia, n = 36); direction was checked in GSE34608 (Germany, n = 26) and GSE81746 (India, n = 6). A LASSO and random-forest classifier was compared with the Berry 393-gene and Sweeney 3-gene signatures. Immune composition was assessed with MCPcounter and CIBERSORTx. Results: We identified a 50-gene core signature dominated by interferon-stimulated genes. All 50 were upregulated and reached FDR < 0.05 in every dataset. ssGSEA gave an AUC of 0.830 (95% CI 0.743-0.917) in GSE28623 and 0.941 (0.868-1.000) in GSE56153. Direction agreement was 95.7% in Germany and 95.8% in India. PTB versus latent TB infection gave 0.848 (0.756-0.940). LASSO selected four genes (BATF2, ANKRD22, GBP5 and EPSTI1). The frozen classifier gave an external AUC of 0.864 (0.785-0.944). The Sweeney 3-gene score, re-tested in one of its validation cohorts, reached 0.912 and exceeded the 50-gene score (47/50 genes; Holm p = 0.0234). Berry 393-gene scoring gave 0.910 with directions reconstructed from GSE19439 (Holm p = 0.0071 versus the 50-gene score). The signed score is a reconstruction, not Berry's published score. MCPcounter showed myeloid expansion and lymphoid suppression; CIBERSORTx recovered the former but not the broader lymphoid suppression. Conclusions: The 50-gene signature was consistent across three overlapping UK discovery datasets. External evaluation was partial, comprising AUCs for 47 of the 50 genes in two cohorts and direction concordance in two smaller cohorts. This is a benchmarking study, not a claim of superiority: the Sweeney 3-gene and signed Berry scores were higher, and the 4-gene classifier did not differ significantly from Sweeney. The classifier warrants prospective validation. The Berry and Sweeney comparisons are not independent.

Title: Electron Transport Chain-inhibiting fungicides increase resistance to widely used azole antifungals
Authors: Pociunaite, S. M.; White, S. A.; Tong, P.; Yeboah, R.; Pidoux, A. L.; Allshire, R.
Abstract: Rising antifungal resistance in human and crop fungal pathogens poses significant challenges. Azole-based antifungals that inhibit ergosterol biosynthesis are a key first-line treatment for human fungal infections. Importantly, azole-based ergosterol-inhibiting fungicides are also widely used in agriculture alongside electron transport chain (ETC) Complex III inhibiting compounds. However, it is unknown whether the combined use of these distinct fungicides is entirely synergistic. We find that exposure of fission yeast, Schizosaccharomyces pombe to ETC-Complex III inhibitors, prior to or simultaneously with azoles, attenuates azole efficacy by inducing mitochondrial dysfunction. Our analyses show that reactive oxygen species (ROS) accumulation as a result of ETC inhibition activates oxidative stress response pathways thereby decreasing azole potency. Related responses in pathogenic fungi indicate that the use of ETC inhibiting fungicides in agriculture may inadvertently promote azole resistance. We conclude that the use of specific fungicide combinations should be re-evaluated in order to preserve both their clinical and agricultural effectiveness.

Title: Emergence of mobile fosA3-blaCTX-M-65 with mcr-1.1 and tet(X4) on conjugative plasmids in avian pathogenic Escherichia coli from industrial poultry in Pakistan
Authors: Umair, M.; Fatima, F.; Mathias, J.; Iannetelli, T.; Mohsin, M.; Farlow, A.; Walsh, T. R.
Abstract: The emergence of plasmid-mediated resistance to critically important antimicrobials poses a growing threat to global health. Here we report the first genomic evidence of plasmid-mediated fosA3 and blaCTX-M-65 coexisting with mcr-1.1 and tet(X4) in multidrug-resistant Escherichia coli from clinically healthy broiler chickens in Pakistan. Among 1,677 high-quality genomes collected through antimicrobial resistance surveillance in Punjab, Pakistan, three isolates recovered between 2022 and 2024 harboured all four resistance determinants. Hybrid genome assemblies showed that fosA3 and blaCTX-M-65 were co-located on IncHI2A plasmids, whereas mcr-1.1 and tet(X4) were carried on separate IncI2 and IncFIA/IncFIC plasmids, all predicted to be conjugative; in one isolate the tet(X4) contig did not circularise. The isolates belonged to sequence type 93 and exhibited resistance to fosfomycin, colistin, tigecycline and cefotaxime. Comparative genomic analysis revealed highly conserved IncHI2A plasmid backbones, with an additional integron-associated resistance region in the 2024 isolates, suggesting acquisition of accessory resistance determinants. Resistance to three last-line antimicrobial classes and a canonical virulence profile now coexist on conjugative plasmids in poultry E. coli, a combination that favours co-selection and argues for plasmid-resolved surveillance in poultry production.

Title: TrES-seq integrates single-cell RNA and nanobody-based histone mark profiles to decode epigenetic and transcriptional axes of cell identity
Authors: Polavarapu, V. K.; Annan, A.; Srivastava, D.; Katanayeva, N.; Epiney, J.; Santamaria-Martinez, A.; Lambercy, K.; Ciriello, G.; Oricchio, E.
Abstract: Histone post-translational modifications and gene expression jointly shape cellular identity and activity. However, systematically assessing their heterogeneity and functional interdependence requires high-quality multimodal single-cell readouts, whose generation still faces significant technological challenges.
