Here, we developed TrES-seq (transcriptional and epigenetic state sequencing), a method that integrates scRNA-seq with species-specific nanobody Tn5 fusion proteins to jointly profile RNA and two histone modifications in the same cells and across multiple samples. In human tonsils, single-cell H3K27ac, H3K27me3, H3K9me3, and RNA data in >25,000 cells revealed a one-to-many relationship where heterogeneous transcriptional states shared similar epigenetic profiles. For example, naive and memory B cells were transcriptionally different but epigenetically indistinguishable, while the epigenetic status of enhancers but not promoters separated germinal center from naive and memory B cells. Moreover, naturally occurring and treatment-induced cell state transitions revealed broad transcriptional changes occurring among genes that already exhibited and retained an epigenetically active state. Overall, TrES-seq provides a robust and cost-effective platform to determine how epigenetic states influence transcriptional heterogeneity, shaping cell phenotypes and function in different physiological and pathological contexts.

Title: ADP-ribosylation governs the repair of topoisomerase IIIβ-induced nucleic acid damage
Authors: Saha, S.; Maidens, T.; Cai, V.; Su, Y.; Chen, J.; Lee, N. C.; Maity, T. K.; Jenkins, L. M.; Zhu, L.; Wu, B.; Zhao, W.; Wilson, G. M.; Pommier, Y.; Sun, Y.
Abstract: Abortive DNA and RNA-linked covalent cleavage complexes formed by the unique dual-activity human topoisomerase III{beta} (TOP3B) disrupt nucleic acid metabolism and can promote cancer cell death. Here, we identify poly(ADP-ribosylation) (PARylation) as a key pathway that regulates the repair and stability of both DNA- and RNA-linked TOP3B cleavage complexes (TOP3Bccs). We show that accumulated TOP3Bccs undergo rapid PARylation in a PARP1-dependent manner and that this modification is dynamically reversed by poly(ADP-ribose) glycohydrolase (PARG). Mass spectrometry identified major ADP-ribosylation sites on TOP3B, and disruption of these sites impaired TOP3Bcc homeostasis. Mechanistically, PARylation recruits flap endonuclease 1 (FEN1) to excise and repair TOP3Bccs. Persistent PARylation caused by PARG inhibition recruits the deubiquitylating enzyme (DUB) USP10 to promote TOP3Bcc deubiquitylation and thereby stabilize TOP3Bccs, presumably by preventing proteasomal degradation. Together, this study identifies a dynamic PARylation-mediated pathway that coordinates the repair of abortive TOP3Bccs. This pathway defines a critical mechanism of TOP3Bcc homeostasis and may influence cancer cell responses to TOP3B-targeting agents.

Title: Biotin-operated ligand trapping enables dynamic spatial redistribution of proteins and organelles in living cells
Authors: Beyers, W. C.; Plutkis, S. E.; Rutcher, K. R.; Grimm, J. B.; Nicolini, C.; Sun, J. L.; Haas, M. R.; Hutton, M. S.; Kim, H. K.; Chavez, A.; Pruett-Miller, S. M.; Vevea, J. D.; Lavis, L.; Chang, C.-L.
Abstract: Controlling protein localization through chemical biology tools is essential for mechanistic interrogations, functional perturbations, and therapeutic development. While existing tools cover a wide range of applications, no single approach simultaneously enables inducible trapping, controlled release, and visualization of a protein of interest (POI). To address this gap, we developed Biotin-Operated Ligand Trapping (BOLT), which combines a HaloTag-fused POI with a streptavidin trap. Desthiobiotin-conjugated Janelia Fluor HaloTag ligands (HTLs) enable POI visualization, trapping, and biotin-operated release. We demonstrate BOLT's capacity in synchronized secretory cargo release, microtubule-directed organelle movement and hitchhiking, and ectopically localizing nuclear transcription factors. Importantly, pulse-chase BOLT further reveals bidirectional endoplasmic reticulum-Golgi trafficking of an endogenous Golgi enzyme and distinguishes recycled from newly synthesized enzyme populations using distinct HTLs. Altogether, BOLT provides an all-in-one platform to interrogate how subcellular localization regulates protein and organelle function.

Title: Deep learning design and in vivo validation of Müller glia-specific cis-regulatory elements
Authors: Fornes, O.; Koh, K. D.; Marton, R. M.; Chen, J.; De Donno, C.; Marroquin, K. A.; Kang, G. J.; Lal, A.; Müller, S.; Eraslan, G.; Shamir, E. R.; Thakore, P. I.; Jasper, H.; Garfield, D.
Abstract: Effective recombinant adeno-associated virus gene therapies require promoters that are compact and cell-type-specific. Ideally, promoters should also exhibit functional conservation when tested in model organisms to ensure that preclinical findings translate reliably to human patients. Here, we introduce a deep learning framework for designing cis-regulatory elements (CREs) meeting these criteria, applied to retinal Muller glia (MG). Using single-cell chromatin accessibility data from human and mouse retinas, we trained species-specific models to predict cell-type accessibility, and designed compact CREs using two complementary strategies. In silico validation predicted that the designed CREs exhibit high MG-specific accessibility (on-target) in both species with minimal off-target accessibility across hundreds of human cell types and tissues. Mechanistic analysis revealed that the predicted MG accessibility is driven by the creation of LHX2 motifs. In vivo validation confirmed that the designed CREs successfully restrict reporter expression to MG in the murine retina. Our deep learning framework is highly generalizable and enables the rapid design of compact, on-target, and species-conserved CREs for precision gene therapy.

Title: Identification of seven candidate structured noncoding RNA motifs in protists by comparative genomics
Authors: zhang, y.; liang, q.; wang, t.; Huang, Y.; duan, A.; wang, j.; wang, w.; yu, h.; chen, b.; ying, z.; jia, y.; fu, c.; Li, S.
Abstract: Protists represent a highly diverse assemblage of predominantly unicellular eukaryotes, including protozoa, algae, and slime molds. Their essential roles in global ecosystems, along with their significance as human parasites, underscore the need for a deeper understanding of their conserved genetic elements. In this study, we employed an integrated computational approach combining CMfinder and R-scape to systematically identify and evaluate structured non-coding RNA (ncRNA) motifs across protist genomes. Through rigorous assessment and functional annotation, we report seven conserved structured ncRNAs that are likely functional RNA motifs involved in regulating the synthesis of the carbon fixation protein ribulose-1,5-bisphosphate carboxylase/oxygenase (RuBisCO), the light-harvesting and transfer protein phycocyanin, subunits of photosystems I and II, as well as mRNA splicing regulation. Notably, we also identified a structured ncRNA motif that may possess a dual function, capable of bidirectionally regulating the photosystem genes psaI and psbJ simultaneously. Our findings provide valuable insights into the diversity and functional significance of structured ncRNAs in microbial eukaryotes.

Title: Organ context dominates cell identity across a multi-organ single-cell atlas of grapevine
Authors: Bonarota, M. S.; Figueroa-Balderas, R.; Cochetel, N.; Cantu, D.
Abstract: How transcriptional programs defining cell identity are maintained or remodeled across organ contexts remains a fundamental question in plant biology, particularly in long-lived perennials. We generated a multi-organ single-nucleus transcriptomic atlas of the dwarf grapevine cultivar Pixie, comprising over 220,000 nuclei from nine organs across vegetative and reproductive development, each sampled in two biological replicates. We annotated 46 distinct cell types and anatomical structures, reconstructed developmental trajectories within selected cell types, and inferred gene regulatory networks at cell-type resolution. Organ identity accounted for 65% of regulon activity variance across the atlas compared to only 17% for cell type, demonstrating that organ context is the dominant driver of transcriptional variation in most shared cell types. Broadly distributed cell types including epidermis and xylem parenchyma underwent extensive organ-specific reprogramming, while companion cells maintained organ-independent regulatory programs across all nine organs, representing the stable end of a continuum of transcriptional plasticity. This finding suggests that companion cell identity is buffered against organ context, consistent with their invariant role in phloem loading. This atlas establishes a reference framework for dissecting gene regulatory network organization across organs in a perennial crop and provides a resource for cell-type-resolved functional genomics in grapevine and other woody perennials.

Title: PAV-spotter: using signal cross-correlations to identify Presence/Absence Variation in target capture data
Authors: de Visser, M. C.; Ploeg, C. v. d.; Cvijanovic, M.; Vucic, T.; Theodoropoulos, A.; Wielstra, B.
Abstract: High throughput sequencing technologies have become essential in the fields of evolutionary biology and genomics. When dealing with non-model organisms or genomic gigantism, sequencing whole genomes is still relatively costly and therefore reduced-genome representations are frequently obtained, for instance by target capture approaches. While computational tools exist that can handle target capture data and identify small-scale variants such as single nucleotide polymorphisms and micro-indels, options to identify large scale structural variants are limited. To meet this need, we introduce PAV-spotter: a tool that can identify presence/absence variation (PAV) in target capture data. PAV-spotter conducts a signal cross-correlation calculation, in which the distribution of read counts per target between samples of different a priori defined classes - e.g. male versus female, or diseased versus healthy - are compared. We test, validate and apply our methodology by studying Triturus newts: salamanders with gigantic genomes that currently lack an annotated reference genome. Triturus newts suffer from a hereditary disease that kills half their offspring during embryogenesis. We compare the target capture data of two different types of diseased embryos, characterized by unique deletions, with those of healthy embryos. Our reciprocal, self-validating findings show that PAV-spotter helps to expose such structural variants, even in the face of medium to low sequencing coverage levels, low sample sizes, and background noise due to mis-mapped reads. PAV-spotter can be used to study the structural variation underlying supergene systems in the absence of whole genome assemblies. The code, including further explanation, is available through the PAV-spotter GitHub repository.

Title: Smyd1 regulates H3K4me3 to support adaptive fatty acid oxidation in the adult heart during lipid overload
Authors: Mukai, R.; Oka, S.; Sung, E.-A.; Takayama, K.; Ikeda, S.; Matsushita, M.; Takada, T.; Sadoshima, J.
Abstract: Obesity and metabolic syndrome are major risk factors for heart failure, and impaired fatty acid oxidation (FAO) is a key contributor to metabolic dysfunction in obesity-related cardiomyopathy. However, how the heart maintains FAO and adapts to chronic lipid overload remains poorly understood. Here, we identify SET and MYND domain-containing protein 1 (Smyd1), a muscle-specific histone methyltransferase, as an early compensatory regulator of cardiac metabolism in response to lipid overload. In wild-type mouse hearts, high-fat diet (HFD) feeding induced transient increases in Smyd1 expression and H3K4me3 levels during the early-to-mid phase of metabolic stress, both of which returned to baseline levels during prolonged HFD exposure. Single-cell RNA sequencing further revealed that this adaptive increase in Smyd1 expression occurred predominantly in cardiomyocytes. In contrast, cardiac-specific Smyd1 heterozygous knockout mice exhibited accelerated cardiac dysfunction, left ventricular dilation, increased myocardial fibrosis, and reduced survival following HFD feeding. Mechanistically, Smyd1 deficiency impaired the adaptive upregulation of key FAO-related genes and reduced cardiac FAO activity. Furthermore, co-immunoprecipitation analysis revealed an interaction between Smyd1 and peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor alpha (PPAR), suggesting a potential mechanism by which Smyd1 supports FAO gene expression. Taken together, these findings identify Smyd1 as an early compensatory regulator that supports FAO-dependent metabolic adaptation and protects the heart against lipid overload-induced cardiac dysfunction. This adaptive mechanism, involving H3K4me3 regulation and the Smyd1-PPAR interaction, may provide potential therapeutic targets for therapeutic strategies aimed at preserving cardiac metabolic flexibility in obesity-related cardiomyopathy.

Title: Single-molecule in situ detection and quantification of mitochondrial DNA heteroplasmy
Authors: Gottardo, S.; Chowdhury, S. R.; Wilson, B. A.; Chandrasegaram, R.; Prudent, J.; van den Ameele, J.
Abstract: The mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) is a multi-copy genome present in most eukaryotic cells and essential for life. The presence of different mtDNA variants within a cell, or heteroplasmy, may cause pathology when the level of deleterious variants exceeds a critical threshold. However, the mechanisms that control heteroplasmy levels remain poorly understood, in part due to a lack of technologies to visualise mtDNA heteroplasmy in situ and correlate it with intracellular processes. mtDNA single-molecule fluorescence in situ hybridisation (mtDNA-smFISH) allows in situ visualisation of mtDNA molecules and sequence-specific detection of heteroplasmic variants. Here, we provide protocols for sequence-specific detection of mtDNA, large-scale single mtDNA deletions and species-specific haplotypes, in fixed human and Drosophila cells and in whole-mount Drosophila tissues. Combining mtDNA-smFISH with immunohistochemistry using biotin-labelled primary antibodies that resist heat-based denaturation, allows concomitant detection of intracellular proteins. We further describe two image-analysis pipelines, one for 3D quantification and one open-source for 2D quantification of mtDNA deletions in Drosophila tissues and cell culture. This enables estimation of single-cell heteroplasmy levels, observation of cell-to-cell variability, and detection of mtDNA variants at a subcellular level, making mtDNA-smFISH a powerful tool to study the intracellular processes regulating heteroplasmy and mtDNA quality control.

Title: Read&Tag enables antibody-independent combinatorial and multifactorial chromatin profiling
Authors: Schneider, M.; Kopp, L. C.; Schwarzlose, C.; Bohara, N. R.; Bollachettira, C.; Campos Sparr, A.; Huschet, L. A.; Robles, M. S.; Villasenor, R.
Abstract: Genome-wide chromatin profiling methods based on in situ tagmentation have expanded access to epigenomic information but generally rely on antibodies, thereby limiting their multifactorial capacity and the direct measurement of combinatorial chromatin states. Here, we introduce Read&Tag, in which engineered chromatin reader domains or intrabodies are fused directly to the Tn5 transposase to target specific chromatin features in situ. Read&Tag profiles active and repressive histone modifications, DNA methylation, and elongating RNA polymerase II, with signal amplitude increasing with target abundance and remaining robust in frozen tissue and low-input samples. Because the targeting module is a protein of defined structure and affinity, two specificities can be combined within a single complex. Tagmentation by such a dual-specificity reader requires H3K4me3 and H3K27me3 to be present together in the same chromatin fragment. The co-occurrence of both marks thus becomes a precondition of the measurement rather than an inference drawn from independently measured profiles. Combining barcoded reader-Tn5 complexes with primer-timed signal augmentation enables the measurement of four chromatin features in a single reaction. Read&Tag therefore provides a modular, antibody-independent platform for combinatorial and multifactorial profiling.

Title: Variation of anti-oomycete activity in Pseudomonas spp.: phenotypic characterization and comparative genomics
Authors: Saric, E.; Miljanovic, A.; Struski, P.; Oberhaensli, S.; Jerjen, L.; Zucko, J.; Schmidt-Posthaus, H.; Pavic, D.; Maguire, I.; Hermanns, J.; Weisskopf, L.; Pretto, T.; Bielen, A.
Abstract: Pathogenic aquatic oomycetes Aphanomyces astaci and Saprolegnia parasitica represent a major threat to biodiversity and aquaculture production, but their interactions with host-associated microbes remain poorly understood. From a collection of bacterial isolates (n = 328) obtained from fish and crayfish hosts, we focused on Pseudomonas spp. (n = 66) and confirmed their previously reported strong inhibitory potential against A. astaci and S. parasitica. However, our results also revealed substantial inter- and intra-species variation in antagonism. To capture this variation, we selected eight isolates belonging to different P. fluorescens, P. putida, and P. syringae species groups and displaying contrasting levels of anti-oomycete activity for further phenotypic assays and comparative genomic analysis. Across these isolates, mycelial inhibition was markedly stronger against A. astaci than against S. parasitica, indicating species-specific differences in susceptibility. Comparative genomic analysis revealed substantial variation in biosynthetic gene cluster (BGC) repertoires among the analysed strains. Strongly inhibitory isolates carried candidate BGCs with similarity to characterised bioactive pathways, including pyoluteorin, rhizoxin, pyrrolnitrin, DAPG, and orfamide, alongside with multiple uncharacterised clusters that were either shared among inhibitory isolates or restricted to individual strains. All analysed genomes also contained clusters related to siderophore and HCN biosynthesis. However, in vitro assays showed that siderophore production was not clearly associated with inhibitory activity and that total inhibition was considerably higher than volatile-only inhibition, suggesting a substantial contribution of non-volatile, presumably diffusible, compounds. Altogether, our results suggest that Pseudomonas anti-oomycete activity is species- and strain-dependent and likely reflects different combinations of multiple metabolites, likely including diffusible compounds, rather than a single conserved mechanism. In conclusion, this study provides a foundation for future work aimed at resolving mechanisms underlying microbial antagonism toward aquatic oomycete pathogens.

Title: LRCP: identifying functionally related SNPs and genes from phenome-wide genetic-effect correlations using GWAS summary statistics
Authors: Chen, L. G.; Thach, T. Q.; Sham, P. C.
Abstract: Genetic correlation describes which traits share genetic causes. The transposed question, which variants act alike across the phenome, has no comparable estimator, although it points directly to shared genes, pathways and regulators. Correlations of GWAS Z scores between variants across many traits are easy to compute, but they are confounded by linkage disequilibrium (LD) and, for any pair of variants, by sample overlap and genetic correlation among the GWAS. We show that in 452 Pan-UK Biobank GWAS the effective number of independent traits is only 58, and that naive tests reject 51-70% of null pairs of distal variants. We introduce LRCP (likelihood and regression on cross-products of Z scores), which estimates the phenome-wide genetic-effect correlation{rho} between SNPs by regressing Z-score cross-products on LD cross components, using per-SNP heritability enrichment from the companion method LRCQ and LDSC-derived plug-ins. For variants in different LD blocks the estimator has a closed form, and its standard errors account exactly for the dependence among GWAS. In simulations LRCP is unbiased (absolute bias at most 0.03), its 95% intervals cover 93-98%, and its type-I error is 5.0-5.7%, whereas naive correlations are attenuated by 41-64% and reject up to 51% of null pairs. In Pan-UK Biobank, LRCP recovers the expected signs among PCSK9, LDLR and APOB variants and estimates{rho} = 0.90 between the TP53 polyadenylation variant rs78378222 and MDM2 rs3730556, whose Z scores correlate at r = 0.67 across traits (conditional bootstrap P = 0.015), although this correlation lies along a shared body-size and red-cell trait axis. Single variant pairs are near the resolution of current biobanks, with precision limited by the number of genetically distinct traits. Genome-wide, among 1,799 strongly enriched LD clumps (1.61 million distal pairs), a conditional test finds 437 pairs at FDR 5%, where naive correlation flags 1.1 million. Simulating the whole screen under the null shows that this test is conservative and that the 386 strongest links (P < 10-5) lie beyond every one of 322 million simulated null statistics. Linked genes share GO biological processes 1.9 times more often than random pairs of enriched loci. The links form 14 modules that match known biology, among them platelet and red-cell production, lipoprotein metabolism (PCSK9, LDLR, APOB, CETP, LPL), myeloid differentiation (IRF8, ITGA4), bone density (WNT16), pigmentation (HERC2, SLC45A2), alkaline phosphatase (ALPL, GPLD1) and IL-6 signalling (IL6R, CRP). Most modules act within one trait domain, where LRCP shows shared trait profiles rather than a tested shared mechanism. Once LD and the dependence among GWAS are modelled, phenome-wide summary statistics can identify functionally related variants and genes.

Title: LRCQ: phenome-wide heritability enrichment of genomic loci from GWAS summary statistics
Authors: Chen, L. G.; Thach, T. Q.; Sham, P. C.
Abstract: Some genetic variants are associated with many traits, but a variant's GWAS statistics are also inflated by the effects of variants in LD with it and by confounding shared by all variants in a study. Existing measures of per-variant pleiotropy, such as counts of significant associations or multi-trait association tests, do not separate these sources. Stratified LD score regression separates them for one trait at a time and only through predefined annotations. We present LRCQ (LD score regression on {chi}2 across many GWAS), which estimates for each locus its phenome-wide heritability enrichment: the variance of its causal effects across a set of traits, relative to an average locus. LRCQ regresses squared Z-scores from 30 or more GWAS jointly on squared LD, with per-trait LDSC intercepts and heritabilities fitted in earlier stages. Its pooled least-squares solution has a closed form whose cost does not grow with the number of traits. Its standard errors account for sample overlap and genetic correlation between GWAS. Squared Z-scores identify enrichment at the resolution of LD clumps, not single SNPs, so LRCQ reports clump-level estimates ("omni-loci"). These estimates can be aggregated over any functional annotation or gene set chosen after the analysis. In simulations with real UK Biobank LD and 30 to 1,000 traits, LRCQ was unbiased for its clump-level estimand. When GWAS share samples its test statistics are strongly right-skewed: normal-reference p-values were up to 10-fold anti-conservative at P < 0.001. P-values matched to the exact third cumulant restored type-I error and FDR control, and matching the fourth cumulant as well kept the far tail within 1.6-fold of nominal down to P = 10-4. Score-type tests, which evaluate the variance under the null hypothesis, kept power at the most enriched loci. Model-based standard errors were calibrated once the enrichment estimates plugged into them kept the polygenic background. It ranked enriched loci better than mean {chi}2, LD-normalised {chi}2, multi-trait omnibus tests and significant-association counts in 13 of 16 scenarios. Its main vulnerability was a misspecified LDSC intercept. Applied to 444 Pan-UK Biobank European-ancestry GWAS, LRCQ found strongly non-uniform phenome-wide enrichment: the SD of true clump-mean enrichment was 8.3, against a genome mean of 1. At a tag-level FDR of 5%, 881 LD clumps were enriched above the uniform expectation; they fall in 638 distinct loci, including FTO, AXIN2, HBS1L-MYB, CST3, CELSR2-SORT1, PCSK9 and MC4R. These ranked only moderately with mean {chi}2 and poorly with counts of significant associations. Gene-level phenome-wide enrichment rose with loss-of-function constraint. Phenome-wide heritability was 3-5-fold enriched in coding, conserved, 5' UTR and promoter sequence, and depleted in repressed chromatin. LRCQ turns hundreds of biobank GWAS into an LD-corrected map of where phenome-wide genetic variance lies, and complements its companion method LRCP, which estimates genetic-effect correlations between loci.

Title: Decoding the molecular cues regulating the transition of Influenza virus polymerase from transcriptase to replicase.
Authors: De, A.; Roy, A.; Mondal, A.
Abstract: Influenza virus polymerase (FluPol) dynamically transitions between distinct conformational states to coordinate viral gene transcription and genome replication. While vRNP-associated monomeric FluPol supports transcription, ANP32-dependent asymmetric and ANP32-independent symmetric polymerase dimers mediate genome and antigenome (vRNA/cRNA) replication. How FluPol coordinates these distinct functional states to maintain the transcription-replication balance remains poorly understood. Here, we identify and characterize interdomain interactions within PB2 that govern the stability of the replication-competent conformation of FluPol. Specifically, a highly conserved salt bridge between PB2 Mid-E282 and NLS-K752 stabilizes the replicase conformation, while the charge state of residue 627 (E or K) dictates ANP32 engagement, together coordinating polymerase dimerization and replication activity. Strikingly, bat influenza A viruses H17N10 and H18N11 harbor unconventional serine substitutions at both positions, compromising polymerase dimerization, ANP32 interaction, and vRNA/cRNA replication. Remarkably, introducing these bat-signature substitutions (E282S/K627S) into human H1N1 polymerase results in phosphorylation at both positions in human cells. These findings suggest that phosphorylation can partially compensate for the loss of negative charge at these residues, revealing a phosphomimetic adaptation mechanism that modulates polymerase conformational dynamics and function. Collectively, our study reveals how a conserved interdomain interaction within PB2 regulates conformational transitions and transcription-replication balance of FluPol, which might have been driven by phosphomimetic adaptations during the course of a diverse range of influenza virus evolution.

Title: Cell-state conditioning predicts the expression response to an unseen stimulus but not stimulus-dependent genetic effects
Authors: He, H.; Sun, J.; Xu, J.; Abudureyimu, M.; Yang, Y.; Huang, Y.; Wang, Z.; Xia, Q.; Wang, S.
Abstract: Background: Second-generation sequence models can be conditioned on a cell state supplied as a single-cell snapshot rather than selected from a fixed catalogue, but whether that conditioning carries an experimentally applied perturbation has not been tested. Results: We conditioned such a model on interferon-{beta}-stimulated and unstimulated monocytes from a published experiment, using cells disjoint from those providing the measurement, and asked whether the predicted expression response tracks the measured one and whether the same conditioning identifies expression QTL specific to the stimulated state. Predicted and measured responses agree at Spearman {rho} = 0.616 across 119 genes (95% CI 0.486 to 0.716), and at 0.607 after all 119 target genes are deleted from the conditioning input; across fifteen conditions the model's response scales with how much each condition's biology genuinely overlaps the target response (slope 0.73, Pearson 0.92), and a near-neighbour monocyte subset receives 0.295 against a measured overlap of 0.336. For stimulation-specific genetic effects we find no reliable evidence: the pre-specified primary arm moves from p = 0.0019 to 0.443 once both conditions must carry a measurable predicted effect, and the separation localises to the resting-condition baseline. Neither model generation's catalogue contains a perturbed sample, 0 of 4,430 tracks and 0 of 2,799 conditions, although both carry activation-state labels, so the gap is experimental perturbation rather than cell state. Two incidental findings apply beyond this model: credible-set membership mislabels over half of putatively condition-specific loci, and gating a ratio statistic on its larger term manufactures signal. Conclusions: Conditioning therefore conveys the state but not the mechanism: transfer between states is supported at the level of expression and unsupported at the level of variant effect, and an evaluation that separates the two is needed before either is claimed.

Title: MASH-in-a-dish reveals fatty acid-driven itaconate crosstalk between Kupffer cells and hepatocytes
Authors: Chang, J.-C.; Sullock Enzlin, A.; Haaker, M. W.; Maiguashca Sorensen, E.; van der Leek, T.; Mascarenhas, B.; Kluiver, T. A.; Wubbolts, R. W.; van Essen, S.; Bongiovanni, L.; Thomas, R.; Peng, W. C.; Paulusma, C.; Zaal, E. A.; Westendorp, B.; de Bruin, A.; Helms, J. B.; Berkers, C. R.
Abstract: Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH) is driven by interactions between metabolically stressed hepatocytes and non-parenchymal liver cells, leading to hepatocyte injury, inflammation, and fibrosis. Metabolites can mediate intercellular communication, yet their contribution to MASH pathogenesis remains poorly understood, partly because tissue dissociation disrupts the local metabolic environment. To address this challenge, we developed a novel in vitro MASH model, "MASH-in-a-dish", a Transwell co-culture system of mouse hepatocyte-derived organoids (HepOrgs), Kupffer cells (KCs), and hepatic stellate cells (HSCs) in a serum-free, chemically defined liver co-culture medium. MASH-in-a-dish modelled key features of clinical MASH, including steatosis, hepatocyte ballooning, inflammation and fibrosis, and allowed for rapid cell separation and cell type-specific metabolomics and stable-isotope fluxomics analysis. Using MASH-in-a-dish, we identified 21 MASH-associated interactive metabolites originating from 6 metabolic pathways, including the tricarboxylic acid cycle and the urea cycle. As a proof of concept, we further characterized itaconate-mediated intercellular crosstalk. Under MASH conditions, fatty acids replaced glucose to drive carnitine palmitoyltransferase I (CTP1A)-dependent itaconate production in KCs. Itaconate exacerbated oxidative stress, steatosis, and hepatocyte injury in lipid-stressed HepOrgs. Inhibiting itaconate production by KC-specific Acod1 knockout in the MASH-in-a-dish system mitigated hepatocyte damage. These findings identify fatty acid-driven itaconate production as a mechanism for lipid stress-induced immunometabolic crosstalk, linking adipose tissue insulin resistance to hepatocyte injury in MASH. In conclusion, our results establish MASH-in-a-dish as a powerful and versatile in vitro platform to investigating cell-cell interactions and metabolite crosstalk in MASH pathogenesis, and identify fatty acid-driven itaconate crosstalk between Kupffer cells and hepatocytes as a novel pathogenic mechanism and a potential therapeutic target in MASH.

Title: Reproducing squat kinematics after total knee replacement with bi-level inverse optimal control
Authors: Song, H.
Abstract: Total knee replacement restores mobility in patients with advanced osteoarthritis, yet many individuals still experience limited ability to perform high-flexion tasks such as squatting. Current preoperative planning relies on static imaging and does not evaluate postoperative high-flexion kinematics. In this study, we developed a simulation framework that uses bi-level inverse optimal control to reproduce postoperative squat kinematics from subject-specific models. Musculoskeletal models were built for six total knee replacement patients from experimental squat recordings. Cost-function weights were identified in an individualised setting and in a group-level setting. The former gives a subject-specific reconstruction when postoperative motion is available. The latter yields one shared cost function that does not need each patient's postoperative trajectory. That shared function was then tested with leave-one-subject-out cross-validation. The individualised setting reproduced experimental trajectories with low errors across all joints (mean apex difference 1.53{degrees}, root-mean-square error 5.15{degrees}, normalised root-mean-square error 11.15%, Pearson correlation 0.96). The in-sample group-level setting yielded higher errors (mean apex difference 5.70{degrees}, root-mean-square error 6.75{degrees}, normalised root-mean-square error 17.53%, Pearson correlation 0.95) while preserving the general pattern and phasing of the motion. Under cross-validation the shared cost function still worked on left-out subjects; the extra error was small when all joints are averaged (7.00{degrees}, 7.36{degrees}, 17.75%, and 0.95 for the same four metrics), although that loss was concentrated at the hip. The full stand-to-squat-to-stand cycle was generated in a single optimisation without prescribing a target squat depth. A shared cost function can therefore still reproduce squat kinematics in patients who were left out of the fit. That is required before the method could be used preoperatively. It does not itself predict a squat from preoperative data. Larger and independent cohorts are needed before the method could be used to compare alignment choices.

Title: GENECraft: A Function- and Prior-Constrained Discrete Dynamical System for Controllable Regulatory DNA Design
Authors: Wang, J.; Xu, T.; Tan, C.; Zhong, W.; Guo, G.; Zhang, L.; Qiu, Z.; Li, S. Z.
Abstract: Designing regulatory DNA requires reconciling two complementary modeling paradigms: genomic language models (gLMs) capture evolutionary syntax without guaranteeing targeted regulatory activity, whereas sequence-to-function predictors provide explicit functional supervision without enforcing native-like sequence plausibility. We introduce GENECraft, a training-free Function- and Prior-Constrained Discrete Dynamical System (FP-DDS) that couples a genomic language model (Carbon) and a functional oracle (AlphaGenome) during inference-time optimization to balance predicted regulatory activity and consistency with genomic sequence priors. GENECraft evolves continuous latent nucleotide logits while evaluating strictly decoded discrete DNA sequences under a time-dependent composite vector field that fuses normalized functional utility, bidirectional contextual prior guidance, and compositional quality penalties, followed by feasibility-first trajectory readout. Across 2,185 loci spanning promoters, multi-constraint enhancers, and 18 transcription factors (TFs), GENECraft achieves full-joint success rates of 62.70%, 65.23%, and 94.56% (macro-averaged), substantially outperforming seven optimization, evolutionary, and generative baselines (which reach at most 2.15% on enhancers). In matched 336-locus ablations, in-loop Carbon guidance reduces native-relative dinucleotide divergence by 7.8--11.5%, enhancer context sensitivity by 10.5%, and TF mutation sensitivity by 11.0%, establishing FP-DDS as a principled framework for controllable regulatory DNA design.

Title: A structural grammar of truncation across the human homodimer landscape
Authors: Karagöl, T.; Karagöl, A.
Abstract: Alternative splicing and proteolytic truncation generate tens of thousands of protein isoforms in the human proteome. Their consequences for quaternary state, the level at which most protein function operates, have been examined largely one molecule at a time. Using the AlphaFold Protein Structure Database expansion to predicted human homodimers, we compared 5,168 canonical-versus-truncated pairs on four interface metrics distributed with that release. Truncation partitions high-confidence canonical homodimers into structural conservation (56.4% of pairs), complete interface ablation (26.1%) and partial destabilization (17.5%). The partition holds on predicted interface size and not only on interface confidence. Conservation events retain a median 0.938 of the canonical interface residues, destabilization events 0.622, and ablation events 0.000. Interface loss is graded by deletion magnitude, falling from 0.997 of the interface retained below a tenth of the chain removed to 0.192 above a half (Spearman rho = -0.552, p = 4.5 x 10-61). Deletion topology, derived by global alignment, is 53.3% N-terminal and 42.7% C-terminal. C-terminal truncation lowers interface conservation from 65.4% to 37.5%, an asymmetry confined to deletions above the cohort median of 89 residues. Of 208 pairs in which ipTM reports emergence from a sub-threshold canonical baseline, 42 reproduce on ipSAE, the metric on which the release defines its tiers. Canonical disorder content shows no detectable difference between emergence events and controls matched on canonical confidence. Predicted confidence tracks deposited structures, with two or more copies in a deposited assembly for 95.3% of high-confidence canonicals against 49.9% of low-confidence canonicals. Emergence-cohort canonicals are enriched for established homomers, 75.0% against 48.7% for other canonicals of the same confidence, so emergence marks full-length predictions that fail and not interfaces created by truncation. Truncation-associated remodeling of homodimer architecture is a graded, topology-asymmetric property of the human proteome, readable from interface size and operating across gene-functional categories.

Title: Bounded by compartment, composition and time: efferocytic transcriptional readouts after ischaemic stroke
Authors: Ding, S.; Liu, Y.; Zeng, Y.; Huang, Z.; Yuan, Z.
Abstract: After ischaemic stroke, efferocytosis is usually inferred from a single bulk-tissue transcript score. Such a score cannot distinguish more phagocytes from more active ones, nor separate clearance from the inflammatory output that follows. We scored apoptotic demand (DEMAND), clearance machinery (CAPACITY), immunogenic output (OUTCOME) and an inhibitory brake separately across 38 datasets (30 numeric) spanning brain, blood and sorted human parenchyma, rating a program only where 75% of its genes were detected. Each difference was compared with expression-matched random gene sets, checked against leukocyte composition, and reported against the smallest difference its design could resolve. Energy supply and demand were scored on the same scale. Whole-blood CAPACITY was higher after stroke (+0.613/GSE58294, +0.374/GSE16561), exceeding matched random gene sets. Five lineage proxies left it intact in one cohort (+0.473, 95% CI +0.350 to +0.588) and removed it in a second (+0.014), after age and sex had raised it to +0.488; a third could not be adjusted. Adding the array gradient cut that attenuation to 77.7% ({rho} = 0.814), so 97.1% is an upper bound and the cohort difference partly reflects platform. Matched mononuclear cells showed no effect (-0.054; 90% CI -0.218 to +0.110). In rodent brain, supply rose before clearance machinery in three cross-dataset snapshots (oxidative phosphorylation +1.512 in day-3 infiltrating macrophages), with CAPACITY rising and its carrier shifting from microglia at day 3 to macrophages at day 7 - a suggested, not demonstrated order. In the only sorted human parenchyma series, non-microglial myeloid cells made up 37.1% of cells from a CD45-positive sort in stroke donors versus 19.9% in controls (p = 0.057; q = 0.30), and no microglial layer exceeded that series' resolution limit. Supply and demand ranked samples almost identically, so no transcript-only design can show which sets the limit. An efferocytic transcript score is bounded by compartment, composition and time: not a flux assay, not a validated stand-alone biomarker in these datasets. Energy supply rises with the work of clearance and can rise in cells that do not engulf, but the two scores move too closely for a transcript-only design to establish which sets the limit.

Title: Layer-Weighted Source-Anchored Transfer Learning for Multi-Omics Survival Prediction and Risk Stratification in Younger Breast Cancer Patients
Authors: Guo, W.; Wang, B.; Tatsuoka, C.
Abstract: Background- Younger breast cancer patients (<50 years) often present with more aggressive disease and distinct molecular characteristics, yet predictive models for this group are underpowered due to small sample sizes. Most existing models are built on older populations and may not translate directly, particularly across multiple omics data types. To address this, we developed Layered Source-Anchored Transfer Elastic Net (LSAT-EN), which adaptively borrows from the older source cohort while allowing borrowing strength to vary across omics layers according to their similarity between source and target cohorts, while performing EN variable selection. Methods -Patients aged [≥]60, [≥]55, and [≥]50 years were used as the source to improve prediction in patients aged <50 years. LSAT-EN were evaluated in group-correlated simulations and in TCGA-BRCA integrating 6 omics layers. Binary survival at 2-4 years was assessed by AUC; censored survival by Harrell's C-index and 2-5-year inverse probability of censoring weighted (IPCW) AUC. Results - In simulation, LSAT-EN achieved the highest AUC under moderate source-target heterogeneity ({sigma}=0.25; 0.747-0.802), outperforming GAS-EN (0.735-0.767), overall EN (0.683-0.710), individual EN (0.646-0.767), and glmtrans EN (0.640-0.733) across target training sample sizes (nT). Its advantage was greatest under higher source-target heterogeneity ({sigma}=4), particularly with small nT, where LSAT-EN achieved AUCs of 0.689-0.789 compared with 0.590-0.771 across competing methods. In TCGA-BRCA data, LSAT-EN improved discrimination relative to overall and individual EN in all binary and Cox models across all time horizons and source age groups. LSAT-EN was robust in stratifying high and low risk groups across molecular and clinical subgroups, while LSATEN-derived risk scores captured breast cancer-relevant pathway in survival models across time horizons, along with identifying most important miRNA signals. Conclusion- LSAT-EN is a powerful TL method for improving prediction and risk stratification for younger breast cancer patients; The framework may support prediction in other underrepresented populations with limited target-cohort data to advance cancer disparity ML research.

Title: Myhre syndrome variants form long-lived SMAD heterotrimers through a rewired polar interface at the variant site
Authors: Torner, C.; Pluta, R.; Condeminas, M.; Khan, R. J.; R. de Regil, M.; Ruiz, L.; Pous, J.; Ramos, I.; Caballero, M.; Humm, A.-S.; Niebling, S.; Garcia-Alai, M. M.; Marquez, J. A.; Martinez, A.; Fromm, S.; Martin-Malpartida, P.; Macias, M. J.
Abstract: TGF-{beta} signaling through SMAD transcription factors governs development and tissue homeostasis. Most disease-associated SMAD4 mutations cause loss of function, but five germline variants at only two positions in the MH2 domain, Arg496 and Ile500, instead cause Myhre syndrome, a rare condition inducing pathway dysregulation. We show that the two most common Myhre variants form more stable heterotrimers with SMAD3 than wild-type SMAD4, with affinities increasing two- to threefold and complex half-lives lengthening about fivefold. Cryo-EM reconstructions and twelve crystal structures show that a few interfacial hydrogen bonds shorten to 2.5 [A], reorganizing the binding interface. Our models also identified the SMAD4 C-terminus bound oriented resembling a phosphorylated R-SMAD tail, and two non-equivalent SMAD3 N-termini observed in the absence of cofactors. To the extent that these structural features reflect the cellular environment, they provide a mechanistic basis for the altered signaling dynamics observed in Myhre syndrome and outline concrete avenues for pharmacologically targeting these stabilized complexes.

Title: Inactive X chromosome DNA methylation erosion with age in human dermal fibroblasts
Authors: Ijaz, J.; Kafetzopoulos, I.; Park, N.; Krueger, F.; Clarke, J.; Temple, J.; Colaco, R.; Fernandez de Ara, M.; Coupland, P.; Argelaguet Calado, R.; Parry, A.; Lismer, A.; Taubenschmid-Stowers, J.; Manakov, S.; Santos, F.; Reik, W.
Abstract: X chromosome inactivation is an epigenetic process that establishes dosage compensation between the sexes through the monoallelic silencing of one X chromosome in karyotypically normal females. The allele that becomes inactivated is determined randomly during early development, resulting in females being mosaic with respect to whether the maternal or paternal allele is inactivated. This mosaicism makes it technically challenging to separate the active and inactive chromosomes in bulk populations, and consequently it has been historically difficult to study X chromosome inactivation in human cells. Here we use long read sequencing of 31 single cell clones derived from primary human dermal fibroblasts from 7 donors aged 25-80 years, and generate a method to distinguish DNA methylation state of the active versus the inactive X chromosome. As expected, CpG islands (CGIs) on the inactive X chromosome have high levels of methylation, while CGIs on the active X chromosome are very lowly methylated. Notably, we observe substantial loss of DNA methylation across multiple CGIs on the inactive X chromosome in an age dependent manner. We also observe this DNA methylation erosion in bulk samples by quantifying CGI methylation levels across individual sequencing reads. The genes that show age-related erosion of CGI methylation are associated with increased total transcription suggesting this methylation erosion generates a transcriptional permissive state. Overall, our study provides evidence of erosion of X chromosome inactivation with age in cell lines derived from primary human samples and implicates a role for loss of DNA methylation in the increased dosage of X chromosome linked genes in females with age. These findings shed new light on the epigenetic instability of the inactive X chromosome during human ageing and may be linked to age-related cellular dysfunction in females.

Title: Spatial genomics of the cardiac sarcomere
Authors: Cadisch, C.; Parikh, V. N.; Grove, M.; Singh, A.; Abrams, D.; Lakdawala, N.; Ho, C.; Miller, E.; Ryan, T. D.; Rossano, J.; Lin, K. Y.; Raja, A. A.; Bundgaard, H.; Michels, M.; Zwetsloot, P. P.; Ingles, J.; Pereira, A.; Helms, A. S.; Saberi, S.; Crotti, L.; Owens, A.; Day, S.; Gray, B.; Stendahl, J. C.; Lampert, R.; Olivotto, I.; Argiro, A.; Maurizi, N.; Powell, G.; Ware, J. S.; Kawana, M.; Ashley, E.
Abstract: Structure-function mapping of proteins has improved our understanding of disease mechanisms and protein domains while human population genetics has provided a window into variational tolerance that can be modeled at a structural level. Here, to reveal novel insight into the cardiac sarcomere, the motor unit of the heart, we develop a novel analytical framework to integrate data from over 17,000 patients with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM) and combine it with two population-scale genomic databases that incorporate data from more than 1.2 million individuals. We integrate in silico genetic predictions of gene variant pathogenicity with 3 dimensional integrative spatial scanning across multiple structural models of cardiac motor proteins. Results reveal both recognized and novel regions of structural variant intolerance across the critical genes of the cardiac sarcomere including novel insights into protein function. We discuss the structural relevance of mutational enrichment in the context of sarcomere organization and destabilization of sequestered myosin leading to hypercontractility seen in HCM, by incorporating the recently defined high-resolution structure of human cardiac myosin filament. We extend and validate these findings through pathogenic variant class enrichment and reveal novel associations with the earlier onset of disease in a large clinical cohort. In summary, our study provides a multi-dimensional framework for integrating structural, genomic, and modeling data to reveal novel insight into the cardiac sarcomere.

Title: Enabling Genotyping of Low-Biomass Zebra Mussel Samples via Multi-Displacement Amplification (MDA)
Authors: Elizarraga, V. H. H.; O'Brien, L. G.; McCartney, M. A.; Gohl, D. M.
Abstract: Next-Generation Sequencing (NGS)-based genotyping enables population genomic studies of the history of biological invasions, allowing for inference of source populations and routes of spread. Methods for genotyping include whole genome sequencing (WGS), as well as lower-cost targeted approaches, such as microarrays, hybrid capture, or Genotyping by Sequencing (GBS). Using GBS, we previously genotyped ~2,000 adult zebra mussels collected from over 100 populations across Minnesota, the Great Lakes, and the Upper Mississippi River. The need for sufficient template DNA restricts such genotyping approaches to adult animals, while genotyping lower biomass samples, such as zebra mussel veliger larvae remains challenging. Here, we applied Multiple Displacement Amplification (MDA) to increase DNA concentration from low-biomass samples. We demonstrate that MDA yields reproducible WGS and GBS data from as little as 1 ng of starting material and genotyped single veliger larvae from MDA amplified DNA, accurately assigning them to their known source populations. Furthermore, we showed that inheritance patterns can be tracked in MDA amplified DNA from veliger larvae and demonstrated an approach for forensic genetics of juvenile zebra mussels that were found contaminating "moss balls" and sold in the aquarium pet trade. Pairing MDA with high-resolution genomic workflows overcomes biomass limitations and represents a powerful toolkit to enhance early detection, trace invasion pathways, and mitigate the spread of the invasive zebra mussel. This approach is readily generalizable to other organisms or developmental stages where limiting quantities of DNA are available.

Title: Degron-Informed Design of DCAF10 Recruiter for Targeted Protein Degradation
Authors: Zhou, C.; Aketa, Y.; Vaz de Castro, P. A. S.; Zhang, C.; Jing, X.; Cui, W.; Zhang, X.
Abstract: Targeted protein degradation (TPD) is an emerging biological and therapeutic strategy that harnesses small molecules or biologics to eliminate proteins of interest by engaging the cellular protein degradation machinery. Here, we report DCAF10 as a TPD-competent E3 ligase. Guided by DCAF10's endogenous recognition of N-terminal acetyl-glycine degrons, we developed an Ac-Gly-Phe-Gly (Ac-GFG)-based recruiter capable of inducing DCAF10-dependent degradation of FKBP12 and multiple protein kinases. Interestingly, the Ac-GFG-based recruiter also exhibited a minor dependence on a secondary E3 ligase, FBXO22, potentially due to metabolic conversion that generates a terminal amine-containing species. Structure-activity relationship studies further identified an optimized N-propionyl-Gly-Phe-Ile (Pr-GFI) motif that enables potent degradation of FKBP12 (DC50 = 1.56 nM, Dmax = 96%) with exclusive dependence on DCAF10. We further leveraged this recruiting motif to develop a BRD9 degrader that induces potent, selective, and DCAF10-dependent degradation. Our findings establish the Pr-GFI motif as a potent and selective DCAF10 recruiter and provide a new chemical handle for expanding the scope of TPD.

Title: An open long non-coding RNA foundation model for generalizable prediction
Authors: Chang, A.; Zhu, H.; Li, R.; Chen, H.; Wang, C.; Tang, F.; Yao, Q.; Xiong, P.; Zhou, S. K.
Abstract: Long non-coding RNAs (lncRNAs) play essential roles in transcriptional regulation and chromatin organization, yet predicting their functional properties from sequence remains challenging because informative signals span both local motifs and long-range base pairing across kilobase-scale transcripts. Current RNA foundation models are restricted to short sequences and existing lncRNA prediction models narrowly focus on isolated tasks, leaving a dedicated foundation model notably absent. Here we present LncRFM, a dedicated lncRNA foundation model, supported by the LncCorpus pretraining data and the LncBench evaluation suite, which stand for a systematic framework to decode lncRNAs. For foundation model pretraining, we develop a hybrid bidirectional state-space encoder trained with a structure-guided masking strategy to effectively capture both local sequence patterns and long-range contexts. For pretraining data, we contribute over 9.6 million lncRNA sequences to assemble LncCorpus, a pretraining corpus of 24.7 million sequences. For benchmarking evaluation, we construct a comprehensive benchmark, LncBench, comprising 15 datasets and totaling over 1,010,000 sequences across 10 prediction tasks: six core lncRNA functional and annotation tasks and four structural and regulatory RNA assay tasks. Evaluated against seven RNA foundation models under a unified frozen-encoder protocol, our LncRFM achieves the state-of-the-art primary-metric scores on 11 of the 13 datasets that allow downstream adaptation. On two external generalization benchmarks evaluated without further adaptation, LncRFM matches the best structure-specialized baseline in F1 (0.141) and achieves the highest AUROC (0.962) on lncRNA contact prediction, while maintaining competitive cross-species coding-potential transfer (F1 of 0.374) under severe multi-kingdom domain shift. To benefit the scientific community, we make all datasets, source code, and pretrained models publicly available.
